#4895. Electric trucks hit 50% of China’s heavy truck sales, diesel demand falls

Electric trucks made up 50.3% of all heavy trucks sold in China in September. That’s 33,100 electric big rigs in a single month, up 37% from a year ago, while the overall heavy-truck market shrank by 21%.

And it’s showing up in the oil data. China’s diesel demand is on track to fall by about 230,000 barrels per day this year, and trucks running on batteries and natural gas are doing most of the work.

In 2024, new-energy vehicles accounted for 13.6% of heavy trucks (12 tonnes and up) sold in China. In 2025, sales nearly tripled to 231,100 units, up 182%, for a 28.9% share.

December 2025 hit 53.9%, but that was a rush. Buyers piled in before trade-in subsidies expired and new purchase tax costs kicked in, and the share dropped back to about 23% by March.

Then it came right back. Through the first nine months of 2026, China sold 226,400 electric heavy trucks, up 64%, for a 38.1% share. That’s already almost as many as in all of 2025, with a quarter still to go. In tractors, the big rigs that pull long-haul trailers, the September share hit 64.5%.

That’s well ahead of Beijing’s own plan. This year, 11 government bodies set a target of 40% new-energy heavy-truck sales by 2030, along with 1.6 million of them on the road, 30,000 km of zero-carbon freight corridors and about 3,000 charging and swap stations. The market blew past that sales target four years early on a monthly basis, and CATL now says new-energy trucks will be half of China’s annual truck sales by 2028.

It comes down to cost. In most uses, an electric heavy truck in China is now cheaper to own and run than a diesel one, and fleets run that math every day.

CATL claims savings of about 0.6 yuan per km. Independent numbers are more measured, but still favorable: a study by the ICCT and China’s CATARC found battery-electric trucks about 19% cheaper per tonne-km than diesel in good conditions, though they lose that edge at low annual mileage or when battery weight eats into payload.

Charging time is the other objection, and China’s answer is swapping. CATL’s Qiji brand operated about 300 heavy-truck swap stations at the end of 2025 and plans 900 by the end of this year and 2,000 in 2027. In August, it agreed to pay 2.56 billion yuan (about $370 million) for nearly 25% of Qiyuan Green Power, China’s largest heavy-truck swap operator with more than 1,600 charging and swap stations. Its new standardized packs hold 432 kWh and 513 kWh and swap in about five minutes.

CATL is already taking the swapping model to Europe with Octopus Energy.

The trucks themselves are domestic. XCMG led the segment in 2025 with a 15.4% share, ahead of SANY and FAW Jiefang, and the top three held 42.9% of the market. CATL supplied 60% of the batteries.

For years, the alternative to diesel trucks in China was liquefied natural gas. LNG trucks took nearly 30% of the market in 2024, when gas was much cheaper than diesel.

Now they’re losing to batteries. According to Kpler, LNG trucks had a 37% share of heavy-duty registrations in March, against 23% for electric. By July, electric was at 47% and LNG had collapsed to 11%. Monthly LNG truck registrations fell from more than 30,000 to about 6,200.

So China is skipping the “bridge fuel” phase for trucks almost as fast as it started it.

China’s diesel consumption already peaked. Rhodium Group found that diesel refinery runs topped out in April 2023, and apparent consumption dropped from 4.7 million barrels per day then to 4.0 million barrels per day in April 2025.

2026 is the steepest drop yet. Kpler estimates diesel demand fell about 420,000 barrels per day year-over-year in May, roughly 10%, and 460,000 in June. It expects a decline of about 230,000 barrels per day for the full year and only a 64,000 barrel-per-day rebound in 2027.

Kpler puts the gross diesel displacement from alternative trucks at about 680,000 barrels per day this year: roughly 450,000 from the LNG fleet built in recent years and 230,000 from electric trucks. Road freight still grew about 3% through July. China is moving more goods with less diesel.

There’s a catch. The fuel price spike this spring, tied to the Iran war, cut demand on its own and pushed more fleets toward electric. But that only explains part of it, and the fleet is still early: electric trucks will be only about 8% of China’s heavy trucks on the road by the end of 2026, according to Kpler. Every year of 40-50% sales shares compounds the diesel losses.

Europe is growing fast from a tiny base. ACEA data shows 5,120 heavy electric trucks (16 tonnes and up) registered in the EU through September, up 59.9%, for a 2.5% share. That’s up from 1.7% a year ago, but diesel still took 91.7% of all EU truck registrations.

A few countries stand out. Switzerland is at 24%, Norway 14.4%, the Netherlands 11.1% and Sweden 10.3%. Germany registered the most units at 1,722, but that’s only a 4.2% share.

The US doesn’t publish an official electric Class 8 sales figure, and that tells you something. The best indicator is the recent order for 2,500 Tesla Semis through ZET SCALE, which would roughly double the number of electric Class 8 trucks on US roads. Against about 230,000 Class 8 trucks sold per year, the electric share is well under 1%.

Price is the big difference. The ICCT puts the median electric Class 8 tractor in the US at $411,200, against $172,500 for diesel. Federal tax credits for commercial EVs ended in 2025, and California shelved the rule that would have required fleets to buy zero-emission trucks.

This is the biggest under-covered story in the EV industry right now.

Everyone argued for years about whether electric semis could work. Range, weight, charging, cost. China settled it the boring way. It got the price of a battery-electric heavy truck close enough to diesel, built swap stations along freight routes, and let fleet operators do what fleet operators always do: pick the cheapest truck per kilometer.

And the result is showing up where it matters, in oil demand. Trucks are where diesel lives. Displacing a quarter of a million barrels a day in one year, with electric trucks still only around 8% of the fleet, means we’re still early on this curve.

The contrast with the US is hard to watch. America has Tesla, a Semi factory in Nevada built for 50,000 trucks a year, and some of the best freight corridors in the world for electrification. But electric Class 8 trucks cost 2.4 times as much as diesel here, the federal incentives are gone, and the market is under 1%. The ZET SCALE order is real progress. But it came from shippers pooling their demand, and twe have yet to see these trucks get delivered.

China having a lot of phev and EV vehicles has helped with oil pricing around the world, more notably in the current american-caused oil crisis. It would be worse if they were all traditional powered cars and trucks.

Now to be clear, I'm not saying that it has made a massive impact or is even the only reason why the oil crisis isn't much worse, it's just one of a few steps China made to reduce the impact of the oil crisis. But going electric everywhere we can has a stabilizing effect when oil shocks show up

Europe at least has the regulation, and its best markets, at 10% to 24%, are roughly where China was in 2024 and 2025.

The question now is how long Chinese truck makers stay home. SANY and BYD already sell electric trucks in Europe, and CATL is building the swap network for them. If those trucks can come close to China’s pricing, how long can Western truck makers keep charging 2x diesel?

Diesel trucks aren’t the only thing batteries are displacing. At home, pairing solar with an EV or a home battery can cut your energy bills dramatically. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4893. Artists Helen Marden and the Late Brice Marden Refashioned a Decommissioned 19th-Century Ferry Terminal

Over the course of their more than 50-year marriage, artist Helen Marden and her late husband, the eminent painter Brice Marden, amassed an international collection of seriously eccentric—and deeply magical—houses, gardens, and studios, each designed around the double helix of art and family. They bought their first house, a cliffside cottage on the Greek island of Hydra, in 1973, and since then real estate and art have been entwined in their life, art facilitating the purchase of property, the properties both catalyst and carapace for the evolution of their art. An Italianate villa in upstate New York, a pair of traditional riads in Marrakech, a hotel set among the ruins of a 19th-century sugar plantation in the Caribbean, a second house by the port in Hydra, a Renaissance Revival town house in Manhattan, a stately manse on a sprawling estate in Pennsylvania—every one of their idiosyncratic properties has its own fascinating history, reflected in its interior. The homes are all documented in the upcoming book Brice & Helen Marden: Houses, Gardens, Studios (Gagosian), edited by this writer, with photography by Stephen Kent Johnson.

Helen Marden in the living room. Chair and side table by the Campana Brothers. The chimney is clad in Clé Tile. A watercolor by Henri Michaux rests on the mantel.

The living room includes chairs by Marcel Wanders (far left) and the Campana Brothers. Sculpture at right by Michael Wang.

In the dining room, a Paavo Tynell pendant hangs above a rustic farm table with chairs by Jonathan Olivares and Maarten Baas. Amazonia marble covers one wall.

The Mardens were instinctively drawn to residences with endurance, places that have seen a few things, not newly built pleasure domes devoid of texture and soul. Swan House, the riparian hideaway in the middle of the Hudson River, epitomizes the couple’s embrace of the strange and the enchanted. Accessed by a long, narrow causeway that leads off the shore of Saugerties, the structure was built in 1877 as part of Long Dock, a ship terminal and moorage for large vessels conveying people and goods the length of the Hudson. It was also a landing for ferries crossing the river between Saugerties and the village of Tivoli. One can see Swan House shimmering in the landscape from the edge of Rose Hill, the Marden family’s 19th-century Tivoli estate.

The Depression, along with the advent of more efficient modes of transport, scuppered the last of the large ships landing at Long Dock in the early 1930s, but ferries continued to make the two-minute trip across the water until 1938. After that, the structure was decommissioned from professional service and sold, becoming the only privately owned peninsula on the Hudson. The Mardens purchased the property in 2011, but it took a full decade before they engaged designer Daniel Sachs and architect Kevin Lindores of the AD100 firm Sachs Lindores Architecture, Interiors to execute a full-scale renovation.

The primary bath features custom zellige tiles, a vintage Vistosi chandelier, an antique marble sink, and a tub by The Water Monopoly.

Sachs Lindores remodeled the entry with a windscreen of glass brick. The chair is by Gaetano Pesce.

Yellow zellige tiles meet a pale pink Aga range beneath a custom zinc hood in the kitchen. The pendant light is by Adolf Loos from WOKA.

Brice Marden’s For Helen – Valentine 2019 (2015–18) hangs on the black-tiled fireplace tower that mediates the bedroom and living room.

A custom bed is flanked by an antique French console table and a Charles Rohlfs hall chair. Lighting includes a Franz West chandelier and a floor lamp by Achille and Pier Giacomo Castiglioni.

“Early on we demolished a few walls to open up the views, but it was pretty raw. We’d just go over and watch the boats go by,” Helen recalls. “You have a completely different relationship with the river when you’re sitting in the middle of it.”

Given the famously cultivated, idiosyncratic tastes of the homeowners, the collaboration between Sachs Lindores and their clients was unusually fertile. Together, they reimagined the derelict building as a trick box for trapping the natural light that bounces off the water on all sides, with reflective, lead-coated copper siding and a zinc roof on the exterior and fields of luminous plaster, tile, and marble within. “Helen never shies away from a bold gesture. At first, she told us to paint the house red, but when we presented the idea of a glistening metal-clad box with light dancing on the skin, she immediately went for it,” Sachs recalls. “Brice and Helen were very interconnected in their aesthetic tastes and decision making,” Lindores adds. “As you might imagine, they studied every paint color and trim detail.”

Ruins of the 19th-century dock remain alongside the house.

A guest room is outfitted with a Pierre Jeanneret daybed, lounge chairs by Monika Mulder for IKEA, a vintage Kevin Walz standing lamp, and a Mathieu Matégot magazine rack. Painting by Helen Marden.

Sigmar Polke’s Untitled (1998) hangs above a vintage Walter Knoll sofa in the first-floor sitting room.

While retaining the shape of its original architectural envelope, the house was essentially rebuilt, with new window configurations, open circulation, and an exposed ceiling, all in service of maximizing watery vistas and ease of use. On the lofty upper level, the existing chimney, newly revealed in its full floor-to-ceiling height, was clad in glossy black brick tile. The monolithic form now feels like a high altar in a temple of light. Custom zellige tiles imported from Fez cover the walls of the kitchen and baths, where Helen’s genius for juxtaposing colors and materials comes into high relief.

The polyglot ensemble of furnishings hews closely to the signature Marden mix: Moroccan rugs; bold contemporary designs by the likes of Gaetano Pesce, Marcel Wanders, and the Campana Brothers; humble American folk pieces; 20th-century classics by Paavo Tynell, Adolf Loos, and Pierre Jeanneret; and a few Continental antiques to leaven the brew. “I just pick things that I like, things that make me happy,” Helen says, pooh-poohing the idea of some grand decorative vision. Her designers would demur. “She has an incredible eye,” Sachs insists. “The more crazy Helen would get, the more Brice liked it.”

#4890. Lexus is taking a page from China for its next electric SUV launching in 2027

Toyota’s luxury brand Lexus is launching a new electric SUV in 2027, its first vehicle built in China in over two decades.

It’s official. Toyota is breaking from tradition, planning to develop and produce the new vehicle in China rather than its home market of Japan.

Lexus confirmed the new vehicle will be made at its new manufacturing plant in Jinshan, Shanghai, and will go on sale in 2027.

As the first Lexus factory built from scratch overseas, the company said the new plant will bring together its global manufacturing capabilities.

Toyota broke ground on the facility in June 2025, saying the new facility will unlock “Lexus speed” as it aims to keep pace with domestic brands like BYD. Construction was expected to be completed this past August, with the first vehicle scheduled to roll off the assembly line in the fall of 2027.

The first Lexus model will be an electric SUV, produced using advanced manufacturing methods such as gigacasting to reduce costs and speed up output.

The facility will be a cornerstone of Toyota’s comeback plans in China, where it’s struggled to compete with local brands.

Production capacity will be around 1,000 units per month in 2027 as Toyota ramps up to “tens of thousands” in 2028.

Toyota’s sales plunged nearly 20% in China last month, marking its eighth consecutive month with lower sales than the year prior. The market in China “remained weak due in part to rising gasoline prices, while the market for gasoline vehicles and hybrid vehicles was particularly affected,” Toyota said.

In the first nine months of 2026, Toyota sold just over 1.05 million vehicles in China, 18.9% fewer than in the same period last year.

Lexus’ new Shanghai facility is wholly owned by Toyota, enabling it to produce vehicles in China through its joint ventures.

The new electric SUV will go on sale in China in 2027. Specific details, including battery, range, and prices, have yet to be announced.

As part of its “with China, for China, strategy, Lexus said it will “continue to use China as a source of innovation,” adding it will “deepen localization efforts” to bring classic models to the market that meet local needs.

Toyota joins the growing list of major OEMs that are already tapping, or plan to tap, China for its next-generation electric vehicles.

While in other global markets, Toyota is sticking to its “multi-pathway” strategy, which includes all powertrains from electric to ICE; in China, it’s being forced to adapt.

China is Toyota’s third-largest market, following the US and Japan. To stay competitive and turn things around in China, Toyota will rely more on local partners and suppliers.

Developing the new Lexus electric SUV in China first rather than Japan is significant given Toyota’s traditional ways.

Typically, it takes Toyota about four to five years to fully develop a new vehicle. In China, automakers are now building them in as little as two years.

Toyota, like many automakers at this point, is turning to China for new tech, batteries, production methods, and other EV components to keep pace.

#4888. Where Does Joe Burrow Live? Unpacking the Bengals Quarterback’s Real Estate Portfolio

He signed a record-breaking contract with the Cincinnati Bengals in 2023, but where does Joe Burrow live when he’s not on the field?

The NFL quarterback was born in Ames, Iowa, in 1996. His family moved to Ohio when he was eight, and he has resided mostly in the Buckeye State ever since. Burrow played for Ohio State University from 2015 to 2017, then transferred as a graduate student to Louisiana State University, where he won the Heisman Trophy shortly before graduating in December 2019. He was drafted into the NFL the following year by his hometown Bengals, with whom he inked a $36.1 million, four-year contract—plus a $23.9 million signing bonus. Three years later Burrow signed a $275 million five-year extension, making him the highest-paid player in NFL history at the time, according to ESPN.

It’s unsurprising, then, that Burrow has put down roots in the Buckeye State. Below, we’re examining the quarterback’s real estate portfolio.

In May 2020, a month after being selected first overall in the NFL Draft, Burrow revealed that he was spending the pandemic lockdown in his old bedroom at his parents’ house in The Plains, Ohio, just outside of Athens. Interior design apparently wasn’t at the forefront of his mind; the room still had his childhood Star Wars curtains and posters on the wall, though he had given the bed a king-size upgrade in high school, replacing the Star Wars comforter that once rounded out the room’s theme. According to The Sun, the 1997-built residence sits on a cul-de-sac and has four bedrooms and three bathrooms.

The Bengals play at Paycor Stadium, formerly known as Paul Brown Stadium.

In June 2020, Burrow spent $835,000 on his first house: a 2,900-square-foot Cincinnati dwelling just five miles from the Bengals’ home stadium. Located in the city’s historic Columbia-Tusculum area, the two-story property was built in 2014. Further details on the dwelling are scant—including whether or not Burrow still owns it. However, its location would make it a convenient place to stay during the NFL season.

#4887. BYD sold more EVs last month than the US did all quarter, topping 300,000

BYD sold over 300,000 electric vehicles in October, a new record and more than the US managed in the entire third quarter.

The world’s leading EV maker is showing no signs of slowing down. BYD sold 490,168 new energy vehicles (NEVs) in October, up 11% from the prior year and the company’s highest monthly total in 2026.

BYD’s battery electric vehicles drove the growth, with a record 305,743 units sold, up 37% year over year and marking the first time its EV sales have crossed the 300,000 mark.

To put that into perspective, just over 262,500 EVs were sold in the US in the entire third quarter combined, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates.

October marked BYD’s sixth straight month of higher sales growth and its third straight month of higher EV sales. Through October, BYD sold 1,953,700 electric vehicles, up 6% from the same period last year.

BYD’s all-electric vehicles (EVs) accounted for about 63% of total sales last month. Plug-in hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, fell 17% in October to 177,382 units. Through October, BYD’s PHEV sales fell 11% to 1,625,969 units.

According to BYD’s filing, the company exported 170,194 vehicles in October as it expands overseas to drive growth in markets like Europe, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America.

Through October, BYD exported over 1.5 million electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles, nearly double compared to last year.

By the end of 2026, BYD expects overseas shipments to reach about 2 million vehicles. In 2027, that number is expected to rise to more than 2.5 million vehicles.

#4886. The 7 Best Garmin Watches, Tested by Our Fitness and Tech Experts

Garmin has a watch for every type of athlete and budget.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Brands like Whoop, OURA, and Apple offer some of the best fitness trackers available, but Garmin watches remain the go-to for serious athletes and outdoor enthusiasts. Men’s Health editors have trusted these wearables to go the distance during ultramarathons, multi-day hikes, and backcountry ski trips thanks to their weeks-long battery life and pinpoint GPS accuracy. But they’re equally useful for everyday life and weekend warriors—we love wearing the Garmin Approach S70 for golf rounds because it comes preloaded with more than 43,000 courses from around the world.

The current Garmin lineup is more robust than ever, from entry-level running watches to premium expedition-ready models that cost upwards of $1,000. Several models come with full-color topographic maps, military-grade durability, and hardcore activity-specific metrics. For instance, runners get detailed stride analysis, cyclists receive power metrics, and swimmers enjoy stroke detection. They also offer specialized outdoor capabilities, including barometric altimeters for precise elevation tracking, compass sensors for navigation without GPS, and pulse oximeters that help monitor your acclimation at high altitudes.

The Garmin Vivoactive 6 offers health monitoring features like sleep coaching, recovery time recommendations, and training readiness scores. Meanwhile, adventure-focused models like the Garmin Instinct 3 and Garmin Fenix 8 Pro incorporate multi-band GPS for accuracy in dense forests, plus emergency features like fall detection and SOS alerts. Whether you’re tracking your first 5K or planning a summit attempt on a remote peak, there’s a Garmin designed specifically for your needs. We’ve logged thousands of miles testing these watches to help you find the perfect match.

Over the years, our editors have done it all: ultramarathons, multi-day backpacking trips, open water swims, and mountain expeditions. Through our adventures, Garmin watches have consistently proven their worth on our wrists. To find the best Garmin watches, we evaluated several models across multiple activities, testing their GPS accuracy, battery performance, and usability. We also considered factors like comfort during prolonged wear and durability when subjected to the elements. This testing allowed us to see how each watch performs out in the real world beyond the spec sheet.

The Fenix 8 stands as Garmin’s ultimate performance watch, offering detailed training insights and reliability for marathoners, ultra-runners, and multi-sport competitors. The watch doesn’t doesn’t track your runs—it analyzes every aspect of your performance with features like training readiness, recovery time, and PacePro technology, allowing you to plan your race-day strategy with GPS-based pace guidance. These features can help you optimize your performance.

Battery life remains exceptional even during GPS-intensive activities. While the standard 51mm AMOLED version delivers approximately 29 days, the solar-equipped model extends this to 48 days with adequate sun exposure. The watch offers multiple power management profiles that let you customize battery usage based on what you have planned that day. This ensures you have the data you need from start to finish without worrying about mid-race charging.

Beyond its training capabilities, the Fenix 8 serves as a reliable navigation tool during unfamiliar routes and trail races. The full-color topographic maps, turn-by-turn directions, and ClimbPro feature help you strategize your effort on challenging courses. You also get comprehensive recovery features, with detailed sleep tracking, HRV status, and body battery energy monitoring that help prevent overtraining.

While the Fenix 8’s price places it among the most expensive sport watches available (especially for the new Fenix 8 Pro), serious athletes who spend hundreds of hours training for major events will find the watch’s performance insights and bulletproof reliability well worth the investment. "This watch has everything that Garmin has to offer into a low-profile casing," says MH Fitness and Commerce Editor Charles Thorp, NASM. "Rugged enough to perform in tough terrain, but sleek enough to fit in everywhere else."

The Vivoactive 6 is one of Garmin’s more lifestyle-oriented models, offering a balance between everyday smartwatch functionality and robust fitness tracking. With its sleek design and comprehensive tracking features, it’s a solid alternative to the Apple Watch SE for those who want longer battery life (up to 11 days) and more comprehensive fitness metrics.

Through running and strength training sessions, the Vivoactive 6 offers detailed metrics about VO2 max, aerobic and anaerobic output, and exercise load. These insights provide a clearer picture of fitness progress than basic calorie and distance tracking. The responsiveness during workouts particularly stood out during our side-by-side comparison with the Apple Watch SE. When increasing running pace, the Vivoactive 6 updated immediately, while the Apple Watch lagged noticeably behind. During strength training, we appreciated the live heart rate zone updates, making it easier to gauge workout intensity in real time.

The most significant advantage over the Apple Watch is battery life. While our SE required daily charging, the Vivoactive 6 kept going for days between charges—a game-changer for active users. The comfortable fit works well even on smaller wrists, and at $299, it offers more fitness functionality than similarly priced competitors while maintaining everyday usability. It supports contactless payments and can even store music from your favorite Spotify playlists. If you want comprehensive fitness insights without the premium price, the Vivoactive 6 hits the sweet spot.

The Forerunner 970 is Garmin’s new flagship running watch, built for athletes who want every data point without sacrificing everyday usability. It pairs a brighter 1.4-inch AMOLED display with a built-in speaker and microphone, plus a tougher sapphire lens and lightweight titanium bezel, so it feels premium yet rugged enough for hard training.

During intervals and long runs, the interface is intuitive—pace, heart rate, and distance are all visible at a glance, and after each session the watch prompts you to rate how the run felt. The 970 also offers deeper performance tools, including running economy, running tolerance (when paired with Garmin’s HRM 600 chest strap), hill score, endurance score, and more detailed load analysis to show how hard you’re pushing week to week.

Battery life remains a major selling point. Garmin claims up to 15 days in smartwatch mode and 26 hours in GPS mode with multi-band SATIQ, so you can stack long runs, races, and daily training without worrying about charging. Built-in full-color maps, turn-by-turn directions, dynamic round-trip routing, ClimbPro, and Up Ahead make the watch just as useful on unfamiliar trails as it is for neighborhood miles.

Recovery and health tracking also see significant upgrades over older Forerunners. Training Readiness delivers a simple morning score based on recent sleep and workload, so you know whether to push or back off. Upgraded sleep tracking, nap detection, and newer tools like ECG readings also provide a clearer picture of how your body handles stress, illness, and heavy training weeks.

If you’re looking for something that’s durable, look no further than the Instinct 3. The watch offers military-grade construction that can withstand some real punishment, with a rugged design that proved its worth throughout testing. We accidentally banged it against doorways and scraped it against kettlebells during workouts, yet it emerged without a scratch. The distinctly masculine aesthetic features a substantial case housing an impressive array of sensors while maintaining water resistance to 100 meters.

Battery performance is one of the Instinct 3’s most impressive features. While Garmin claims 18 days between charges, our testing revealed closer to 21 days of regular use without heavy reliance on battery-intensive features. It makes it one of the longest-lasting watches in Garmin’s lineup, while providing a significant advantage over other mainstream smartwatches. When you do need a recharge, a quick 10-minute session can add several hours of use—perfect for those who forgot to charge before heading out the door.

For trail runs and hikers, the watch includes a digital compass that shows your precise directional heading, multi-band GPS with SatIQ technology, and a built-in flashlight with multiple intensity levels including a red light option. The Instinct 3 also features ABC sensors that provide real-time environmental data. Of course, the watch also offers powerful health and fitness features, including HRV status, stress tracking, and the ability to track your blood oxygen levels.

Read more: Our Garmin Instinct 3 AMOLED Review

Don’t let the lower price tag fool you: The Forerunner 165 packs serious running tech into a $249 package, making it the ideal option for runners who are just getting started on their journey or those looking to dip their toes into fitness trackers. This relative newcomer to Garmin’s lineup boasts an AMOLED display, a lightweight design, and advanced training metrics runners will appreciate.

Despite being positioned as an entry-level running watch, the Forerunner 165 outclasses similarly priced competitors with its premium build quality and thoughtful design. It’s incredibly comfortable, especially compared to Garmin’s bulkier models, while still maintaining the brand’s impressive durability. The AMOLED screen offers excellent readability even in bright sunlight, and text looks crisp. We particularly appreciated the intuitive physical button navigation combined with touchscreen functionality.

For runners who want their first serious training companion, the Forerunner 165 hits the sweet spot by delivering Garmin’s core running analytics without overwhelming users. While it lacks some of the advanced recovery tools found in the Forerunner 965 like Training Readiness, it covers all the essentials with accurate GPS tracking and guided workouts.

The Venu 4 is Garmin’s latest lifestyle smartwatch, and it feels like a smarter, more polished upgrade from the Venu 3. Available in 41mm and 45mm sizes, it pairs a bright AMOLED display with a metal case and a low-profile design for a clean, casual look that looks great both at the office and at the gym.

In testing, the Venu line has always stood out for being easy to live with, and the latest model doubles down on that. Battery life stretches up to roughly 12 days in smartwatch mode depending on how often you’re working out and using the always-on display, which means you don’t have to baby it with nightly charges—topping it up during a shower a few times a week is usually enough. The built-in LED flashlight is also a welcome addition for running at dusk or dawn, helping you stay visible to drivers. You also get a speaker and mic for taking calls and using your phone’s voice assistant from your wrist.

What makes the Venu 4 more than a standard smartwatch is that it treats your health as more than just steps and heart rate. Health status and lifestyle logging show how daily choices—like drinking caffeine later in the day—actually affect your sleep, stress, and heart rate variability, so the data feels more useful than just a bunch of charts. The Venu 4 also has the new Garmin Coach feature, with over 80 preloaded GPS and indoor sports apps that cover everything from walking and HIIT to yoga and strength training.

Its app and ecosystem integration still isn’t as far-reaching as an Apple Watch, especially on iPhone, but if you care more about deeper health tracking and better workouts, the Venu 4 is a great alternative that offers multi-day battery life and more recovery-focused insights.

The Approach S70 is the ultimate golf companion, delivering comprehensive course coverage—with over 43,000 preloaded courses worldwide—in a sleek, lightweight design. Available in two sizes (42mm and 47mm), this premium golf watch displays detailed course maps showing precise distance to greens, hazards, and doglegs, while the Virtual Caddie feature provides club recommendations based on your playing history and current conditions.

What truly sets the S70 apart is its attention to golf-specific details. The watch provides front, center, and back distance readings to every green, along with precise yardages to hazards. This is extremely helpful as sometimes you can’t even fully see a hole and have no idea that a water hazard is lying within distance of your next shot, so that overview of the hole is crucial info to have. The "plays like" feature accounts for elevation changes and wind when calculating distances, something that can be difficult to gauge on your own.

Beyond the thousands of preloaded courses, the S70 also displays green contour data to improve your putting strategy (Garmin Golf membership required). During our testing, the functions and how to navigate them took a little getting used to, but once we got that down, it was pretty easy after every shot just to twist our wrist to get our next distance. The AMOLED display has also been crisp and never difficult to see out in the sun.

At $699, the S70 is a significant investment, but for golfers who regularly play and want and easy way to gauge the shots to hit, the combination of golf-specific features and modern smartwatch functionality makes it a great companion on the course.

Read More: Our Review of the Garmin Approach S70

Depending on the Garmin you choose, you can expect battery life to last anywhere from a few days to a few weeks. The Fenix 8 AMOLED’s battery can stretch for up to 16 days, while the Fenix 8 with solar will go up to 21 days (28 days with solar). Of course, real-world battery performance can vary based on how you actually use your watch. Running a marathon with continuous GPS tracking? You’ll drain the battery much faster than if you’re just checking notifications and tracking daily steps.

Garmin has a reputation for offering several advanced training and recovery metrics, which can help you understand how ready your body is for exercise and optimize your training schedule. The Forerunner 970 offers Training Readiness, which synthesizes your sleep score, recovery time, acute training load, sleep history, and more to show "when you are most likely to benefit from a hard workout and when to consider dialing down to let your body catch up," Garmin says.Even if you don’t train every day, you can still benefit from Garmin’s more basic tracking features, like daily step count, calories, and sleep. Some models can even track your stress, monitoring your body’s physiological responses throughout the day. During a hectic workday or high-pressure meeting, knowing when you’re stressed can prompt you to take action—i.e., perform breathing exercises—which can make a difference in your overall well-being.Additionally, Garmin’s various models analyze detailed performance metrics to determine if your training is productive, offer built-in coaching features to prepare you for races, and suggest workouts tailored to your fitness level and goals. What makes Garmin’s approach so good is its flexibility—serious athletes can drive into the data, while casual users can stick with simpler metrics and guided programs.

GPS and Garmin go hand in hand, so it’s no surprise that the brand’s watches offer robust tracking and navigation. These features can be essential for runners, hikers, and outdoor athletes. Most Garmin watches provide detailed maps, turn-by-turn directions, and breadcrumb trails that help you retrace your steps. Some high-end models, like the aforementioned Fenix 8, offers offline maps with enhanced satellite imagery, SATIQ technology, ABC sensors, and more. These features can be invaluable for precise tracking even in steep valleys, offer reliable compass headings, and deliver accurate elevation readings.

Garmin watches traditionally prioritize function over fashion, packing them with a lot of tech and large batteries. As a result, they generally skew larger compared to many competitors. Some models come in multiple sizes—the Venu 4 is available with screen sizes of 41mm and 45mm, similar to the Apple Watch Series 11, which comes in 42mm and 46mm. However, the Venu 3 is still noticeably larger; it boasts a width of 45mm and a thickness of 12mm (compared to the Series 10’s 36mm and 9.7mm). That said, some of Garmin’s watches, like the Forerunner 970, only come in one size. If you have smaller wrists like I do, you have two options: Buy your preferred model and accept that it might look oversized on your wrist, or opt for one of Garmin’s more lifestyle-oriented models like the Vivoactive 6, which is 10.9mm thick. Garmin does offer "S" variants of several models specifically designed for small wrists—the Venu 3S, for example, is thinner and lighter than the normal Venu 3. However, these S models typically sacrifice battery life for their smaller footprint, so you’ll have to consider if that’s a compromise you’re willing to make.

There are a lot of Garmin watches to choose from—the brand lists five major lineups on its website. The Forerunner 165 is one of Garmin's most affordable models at $249, providing you essential training metrics, built-in GPS, and up to 11 days of battery life. The more full-featured Venu 4 jumps up in price to $549, offering more detailed health insights, better battery life, and a larger, more vibrant display. Garmin’s premium adventure watches command the highest prices, with the Fenix 8 starting at $899 and climbing to $1,099 for solar-equipped models with sapphire crystal displays. When deciding which Garmin is right for you, consider what features you truly need versus what’s nice to have. If you’re a casual runner, you might be best served by something in the Forerunner lineup. But if you regularly go hiking in the backcountry, you might find the premium price of a Fenix justified by its comprehensive navigation tools and extended battery life.

#4884. The Six Bells Madewell Collection 2026

Whimsical design flourishes, cozy interiors, and close proximity to upstate antiquing all make The Six Bells Countryside Inn one of the best weekend escapes in the Empire State. Now, thanks to Madewell, you never have to check out. Launching today, the two brands have joined forces on a 28-piece holiday capsule of heirloom-worthy wardrobe and home essentials inspired by The Six Bells’ vintage aesthetic. Pieces specifically pay homage to the hotel’s interiors through references to archival patterns and wallpaper prints found throughout the Inn’s rooms and communal spaces.

“We fell in love with [The Six Bells’] distinct, whimsical world—the mix of patterns, the nostalgic sentiment, and the personality in every detail,” says Madewell creative director Steven Cateron. During initial planning for the clothing brand’s holiday collection, the hotel in Rosendale, New York became an unexpected source of inspiration for Cateron and his team because of the shared appreciation for heritage and storytelling. “Each piece has intention, whether it’s to wear day-to-day or for a celebration, a gifting moment for a loved one or hostess, or pajama pieces that lean into cozy season,” he says.

Sock slippers from the collaboration and Madewell’s classic denim make a perfect pairing.

Founded by Audrey Gelman in 2025, who designed the hotel in collaboration with interiors firm GrecoDeco, The Six Bells Countryside Inn has quickly risen in popularity—even earning a spot in AD’s list of Great Design Hotels last year. “This project is so rooted in a shared love of the decorative arts and global human history,” designer Adam Greco previously told AD. Design-wise, maximalism dominates the interiors. Picture: rooms wrapped in fretwork wallpaper and deep cinnabar paint, with pistachio window shades and striped seating.

The collection also builds on the fantasy of Barrow’s Green, the fictional English village dreamed up by Gelman that includes its own imaginary landmarks and distinct locals (including a town gossip and poignant editor). “It was so interesting to broaden our imaginations and think about how The Six Bells’ style could be brought to life through clothes,” says Gelman.

A cheeky message makes this classic needlepoint pillow pop.

At the same time, the collaboration was an opportunity to venture into Madwell’s less-explored categories—specifically the home space. The collection’s interior goods are a practice in curated nostalgia: There are holiday ornaments you’ll reach for year after year, scented candles and soaps to integrate into your daily winter routine, and cozy pajamas inspired by vintage sleep silhouettes. “If it’s something we don’t currently offer, we want to work with people that do the category best,” says Cateron. “The Six Bells team were the perfect partners to bring this collection’s home accessories to life.”

Still, versatility isn’t lost in the assortment. In designing the clothing, Cateron made sure to include “pieces to wear upstate, in the city, or for day-to-day celebrations.” Classic denim jackets are neutral staples that you can reach for any day of the week, while Fair Isle wool knits are seasonally appropriate while still feeling adaptable enough to wear after the holidays. “There’s a real point of view behind every detail [at The Six Bells Countryside Inn], from the interiors to collected vintage pieces,” says Cateron. “This collection captures that sensibility in a way that felt authentic to both brands.”

The collection is available to shop on Madewell.com and in Madewell stores starting today, November 12.

#4881. Nickey Kehoe’s New Collection With The Lacquer Company Takes Its Cues From Beloved Antiques

In 2024, AD heralded the return of lacquer. In our April 2026 issue, cover star Athena Calderone was pictured leaning over an enormous burgundy-lacquered kitchen island, and in May, cover star Mark Grattan showed off his parrot green lacquer walls. Today’s collaboration between AD100 design firm Nickey Kehoe and The Lacquer Company brings the glossy finish down to a slightly more manageable scale, applying it to coffee tables, desks, trays, and tissue boxes. Nickey Kehoe founders Todd Nickey and Amy Kehoe designed the 30-piece collection with The Lacquer Company founder James Lowther, drawing on antique furniture and objects the three have collected over the years.

The Bonne Nuit nightstand in Cassis staged among various Nickey Kehoe textiles and an upholstered headboard.

The Florin Tray in Carreaux & Marine Blue is styled with all small pieces from the Nickey Kehoe collection.

Many of the pieces, as is often true of Nickey Kehoe’s in-house catalog, draw on the founders’ personal vintage collections. The Pastis side table is based on a bamboo folding table that belongs to Nickey. The Hugo desk is a Louis XVI–style writing desk, with tapered, fluted legs, brass details, and three soft-close drawers in a bright red lacquer. The colorways sound like a very civilized, French late lunch: cassis and lettuce green, carreaux and marine blue, khaki and chocolate brown. The Jules catchall tray comes with a matching tissue box cover for the powder room.

Lacquer trays, tissue boxes, side tables, and the collection’s coffee table are staged together here to show the full line.

The Pastis side table references a vintage style with the lacquer and bamboo combination reminiscent of Regency Chinoiserie.

Lowther bought his first piece of lacquer, a burnt-orange betel box, while traveling in Burma in 1999, and it’s still one of his favorite things. He later found the craftspeople he was looking for in Saigon, and every piece from The Lacquer Company is still made there in Sơn Mài lacquer, a Vietnamese art form that goes back centuries. The process is lengthy: Wood is first sealed with a resin called Sinh. It’s then coated repeatedly with natural lacquer mixed with ground mountain rock, alluvial soil, and cashew nut shell oil. Each coat is wet-sanded until it’s smooth before the next coat is applied. “There is no prescribed drying time, no set number of layers,” according to the company. That makes the eight- to 12-week lead time on larger pieces easier to forgive.

Nickey Kehoe’s goal is for its furniture to feel “as if it was acquired, not purchased.” With these pieces so rooted in vintage styles and techniques, they make good on their promise.

The collection is available to shop on NickeyKehoe.com.

#4877. How One Designer Brought a Discerning Eye to Her Deeply Personal Manhattan Apartment

Ask an interior designer about their most difficult client, and there’s a good chance they’ll name themselves. Dani Dennis spent more than a decade at Mark Cunningham Inc. before founding her own New York–based practice, Danielette Dennis Interiors, translating other people’s tastes into rooms. “I’m such a decisive person,” she says of her approach to projects ranging from a traditional Brooklyn Heights townhouse to a sleek Park Avenue pied-à-terre. But when it came to decorating her own Gramercy Park apartment that she shares with her husband and two daughters, Dennis had no client brief to answer to—and no one to make the final call but herself.

When the family moved in three years ago, the apartment had plenty going for it: tall windows, handsome moldings, and an airy living and dining area. Dennis left the architecture alone, putting furniture, textiles, and her growing art collection to work instead. Benjamin Moore’s Steam keeps the walls a warm white, though the rooms are anything but hands-off. “I almost wanted it to feel like a gallery,” she says. “But, obviously, it’s lived in, and I have kids, so nothing is too precious.”

A portrait by Patrick Eugène, sourced via Mariane Ibrahim, anchors one end of the living room. Nearby are an Alfred Grenander chair upholstered in Toyine Sellers fabric, a black mushroom side table by Emma Donnersberg, and Christian Woo’s Noga Cube side table.

A portrait of a young girl by Jerrell Gibbs hangs near a Pierre Augustin Rose Cadillac ottoman upholstered in Rosemary Hallgarten’s alpaca bouclé. Vintage Saint-Louis crystal, sourced at the Paris flea market, sits atop the credenza.

The living room’s opposing sofas encourage conversation. The sofa (right), upholstered in Pierre Frey wool and mohair, is by Marked NYC. The ceiling fixture is a reedition of Pierre Chareau’s Quart de Rond lamp, and the rug is by Scott Group Studio.

Joseph-André Motte chairs surround the dining table, while a 1960s Italian burlwood credenza from Naga Antiques sits beneath an abstract painting by Carmen Neely. The dining rug is by Crosby Street Studios.

A first-generation American of Liberian heritage, Dennis has built a collection of art that includes contemporary Black artists from across the diaspora. A painting of girls playing in a circle takes her back to her school days in Côte d’Ivoire. Others show Black women in moments of rest and repose. “I want my kids and my family to be surrounded by reflections of us,” she says. Her clients’ collections tell their own stories; this one tells hers. Black joy runs through the collection, but Dennis doesn’t shop by theme; she listens to her gut. “I buy what I love,” she says. “I don’t buy for decoration.”

Dennis is equally at ease with an English-country chintz and a graphic geometric. In her own home, she borrows a little from everywhere, favoring clean lines and unexpected combinations. A custom sofa in Sanderson velvet faces a curved Marked NYC design in Pierre Frey wool and mohair. Camel-colored lounge chairs play against the sharp geometry of a Roger Sprunger coffee table; a 1906 Josef Hoffmann side table and an early-20th-century Alfred Grenander chair join the mix. “When the harmony comes from shape and proportion and feeling, I think that’s what makes spaces dynamic,” she says.

An expressive Ferrari Sheppard painting, acquired through Massimo De Carlo in Milan, hangs above a custom sofa upholstered in Sanderson’s indigo Quartz velvet. Camel-colored chairs wear Holland & Sherry fabric. A glass-and-metal coffee table by Roger Sprunger joins a modernist stool by Charles Vandenhove and JM Szymanski’s slender Table No. 3.

Dennis took a moodier approach in the library, where the family gathers. The walls and ceiling are painted the same dark hue, creating a cozy retreat for her two daughters, who prefer sprawling on the soft rug to sitting on the sofa. Artwork includes a floral painting by Alexandria Tarver and Hazel Mphande’s Stone or Lavender (2021). The striped pillows are in Fortuny fabric.

The dining table seats 10. Dinner guests, however, are still forthcoming. “I haven't had people over yet, because in my head it’s not done,” Dennis says. Joseph-André Motte chairs surround the table, while a 1960s Italian burlwood credenza and a Crosby Street Studios rug anchor the dining area. The living room sofas were positioned for entertaining too, although the family’s day-to-day use of the space is less formal. For Dennis’s daughters, 10 and seven, the mohair-and-wool sofa comes with ground rules: “You guys can sit on it, you can perch, but if we want to play, let’s do it elsewhere.”

The library, on the other hand, is fair game. The girls can sprawl out with a book or watch TV, though they rarely bother with the sofa. “They’re always lying on the rug,” Dennis says. She painted the walls a deep olive-green, carrying it across the ceiling for an enveloping effect. The art also takes a moodier turn, with a floral painting by Alexandria Tarver and a black-and-white self-portrait by Hazel Mphande. The primary bedroom, meanwhile, provides a brighter, quieter escape. “I always wanted to be in a cloud,” the designer says of the neutral palette. The upholstered bed, 1970s steel bench in alpaca wool, and leather-bound nightstands supply the texture.

Since the photo shoot, Dennis has switched out accessories and rearranged objects. When she recently swapped a lamp in the living room, even her husband took notice. “Another one?” he asked. At work, Dennis knows when to call a room finished. At home, she’s beginning to wonder why she should.

“I always wanted to be in a cloud,” Dennis says of the primary bedroom, where texture takes precedence over color. A vintage 1970s steel bench with alpaca upholstery sits at the foot of the bed, while leather-clad nightstands add another tactile element. The ceramic lamp is by Christiane Perrochon, and the understated artwork above the bed is by Carmen Neely.

#4875. Toyota’s Corolla Cross EV spotted for the first time [Images]

Toyota is giving its best-selling Corolla a major makeover, and an all-electric version is part of the plan. The upcoming Corolla Cross EV was captured in public for the first time ahead of its expected 2027 debut.

The Corolla has always been “a car for everyone,” Toyota’s former president and current CEO, Koji Sato, said after unveiling the next-gen Corolla Concept at last year’s Japan Mobility Show.

Since it went on sale 60 years ago, over 57 million drivers have chosen the Corolla, making it Toyota’s best-selling vehicle ever.

The Corolla has undergone 12 model changes since 1966, but the compact car is about to undergo its biggest transformation yet.

Although it’s still a top seller, the Corolla has lost some of its appeal as new, more advanced, and efficient options have emerged. Toyota looks to change that with the next-generation model.

It will remain “a car for everyone,” as Sato said, but the next-gen Corolla will come in multiple powertrains, including an all-electric version.

“Whether it’s a battery EV, plug-in hybrid, hybrid, or internal combustion engine vehicle―whatever the power source―let’s make good-looking cars that everyone will want to drive,” Sato said at the Japan Mobility Show last October.

Ahead of its expected debut sometime in 2027, a disguised Corolla Cross EV was spotted driving near Toyota’s European headquarters and R&D center.

New images from Chinese media outlet Autohome show what’s expected to be the all-electric Corolla Cross, with a closed-off grille and a unique body design.

The new Corolla will be the first to use Toyota’s new “multipathway” platform that will support electric, hybrid, gas, and other powertrains.

Toyota hasn’t revealed specifics, including battery or powertrain specs, but the next-gen Corolla EV is expected to remain close in style to the Concept. Aside from the massive COROLLA badge on the back, it looks like an entirely different vehicle with a near sports-car-like silhouette.

In an exclusive interview with Japanese media NHK in July, Toyota’s current chairman and former CEO, Akio Toyoda, warned that the company “cannot survive” if it does not adapt amid new competition and technology from China.

During the special, which went behind the scenes at Toyota’s “top secret” development site, several blurred Corolla Concept body types, including a sedan, hatchback, crossover, and GR model, were revealed in the background.

According to a recent Nikkei report, Toyota plans to begin production of the next-gen Corolla in 2028 through its joint venture with Chinese state-owned FAW Group, FAW Toyota Motor.

The Toyota Corolla EV is expected to be available in single- and dual-motor configurations with a driving range of at least 250 miles.

Let's hope that Toyota gets the Corolla EV right, because if it offers the right range for the right price but still feels fundamentally like a Corolla it is an EV that would get consideration from buyers who wouldn't otherwise consider an EV.

They're the buyers that trust Toyota and who consider the Corolla to be a nice safe choice for a car. And by safe, that means a vehicle that may not be all that exciting, but also a vehicle that they won't regret buying. Needless to say, these are not people who read Electrek, or even Car & Driver, for that matter. But there's a lot more of them than there are of us.

The hybrid version will reportedly use a new 1.5-liter four-cylinder engine and an electric motor. Toyota’s engineers told Car and Driver the system would deliver around 134 horsepower. It’s also estimated to be 10% to 20% more efficient than the current Corolla.

Toyota has yet to confirm the electric version will launch in the US. According to Car and Driver, the gas version will likely start at around $25,000, the hybrid around $27,000, and the EV and PHEVs will likely be priced in the $30,000 range.

#4873. 7 Best Cheese Boards for Entertaining Centerpieces (2026)

The calendar pointing toward the holidays also means that cheese board season is here. The platters function as a key part of any festive gathering, serving as the meeting point for people to nibble and mingle before they take a seat. But it’s much more than a way to display finger foods. Often situated in a central location at a party, a cheese board works as a decorative design piece, and when done well, can even be a conversation starter. In fact, some boards themselves read as a still life, even after half the Brie is gone.

The most unique cheese boards combine material and shape, offering something distinct and memorable to house the bites (or function as a surface for slicing a baguette). Designers are creating beautiful centerpieces by carving wood into soft, stonelike forms or cutting marble into asymmetrical ovals. Ahead, find seven cheese boards to invest in now, each one pretty enough to steal the spotlight at any event.

Sarah Sherman Samuel is known for blending character with clean modern lines in her interiors, and her cheese board trio for Lulu and Georgia brings that same sensibility to the table. The set includes two marble boards and one made of acacia, allowing you to layer textures; situating soft cheeses on cool stone and bread on wood. The three sizes allow you to extend your spread down a long table for a crowd or cuddle everything close on the counter.

These amorphous-shaped boards by Danish brand Ferm Living are inspired by cairns, the stacks of stones that hikers leave as markers on the trail. Each is carved from solid ash that’s certified by the FSC—a third-party organization that confirms responsible sourcing of wood—and is given a carbonized finish that turns the wood a deep espresso shade. When you’re not using the boards to display cheese, you can stack them on a counter where they’ll look like a sculptural piece.

For a more artful approach to your cheese board, check out this tortoiseshell option from CB2. Portuguese artisans hand-finish each piece in a reactive glaze, so no two boards come out identical. The amber and chocolate swirls highlight both white cheeses and green accoutrements, such as green grapes and Granny Smith apples, for an especially striking display. And at roughly 10 by 18 inches, the long board runs neatly down the center of a table.

Serena & Lily has made this wave shape its signature, commonly appearing on its crested mirrors and nightstands, and this board brings that coastal edge to the table. The scalloped surface is the relaxed, beach-house counterpoint to the more architectural boards on this list. At 18 inches, the small size suits a cozy night in for two, while the large, 30-inch board option has room to house a full spread with all the accoutrements.

Red marble has been having a moment, showing up on bathroom vanities and living room floors. This tray is a low-lift way to incorporate the material in your space. Cut from deep red stone into a sleek oval with a thick rim, the color of this CB2 cheese board is inherently festive but will look elevated and at home in your kitchen year-round. Because it’s solid marble, the veining and color will vary from tray to tray.

At 13 by 18.5 inches, the generously sized Romie has room for the full spread, with space for several cheeses, cured meats, a cluster of grapes, and a stack of crackers that won’t slide off the edge. Its classic oval shape is made from acacia that’s stained a deep chocolate, bringing out the grain and hiding knife marks. It’s an Anthropologie exclusive and a beautiful board to reach for when you’re feeding more than a few people.

The artist Neil Cohen designed this 15-inch acacia block for the New Mexico–based brand Nambe, and the piece’s best feature is hidden in plain sight. The wood is carved with nooks that hold the knife and spreader flush with the surface, so the tools stay with the board instead of getting lost in a drawer, which is a pretty great feature. The clean shape is modern, making it an easy hostess gift.
