#4818. Wellness Apps, Medically Tailored Meals Help Slow Weight Gain After GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Weight regain is common after stopping GLP-1 medications such as semaglutide (Wegovy, Ozempic) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound).

In fact, previous research has shown that most people regain at least half of their lost weight within 1 year of stopping treatment, with weight regain often accelerating during the first 3–4 months.

However, a new study suggests that structured support, including a weight management app or medically tailored meals, may help slow weight regain after discontinuing GLP-1 medications.

The small study, published October 7 in Obesity Science & Practice, found that participants who received either intervention regained significantly less weight over four months than those receiving usual care.

The study included 39 adults with an average age of 50, an average weight of 189 pounds, and an average body mass index (BMI) of 31.4.

All participants had lost more than 10% of their body weight while taking GLP-1 medications and had stopped treatment within the previous 30 days.

All participants also completed questionnaires at the beginning and end of the study and used Bluetooth scales to track their weight at home throughout the four-month period.

Researchers randomly assigned participants to one of the following three groups:

Participants continued to receive care from their healthcare providers, which may include nutrition, exercise, and lifestyle counseling from a clinician or registered dietitian. The type and amount of support varied depending on the provider’s recommendations and available resources. The researchers did not provide any additional intervention.

Participants received a subscription to Noom, an app that uses behavioral strategies to support weight loss and maintenance. These include tracking food intake, exercise, and weight, as well as educational lessons on the psychological, physiological, social, and environmental factors that influence eating behaviors.

The app also provides tools to help users recognize and manage triggers that may lead to overeating. Participants were encouraged to use the app for at least 15 minutes daily, including completing lessons, logging food, and tracking their weight.

These are typically nutrient-dense meals developed by registered dietitians to meet the nutritional needs of people with specific health conditions, such as chronic kidney disease or uncontrolled type 2 diabetes.

For this study, participants in this group selected 10 portion-controlled, “weight wellness” meals each week from more than 70 options, which were delivered to their homes.

After four months, participants who received either medically tailored meals or access to the digital weight management app experienced significantly less weight regain than those receiving usual care.

The estimated weight regain was 10.75% of body weight in the usual-care group, compared with 3.6% in the Noom group and 3.58% in the medically tailored meals group.

Although participants in all three groups regained weight, the findings suggest that structured nutritional or behavioral support may help limit weight regain after stopping GLP-1 medications.

“These findings highlight the benefits of ongoing support for patients on a weight loss journey,” said Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA. Ali wasn’t involved in the study.

Denise Pate, MD, a board certified internist with Medical Offices of Manhattan who was also not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are significant “because they show that obesity management is multifactorial, not only medication, but the combination of types of meals and behavioral change all play a role.”

However, because this was a small, four-month study, larger, longer-term trials are needed to determine whether these approaches can help people maintain weight loss over time after stopping GLP-1 medications.

Ali noted that research suggests GLP-1 medications are most effective for weight management when taken long-term.

“Obesity needs to be recognized and treated as a chronic condition, similar to diabetes or hypertension,” he said.

Pate agreed, emphasizing that obesity is not always recognized as a chronic condition that may require ongoing treatment.

“I feel that the medical community, insurance, and the population as a whole have yet to fully accept obesity as a chronic medical condition, which it most definitely is for a large part of patients. For this reason, I think patients should stay on these medications long term if needed,” she said.

“GLP-1 medications are highly effective tools for transitioning to a healthier diet and lifestyle, which for most people may require long-term use,” Ali added.

Pate explained that one of the goals of GLP-1 medications is to help people eat smaller portions by recognizing when they feel full and stopping when they do.

“I tell my patients from the start, this is the goal,” she said, adding that she hopes patients will retain those habits after stopping treatment.

Ali recommended maintaining a balanced diet rich in protein and vegetables while limiting added sugars and refined carbohydrates.

He added that tracking apps and regular follow-up appointments with a healthcare professional or registered dietitian may also help people maintain their progress.

“Patients need to understand that the GLP medication is not a miracle drug, although with the dramatic weight loss, it can be perceived as such. It is only a tool to be used in conjunction with an exercise routine as well as a healthy diet,” Pate said.

#4817. How Dwight Howard Built His ‘Superman’ Physique

The NBA center talks training, injuries, and discipline.

MORE THAN OTHER pro athletes, NBA players tend to enter their professional careers as skinny kids, still developing out of high school. To a degree, that’s exactly what happened with Dwight Howard, the first pick of the 2004 NBA draft. “My first year in the league, I got kind of pushed around,” Howard said on MH’s Strong Talk. “I didn’t like it.” Howard spent that offseason “eating weights” and became on the most muscular (and dominant) players ever. He earned the nickname “Superman” and went on to a Hall of Fame career. For almost two decades, Howard played for multiple teams and won an NBA championship with the Los Angeles Lakers in 2020.

Howard’s superhero physique came from more than shooting hoops. The center began building a disciplined training regimen as a high schooler, waking up at 4 a.m. to run track and hit the weight room.

“I told my dad at 10 I wanted to go to the NBA, and he said, ‘Well, you got to learn how to sacrifice now. You know your time and your effort. You have to learn how to be disciplined,’” Howard says in the latest Strong Talk episode.

Howard took his dad’s words to heart, already having the foresight that establishing a routine now would be easier than breaking bad training habits upon entering the NBA. His training over the years has evolved into different fitness challenges: from training in high-altitude terrains in Aspen to taking on Pilates and yoga.

Speaking with MH fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. and exercise physiologist and strength coach Dr. Pat Davidson, Howard goes into detail about the strength exercises he did to stay fit during the season, what he’s learned from trying to play through injuries, and the upcoming launch of the Rize Above with Dwight app next month that will offer fitness guidance to individuals of any age starting a fitness journey.

#4816. DARVO at Work: Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

Simone had done everything right. She had led her department's most impactful projects, trained half the team, and been told twice that she was "next in line" for a senior manager role.

Then the promotion went to Mark. He had been with the company for about a year, created extra work for others by turning in slop, and, as nearly everyone knew, had been in a relationship with their boss, Jody, for the last 6 months.

Simone didn't accuse anyone of anything. She politely asked HR whether the promotion process had been reviewed for a conflict of interest. Before long, Simone was labeled "a troublemaker," and somehow Jody was a victim of "harassment about her private life."

How does the person who raised a legitimate concern end up as the problem, while the person who created the problem ends up as the victim?

Jennifer Freyd (1997) coined the term DARVO— for Deny, Attack, and Reverse Victim and Offender—to describe how people often respond when confronted about wrongdoing. It was first studied in the context of domestic violence and abuse, but it occurs anywhere accountability is brought up, including the workplace.

DARVO can be deliberate and calculated, or reflexive and emotion-driven. Either way, the person who dared to speak up is vilified. Here’s how it might have played out with Simone and Jody.

The organization's attention switches to protecting Jody and Mark, the people with power, and away from advocating for Simone, someone originally harmed by that power. And the original concern, a manager granting a promotion to her lover in violation of conflict-of-interest policy, has disappeared from the conversation. It’s now about "You are attacking my private life and hurting my feelings."

DARVO is used so often because it is effective. Research shows it. In a 2020 set of experiments, people read the same incident with or without the accused person's DARVO response. When DARVO was present, readers judged the victim as less believable and more to blame, and the perpetrator as less responsible (Harsey & Freyd, 2020).

DARVO can also gaslight the original target. Harsey, Zurbriggen, and Freyd (2017) found that the more DARVO people encountered when confronting someone who had wronged them, the more they blamed themselves. Self-blame can lead to self-silencing, and Simone might come to wonder if she really is "just bitter" and should say nothing.

From the inside, DARVO can spur confusion. Simone starts editing her own memory: Was her tone too sharp? Did she misread something? Was she, deep down, just jealous? Each doubt could make sense, and that’s what makes them dangerous. Over time, that self-doubt can harden into silence—a coping strategy that may cost you who you are. So, if you find yourself wondering whether you were the problem, keep asking yourself: What actually happened first?

Research also offers some good news: People who were taught to recognize the DARVO pattern were less swayed by it. They saw the victim as more credible and the perpetrator as less so. Simply knowing the pattern's name weakens its grip (Harsey & Freyd, 2020). Of course, recognizing the pattern requires paying attention. The clearest signal is a subject change. If a question about a decision turns into complaints about the questioner's tone, personality, or propriety, ask why.

DARVO succeeds by making us forget the original question. In Simone's case, it was simple: Was there a conflict of interest? Everything that followed—the denials, the attacks on Simone, Jody's claims of being a victim—was meant to bury it.

Do not be distracted. Hold on to the original concern. Keep asking “what happened first.” And insist on the resolution of the original question.

DARVO depends on changing the subject. These phrases change it back.

Freyd, J. J. (1997). Violations of power, adaptive blindness, and betrayal trauma theory. Feminism & Psychology, 7(1), 22–32.

Harsey, S., & Freyd, J. J. (2020). Deny, Attack, and Reverse Victim and Offender (DARVO): What Is the Influence on Perceived Perpetrator and Victim Credibility? Journal of Aggression, Maltreatment & Trauma, 29(8), 897–916.

Harsey, S., Zurbriggen, E. L., & Freyd, J. J. (2017). Perpetrator responses to victim confrontation: DARVO and victim self-blame. Journal of Aggression, Maltreatment & Trauma, 26, 644–663.

#4814. Michael Strahan Shares the Words That Helped His Daughter Through Brain Cancer Treatment

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

For years, Michael Strahan appeared in commercials for St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital, delivering a message he never imagined would become so personal: “No parent should have to hear that their child has cancer.”

But in 2023, the beloved TV host and former NFL player faced that reality when his daughter, Isabella, was diagnosed with brain cancer at 19 years old.

“[That] line that I used to deliver, usually at the end of the commercial…here I am actually filling that line in my life in real time,” Strahan told Healthline.

Strahan believes his longtime connection with St. Jude was more than a coincidence. After years of advocating for families affected by childhood cancer, he found himself on the other side of that experience.

“When I needed that family…they were there for me,” he said. “I’m just appreciative, and I think things come back to you; give out good, good comes back.”

In October 2023, Isabella began experiencing vomiting, headaches, and balance issues during her freshman year at the University of Southern California (USC). Tests revealed that she had medulloblastoma, a fast-growing cancerous brain tumor located in the cerebellum. She underwent emergency brain surgery, radiation therapy, and four rounds of chemotherapy.

While medulloblastoma typically occurs in children between the ages of 3 and 9, it can also affect young adults like Isabella.

“[The] biology in adolescents and young adults can differ meaningfully from pediatric cases, requiring specialized expertise at centers of excellence for this disease,” Arnab Chakravarti, MD, director of the Brain Tumor Program at The Ohio State University, told Healthline.

Medulloblastoma is sometimes confused with glioblastoma, the most common type of malignant primary brain tumor in adults. Glioblastoma is particularly aggressive, with a median overall survival of just 15 months and a 5-year survival rate of less than 10%.

However, Chakravarti explained that medulloblastoma has a significantly higher cure rate than glioblastoma.

“[This is] a point of genuine hope that deserves to be communicated clearly,” he said.

Radiation therapy is a cornerstone of medulloblastoma treatment. Isabella received proton therapy, which uses precisely targeted radiation to treat tumors while limiting exposure to surrounding healthy tissue.

“For medulloblastoma, this physical precision is transformative,” Chakravarti said. “Proton craniospinal irradiation dramatically reduces [collateral] exposure — preserving cochlear function and hearing, reducing cardiovascular risk, protecting the thyroid, and most critically, sparing developing brain tissue in ways that translate into measurably better neurocognitive outcomes years after treatment.”

He added that multiple prospective studies have shown that children and young adults treated with proton craniospinal irradiation experience less cognitive decline and better quality of life compared to those treated with conventional radiation.

Today, Isabella is back at USC, embracing the everyday routines she once had to put on hold.

“I am back at USC, so…it’s been great, in the midst of exams, so it’s a little stressful, but I actually [am] inviting the stress in because at one point I didn’t have exams, so I’m happy to be back,” Isabella told Healthline.

Along with attending classes, Isabella is enjoying activities such as working out and cooking. She continues to undergo MRI scans of her head and spine every three months, but said that after another year, the scans will become less frequent, occurring every six months.

“But really…I don’t have a lot of doctor’s appointments,” she said.

“It feels like a brand-new life, but it’s a good one. And that’s wonderful,” Isabella said.

Isabella said her family’s support played an important role in helping her through cancer treatment. Spending so much time together in the hospital brought them closer as they watched movies and played cards and board games to pass the time.

“[It] really, really bonds you to people, and just having my dad and my whole family there was something that [you] can’t beat,” she told Healthline.

Michael said that despite the difficult circumstances, he cherishes the time he spent with his daughter. Before her diagnosis, Isabella was a typical teenager who spent much of her time at school or with friends.

“They say you spend the most time with your kid for the first few years of their life, and then once school starts, you don’t get a chance to spend as much time as you would like with them,” he said.

While Michael said he and Isabella already had a close relationship, her diagnosis brought the family even closer and helped them reflect on what mattered most.

“[What] was really important was family, and relationships, and the love that you have for each other, and the support you have to give each other,” he said. “I think that our relationship now is better than ever.”

Today, Michael makes an effort to visit Isabella at USC whenever he’s in Los Angeles during the NFL season.

“Some weekends she [has time for me]. Some she doesn’t,” he said. “But just to have that relationship with your child, where they want to hang out with you, is a good feeling, and that’s the relationship that we have.”

Michael and Isabella are sharing their story to raise awareness about brain cancer and offer hope to other families facing similar challenges.

They recently participated in a fireside chat in New York City hosted by Real Chemistry and SMAC, where they discussed their family’s experience navigating Isabella’s diagnosis, mental health, caregiving, and the impact of sharing their story.

Throughout her treatment, Isabella also documented her experience through a series of YouTube vlogs and the ABC primetime documentary, “Life Interrupted: Isabella Strahan’s Fight to Beat Cancer.”

For Michael, helping others is a value he learned from his parents. He recalled how his father used his transportation business in Germany to support people in need after retiring from the military.

“[He] would take donations, and use his money and his trucks, and drive stuff to Yugoslavia and Czechoslovakia, and drop it off there at local churches and the shelters for people, who he had no connection with,” said Michael. “So for me, I think I do what I feel is on my heart and what’s important to me.”

For parents caring for children with cancer, Michael emphasized that it’s OK to feel overwhelmed or emotional. He encouraged them to show their children love and support while helping them maintain hope for the future.

“I think positivity is the main thing because it was so tough on her at the time when she was [saying], ‘I can’t do it. I can’t do this. I can’t do that,’” said Michael.

Michael said he made a conscious effort to replace words like “can’t” and “if” with “when” while encouraging Isabella during treatment.

“Anytime she got down on herself, I’d say, ‘when you go back to college, when you do this, when you do that,’” said Michael. “And I just think the positive attitude and the love that you can give and the confidence that you can display towards your loved one [or] your child who’s going through something like this is the only thing you can do because you’re at the mercy of medicine.”

Now in her senior year at USC, Isabella is looking ahead to life after graduation.

“[There’s] a lot of interesting opportunities and things that I want to pursue,” she said.

Michael has no doubt she will find her way.

“She’s so talented, and this experience, in my opinion, has opened up my eyes to more talent that she has that I didn’t realize…the talent to connect people, and be in front of a crowd. I always thought she’d be nervous because I get nervous, but she’s better than me,” he said.

#4813. What the Recent Tech Outage Can Teach Us About Balance

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

As I write this, parts of North America and Europe are experiencing a Microsoft outage that is affecting certain parts of the cloud infrastructure, particularly office communication services such as Outlook, Teams, and Microsoft 360. While this is certainly causing disruption and inconvenience in many corporate and business settings, it may also be reminding us of an important reality that we often talk about but rarely implement: work-life balance.

In the United States, it has long been reported that workers struggle with creating healthy boundaries between their lives and their jobs, and a 2025 study found that a staggering 66 percent of American workers reported having experienced “some degree of burnout” in the past year (Robinson, 2025). Additionally, 2024 research indicated that 44 percent of employees and 53 percent of supervisors experienced burnout at their jobs (Malinsky, 2022). It is no secret that many of us struggle to find the “sweet spot” between work and the rest of our lives. Increasingly, this disparity between work and life is being seen as a larger problem that, according to a 2021 study, is more than “an individual-level phenomenon,” and is “a societal concern that necessitates systematic support from a wider range of stakeholders” (Fan, Yuyang, et al., 2021).

Along with the statistical evidence, we can find plenty of anecdotal proof that this is a widespread problem: you would be hard-pressed to find a person who does not report some level of exhaustion or burnout related to their career, myself and those I know being no exception. But if it is such an issue, why are we unable to see something like this Microsoft outage as a gift rather than an inconvenience? I would argue that it has to do with our longstanding relationship with work and our misprioritization of its importance. American attitudes about work have long been centered around productivity, busyness, results, and multitasking. Words like “balance” are simply not part of our career-related vernacular.

When something like a technology outage forces us to let go of our usual outcome-orientation towards our jobs, it can feel odd and somehow “wrong.” Looking at social media comments today, I am seeing more that speak to how annoying and inconvenient this outage is and less that speak to it allowing for a slower workday or an (albeit forced) opportunity to not work as hard. But perhaps we can learn from today’s widespread inconvenience. In some workplaces, you are unable to send or answer emails, communicate as usual, or access cloud-related platforms. In one sense, this is frustrating. In another, it is permission not to do these things that, let’s be honest, are often done from home, from the dinner table, at unhealthy hours, in the midst of other life activities, and at the cost of mindfulness and presence in our lives. I am not suggesting that tech outages are good for business, but rather that they can remind us that creating space between work and life is necessary for our overall well-being.

Sometimes inconveniences can be opportunities. In Buddhist philosophy, the concept that the “obstacle is the path” is applicable to today’s inconvenience. The obstacle (not being able to access the usual work platforms) is the path to allowing ourselves to slow down and create some space between work and life—at least for a day or two.

Bryan Robinson, Ph.D. “Job Burnout at 66% in 2025, New Study Shows.” Forbes, 8 Feb. 2025, www.forbes.com/sites/bryanrobinson/2025/02/08/job-burnout-at-66-in-2025…. Accessed 13 Nov. 2026.

Malinsky, Gili. “There’s More Than One Type of Work Burnout―How to Identify Which You Have.” CNBC, 29 Sept. 2022, www.cnbc.com/make-it/2022/09/29/theres-more-than-one-type-of-burnout-ho…. Accessed 13 Nov. 2026.

Fan, Yuyang, et al. “A Process‐Oriented, Multilevel, Multidimensional Conceptual Framework of Work–Life Balance Support: A Multidisciplinary Systematic Literature Review and Future Research Agenda.” International Journal of Management Reviews, vol. 23, no. 4, 5 May 2021, 10.1111/ijmr.12254.

#4812. BYD’s new luxury electric SUV has one big problem: It weighs over 8,200 lbs

BYD’s new full-size electric SUV, the Denza N9 EV, was revealed in a regulatory filing, weighing in at over 8,200 lbs (3,760 kg). That creates one issue.

The Denza N9 first went on sale last March, a flagship plug-in hybrid (PHEV) SUV with a combined CLTC range of about 807 miles (1,300 km) on a full charge and full tank of gas.

BYD introduced the updated Flash Charging version earlier this year, which uses its second-generation Blade Batteries and delivers a pure electric CLTC range of 260 miles (420 km). Combined, it gets up to 944 miles (1,520 km) under CLTC conditions.

In the latest batch of new energy vehicles (NEVs) approved for sale by China’s MIIT (Ministry of Information Technology) this week, a new all-electric Denza N9 appeared.

The filing revealed the Denza N9 EV will be available with three electric motors, delivering a combined output of 1,193 horsepower (890 kW).

A badge on the back reveals it will use BYD’s tri-motor e3 platform. The setup features a single 362 horsepower (270 kW) front motor and two 415 horsepower (310 kW) rear electric motors.

The electric version measures 5,270 mm long, 2,030 mm wide, and 1,830 mm tall, with a 3,125 mm wheelbase, which is the same as the current Denza N9 PHEV Flash Charging model. It will be available in five- and six-seat configurations.

While the filing reveals it will use a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery with cells from BYD’s battery unit, FinDreams, it does not provide specifics like capacity or driving range.

One relatively big thing to note: the Denza N9 EV has a gross weight of 3,760 kg, or about 8,289 lbs.

Obscene weight , and that applies to other SUVs as well. Vehicle registration taxes should be based on vehicle weight as it wears out roads and endangers other road users and infrastructure and wastes resources.

As AutoNext points out, this makes it too heavy for an EU category B driving license, which covers up to 3,500 kg (7,716 lbs).

Last year, the EU updated the rules, allowing drivers who have held a category B license for two years to drive alternative-fuelled vehicles with a maximum weight of up to 4,250 kg (9,369 lbs).

While the Denza N9 EV would qualify as listed, newer drivers would still need a commercial EU category C1 driving license to drive it.

BYD launched its luxury sub-brand, Denza, in Europe and the UK in March, starting with the Z9 GT and the D9 van. More recently, it introduced the Bao 5 PHEV SUV and the Denza Z electric supercar.

#4811. Emideltide Keeps Getting a ‘No’ for Compounding. What’s the Problem?

Why the government’s renewed interest in peptides excludes this one.

THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION has not been shy about its pro-peptide stance. US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has pushed to make six popular yet unapproved peptides available for compounding to people with a prescription. A recent FDA advisory committee meeting voted in favor of adding six out of seven peptides to a list of substances that U.S. compounding pharmacies are allowed to manufacture and supply.

Six out of seven. So what happened to that last peptide? Emideltide, also dubbed DSIP, is a peptide people have turned to for better sleep. And it was the only peptide the FDA advisory board voted against moving out of the Category 2 list—a substance considered to carry significant safety risks, with compounding pharmacies prohibited from making it. Here’s why.

EMIDELTIDE IS A nine-amino-acid peptide originally isolated from the blood of sleeping rabbits during electrically induced sleep in the late 1970s. Since its discovery, a synthetic peptide version has been administered via injection or a nasal spray.

Emideltide reportedly helps you fall asleep faster and extend the time spent in deep sleep. It’s also been used to avoid waking up multiple times throughout the night and anecdotal reports online have mentioned more vivid, Inception–like lucid dreaming. With better sleep, people online using emideltide have mentioned feeling less stress, more refreshed upon waking, and faster recovery after a grueling workout.

MOST RESEARCH LOOKING into the peptide’s role in sleep, however, took place in the 1980s and 1990s—with mixed findings.

For example, a 1984 case study reported on a 35-year-old guy with 10 years of narcolepsy who had reduced sleep attacks, less daytime napping, and more alertness with weekly emideltide injections administered in the morning.

One clinical trial had 16 people take an emideltide injection or a placebo while measuring how long it took for them to fall asleep once they’re tucked into bed. People who had an emideltide injection said they felt more tired and actually went to sleep quicker than the placebo group. That should be great except when they repeated the experiment a second night, the placebo group knocked out quicker than the peptide group.

Another study in 1992 found the peptide helped chronic insomniacs feel less tired. However, there was such little difference in the time it took to fall asleep and stay asleep in the emideltide group versus the placebo group. The authors of the 1992 study said any small improvements with the peptide were probably “due to an incidental change in the placebo group” and “not likely to be of major therapeutic benefit.”

BEYOND SLEEP, EMIDELTIDE has been explored in animal studies for potentially protecting against cancer and improving motor ability after stroke. Another realm of interest is how emideltide might help with curbing withdrawal after addiction.

A 1984 study found emideltide injections helped reduce the severity of opioid withdrawal symptoms in 97 percent of people with addiction along with alcohol withdrawal symptoms in 87 percent of people with alcohol addiction. Although more peptide injections were needed in people with opiate addiction.

In 1998, researchers gave a single injection of emideltide to seven people with opioid dependence. While they reported improvements in opioid withdrawal, the team also noted “it remains an open question whether DSIP could be an effective alternative detoxification approach.” Some of the issues were the small sample size, lack of a placebo group for proper comparison, and that each person knew they were getting an emideltide injection. The lack of randomization makes it hard to say for sure that a treatment actually worked or if people subjectively felt better because they knew they were getting treatment.

WE KNOW EMIDELTIDE doesn’t act like a sedative that slows down the brain and body’s function. But how the peptide exactly works is still up for debate.

The peptide is often considered a sleep-regulator rather than a suppressant. We know emideltide doesn’t act like a sedative or sleeping pill that slows down the brain and body’s function. But how the peptide exactly works is still up for debate.

One possible mechanism is that the peptide increases delta-wave activity. These are your slowest brain waves at 0.5 to 4 Hz that are indicative of deep sleep. Deep sleep is linked to better memory, energy, and all that good stuff you get from a good night’s sleep. There may also be some neuroendocrine effects going on that could explain why people feel calm enough to pass out. A small study back in the ’80s injected a single dose of emideltide in 11 guys and found lower levels of ACTH, a hormone that stimulates your adrenal glands to release the stress hormone cortisol (though this mechanism has been disputed).

The FDA advisory meeting relied on studies that focused on emideltide’s cross-talk with the opioid system in the brain. While the peptide doesn’t directly interact with opioid receptors, evidence points to emideltide somehow being able to trigger the release of endorphins. This may also provide painkiller properties (which is why it’s been proposed as a way to suppress alcohol and opioid withdrawal syndrome).

EMIDELTIDE WILL PROBABLY stay banned—and found only through the sketchy gray market—because there’s not enough information to know if emideltide might do more harm than good.

Since emideltide interacts with the opioid system, there is a possibility that it could lead to addiction. Right now, there are no animal or human studies that prove emideltide wouldn’t worsen addictive behaviors.

There’s also not enough data on whether repeated emideltide use would cause other safety issues. While the small sleep trials did not report any serious side effects, withdrawal studies noted headaches, nausea, and vertigo. After the second injection, some had low blood pressure although the researchers also said it’s unclear whether those symptoms were because of the peptide or from withdrawal altogether.

#4810. Hormone Therapy May Help Improve Menopause Brain Fog, Mood Changes

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Menopause hormone therapy (MHT), also known as hormone replacement therapy (HRT), helps manage various menopause symptoms.

Currently, MHT is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to help relieve hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, and dyspareunia (pain during sex).

However, recent research has found that MHT may also help improve mental symptoms like “brain fog” and mood changes.

Other research also found that MHT does not affect dementia risk. This research followed the FDA’s removal of the black box warning on these products, which suggested they may increase the risk.

Together, these studies show that MHT may help people experiencing menopause in ways not previously realized and that it is generally safe to use.

Research published in Scientific Reports on September 1 suggests that an estrogen hormone treatment that combines estriol and progesterone may help ease the symptoms of brain fog during menopause.

Brain fog may involve memory lapses, difficulty concentrating, and slower thinking.

Just about two-thirds of women experience cognitive difficulties, like brain fog, during the menopausal transition. However, there is currently no Food and Drug Administration (FDA)- approved treatment for these symptoms.

This study was an observational case series that followed 20 menopausal women with an average age of 53. Each participant was given a baseline assessment for cognitive symptoms prior to treatment.

They were then treated for 12 months with a customized regimen of estriol and progesterone.

Estriol is a natural form of estrogen that occurs during pregnancy and has been used in Europe and Asia to treat other symptoms of menopause.

After 12 months, the participants reported significant reductions in:

“Estrogen plays a well-documented role in protecting the brain, yet there are still no approved type and dose of treatment that specifically targets the cognitive symptoms so many women experience during menopause,” Rhonda Voskuhl, MD, neurologist, member of the Comprehensive Menopause Center at UCLA Health, and senior study author, said in a press release.

“Women are often told to simply live with brain fog, when in fact there is a neuroscience basis for it, and potentially a way to address it. That gap in care is what motivated us to look more closely at estriol,” Voskuhl said.

This was a small, preliminary case series without a placebo group or randomization. More research is needed to confirm the benefits for cognitive symptoms.

A study published September 9 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society, showed that hormone therapy may help improve mood changes in women in midlife.

The researchers noted that mood disturbances, such as depression, irritability, anxiety, and mental exhaustion, affect up to 68% of women during menopause.

“The erratic changes and loss of estrogen associated with this hormonal transition can lower serotonin and dopamine levels, which [are] associated with depression and cognitive changes, including poor concentration, brain fog, and memory loss,” said Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

The study included 260 individuals with an average age of 52 years. Just over half of the participants had a history of anxiety or depression, and 24% were using an antidepressant medication at the start of the study.

Each participant completed the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS) both before and after initiating hormone therapy for FDA-approved indications, such as hot flashes and night sweats.

The average follow-up during the study was 4.5 months. Between the baseline and the follow-up, there was a significant reduction in the MRS psychological scores. The percentage of participants with severe mood symptoms decreased from 62.3% to 24.6%.

Treatment response didn’t appear to differ by age, menopausal stage, psychiatric history, or antidepressant use. These findings suggest that hormone therapy may help improve mood symptoms in midlife, especially for those with higher severity of symptoms before treatment.

“This study supports the evidence that starting hormone therapy for the typical disruptive symptoms of menopause may bring collateral benefits, including improvement in mood,” Ross said. “Communicating with your healthcare provider is always best to manage your symptoms and prepare yourself properly for this next stage of life.”

For decades, women have been warned about the serious potential risks associated with menopause hormone therapy (MHT). This included an FDA “black box” warning citing complications like cardiovascular disease, cancer, and dementia.

However, a recent meta-analysis commissioned by the World Health Organization (WHO) that included data from more than a million women, and was published in The Lancet Healthy Longevity, found that MHT neither increased nor decreased dementia risk.

“The World Health Organisation currently provides no guidance on MHT and dementia risk, leaving a critical gap for women, clinicians, and policymakers. Our work will help inform upcoming WHO guidelines on reducing the risk of cognitive decline and dementia,” Melissa Melville, a PhD candidate and aging researcher in the Department of Clinical Health Psychology at the University College London, and first author of the study, told Healthline in a previous interview.

In the same interview, Melville stressed that the importance of this work is twofold: for clinicians, there is an urgent need for higher-quality research, and for patients, decisions about MHT should be guided by symptoms and well-established benefits and risks.

#4809. Germany’s EV share hits record 37% as BEVs beat gas and diesel combined

Battery-electric cars took a record 37% of Germany’s new car market in October, according to data released today by the Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt (KBA), the country’s federal motor vehicle authority. That’s 94,086 BEVs, up 79.5% from 52,425 a year earlier.

For the second month in a row, German buyers registered more fully electric cars than gasoline and diesel cars combined. And with two months left in the year, Germany has already blown past the auto industry’s EV forecast for all of 2026.

The overall market barely grew in October. Total new car registrations rose 1.7% to 254,492 units, which means the EV growth came straight out of combustion cars.

Gasoline car registrations crashed 40.5% to 38,516 units, a 15.1% share. Diesel fell 21.6% to 23,882 units, or 9.4% of the market. Add them up and pure combustion cars made up just 24.5% of new registrations, 12.5 points less than BEVs alone.

Plug-in hybrids slipped 7.9% to 28,499 units (11.2%). So plug-ins accounted for about 48% of the German market last month, and the average CO2 emissions of new cars dropped 21.1% year-over-year to 79.4 g/km.

As we reported this summer, BEVs became the most popular powertrain in Germany for the first time in June with a 28.4% share. They’ve kept climbing every month since: 32.4% in August, 34.5% in September, and now 37% in October.

Through the first ten months of the year, Germany has registered 698,230 BEVs, up 60.7% year-over-year. That’s about 28.2% of the 2,476,290 new cars registered in 2026 so far, up from roughly 19% for the full year 2025.

And the industry didn’t see it coming. In December, the VDA, Germany’s auto industry association, forecast about 693,000 BEV registrations for all of 2026. Germany passed that in October. At the current pace, it’s on track for somewhere around 875,000 by the end of the year.

The biggest driver is Germany’s new EV incentive, which applies retroactively to cars registered since January 1. It pays €3,000 for a new BEV, bought or leased, and up to €6,000 for lower-income households with children. Households with taxable income above €80,000 (€90,000 with kids) don’t qualify.

The program targets private buyers, and that’s exactly where the KBA data shows the jump. Private registrations rose 20.6% in October, while commercial registrations fell 8.2%. Private buyers now make up 40.7% of the market.

Germany has been here before. The government killed its previous EV incentive overnight in December 2023, and BEV sales fell off a cliff in 2024. This time, the money is going to the buyers who need it most, and it’s moving the needle fast.

Tesla’s German numbers swing wildly with its quarterly delivery cycle. In September, the end of the quarter, it registered 12,552 cars (+268.7%) and the Model Y was the best-selling car in Germany. In October, it registered only 2,932, which is still up 290.9% but from a tiny base, for a 1.2% market share.

Year-to-date, Tesla is up 206.1% to 47,742 registrations. That’s a big rebound from a terrible 2025, but BYD is now slightly ahead with 47,961 (+216.1%). BYD registered 5,173 cars in October (+54.3%), though the majority of its German sales are plug-in hybrids, not BEVs.

The other Chinese brands are growing even faster. Leapmotor registered 3,661 cars in October, up 288.6%, and is at 19,705 for the year. Xpeng was up 284.4% to 1,380 units, and SAIC’s MG was up 48.5% to 4,140.

Volkswagen Group still owns the top of the EV charts, though. Through September, the Skoda Elroq was Germany’s best-selling EV with 30,845 units, ahead of the Tesla Model Y (29,464) and the VW ID.3 (24,352).

The EV boom is happening during one of the worst years in the history of Germany’s auto industry.

In October, the VW brand’s German registrations fell 4%, Audi dropped 8.4%, Porsche lost 5.7%, and Opel crashed 24.1%. BMW was flat (+0.1%), and Mercedes was the exception, up 8.5%. VW is still by far the biggest brand in Germany with an 18.2% share, but it’s down 5.6% for the year.

Last week, Volkswagen Group reported a €5.9 billion operating loss for the third quarter, its biggest quarterly loss since Dieselgate, driven by a writedown of its Porsche stake, weak sales in China, and thin EV margins. The group has already approved a plan to cut 100,000 jobs and close several German plants. Mercedes cut its 2026 car margin guidance to 2-3% last week, mainly because of China.

It’s not a product problem. VW’s new ID. Polo is sold out with over 30,000 orders, BMW has over 50,000 orders for the Neue Klasse iX3, and the Elroq leads the German EV market.

Germany is proving what we’ve been saying for years. Give buyers EVs they can actually afford, and they switch fast. Fully electric cars went from about 19% of the market last year to 37% in October, and the country beat the industry’s full-year forecast with two months to spare. That’s not a slow transition.

One thing to consider when talking about EVs not being Germany-made is that Germany car makers can't make them fast enough. A lot of the models are sold out for months. It's not an excuse but something to keep in mind.

Compare that with North America, where EV sales dropped 44% after the US killed its federal EV tax credit. Same technology, sometimes the same cars. The difference is policy.

Germany’s problem is who’s capturing the demand. Hint: it’s not German automakers.

But whose fault is that? You can’t spend years dragging your feet on electrification and lobby government back and forth on EV incentives and then complain when those who are all-in on EVs are able to take better advantage of the customer shift amid another oil crisis.

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero. #4808. How Gossip Is Good for Us

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

As the saying goes, “If you don’t have anything good to say, don’t say anything.” But in the words of Alice Roosevelt Longworth, perhaps more of us prefer: “If you can’t say something good about someone, sit right here by me.” After all, deep down, we all love some good gossip, don’t we?

In fact, by some estimates of everyday conversations, upwards of 65 percent of what we talk about involves people and social interactions, both self-disclosures and information about others’ escapades. And “gossip,” defined as the telling of stories about the everyday adventures of the people in our lives that we tell to, with, and about others, began deep in our evolutionary history. As soon as we began to use language, we started to gossip!

As we gather around the holiday table this year with friends and family we may not have seen in a while, we will share stories of our lives, stories of their lives, and stories of our friends and family not able to be present at the table. The good news is that this is actually good for us. Whereas gossip has a bad reputation, in fact, it serves a critical function in weaving our lives together and keeping our social groups connected.

Dunbar, an evolutionary anthropologist, argues that gossip began very early in our ancestral history. Living in larger social groups benefited our survival, and gossip is a necessary part of keeping larger social groups cohesive. Through sharing stories about how Uncle Joe and Aunt Louise are settling into their new living arrangements in Timbuktu, we maintain a sense of belonging to the group, and this sense of belonging adds to our own sense of meaning and purpose in life. When we feel socially isolated, we actually experience physical pain; Williams and Nida show experimentally that social exclusion for as little as two minutes leads to physiological pain responses and emotional distress, and longer periods of social isolation can result in depression, helplessness, and alienation. Maintaining social connections by integrating our lives with others through stories and gossip brings us together and creates a sense of well-being.

Gossip also serves to help us with advice and discussion of possible problems—if you are thinking about changing jobs, a story about cousin Bill who just did that could provide invaluable information as you consider your options. With my colleagues David Pillemer and Dorthe Thomsen, we showed how these kinds of vicarious stories, stories about other people that resonate with who we are, can promote successful adaptation, help us make good decisions, and teach us morals and values for how to live a good life. We don’t have to experience things directly to learn from them. We can learn from the experiences of others through gossip.

Vicarious stories are particularly prominent in family storytelling. Alongside stories of shared family experiences, such as the Thanksgiving when Dad dropped the turkey on the kitchen floor, and we all had to eat hot dogs, are stories of the family past: stories about parents growing up or grandparents, aunts, and uncles. When the younger generation hears these stories, whether from the person who experienced them (“When I was your age….”) or third-hand as gossip (“Your grandfather loved Thanksgiving, and every year, he would invite friends from work who had nowhere else to go”), these stories become frameworks for how to live a life. Gossip provides us with maps for how the world works.

Of course, there is a dark side to gossip. As Dores-Cruz and colleagues point out, gossip can be used to purposely damage someone else’s reputation, perhaps in the service of self-aggrandizement, and thus can lead to mistrust within the group. They conducted a series of studies to assess people’s motivations and tendency to gossip, especially when the person being gossiped about was experimentally manipulated to be a victim of malicious rumors. They found that group members were more likely to gossip when a group member was being maliciously maligned in order to protect the victim’s reputation. At the same time, people are motivated to spread the word about members of the group who violate norms, suggesting that gossip serves to keep everyone in line. Gossip is a little bit like herding sheep, making sure the group maintains positive bonds and bringing those who deviate from this back into the fold.

This holiday season, there will be gossip! I will spend Thanksgiving with my “framily” (friends and family), and there will be some dear framily we will miss who are not able to be there. But we will gossip! “Did you hear about so-and-so?” and “Let me tell you what happened…” We will laugh, and we will shed tears. And we will cement our bonds. So, this Thanksgiving, if you have something juicy to tell, come sit by me!

Dunbar, R. I. (2004). Gossip in evolutionary perspective. Review of general psychology, 8(2), 100-110.

Williams, K. D., & Nida, S. A. (2022). Ostracism and social exclusion: Implications for separation, social isolation, and loss. Current Opinion in Psychology, 47, 101353.

Pillemer, D. B., Thomsen, D. K., & Fivush, R. (2024). Vicarious memory promotes successful adaptation and enriches the self. Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition, 13(2), 159.

Dores Cruz, T. D., Nieper, A. S., Testori, M., Martinescu, E., & Beersma, B. (2021). An integrative definition and framework to study gossip. Group & Organization Management, 46(2), 252-285.

I wore this during New York City’s shoulder season, and it regulated temperature really well. I never got hot walking to work or felt chilly when the office AC kicked on. The fabric breathes better than most wool sweaters I’ve tested, and it never got that itchy, fuzzy feeling that cashmere can sometimes pick up after a few wears. Plus, the quarter-zip collar gives it versatility, too: zipped up, it looks sharp for the office; unzipped, it leans casual for the weekend. You can choose from a range of easy-to-wear neutral tones; think navy, black, and charcoal, which all pair effortlessly with chinos or dark jeans.

Look for high-quality materials that ensure warmth, comfort, and longevity. By understanding what each fabric brings to the table, you can select the sweater that fits both your lifestyle and your wardrobe goals. Here’s a closer look at what you can expect from the most common options:

Cashmere is the gold standard for softness and luxury. It’s made from the undercoat of cashmere goats, resulting in an ultra-fine, buttery fabric. Expect it to feel lightweight yet warm, perfect for layering without adding bulk. Cashmere sweaters often have a higher price tag, but their timeless appeal and plush feel make them a worthwhile investment. Just remember: cashmere requires delicate care, like handwashing or dry cleaning, to maintain its softness.

Merino wool is a performance powerhouse. Derived from Merino sheep, this wool is fine, soft, and naturally moisture-wicking, making it ideal for regulating body temperature. Merino wool sweaters keep you warm without overheating and are often odor-resistant, so they’re great for active or travel-heavy lifestyles. Bonus: Many are machine washable, adding a dose of convenience.

Cotton sweaters are breathable, lightweight, and perfect for transitional weather or layering indoors. They’re soft on the skin and great for those who find wool too itchy. Cotton doesn’t retain as much heat as wool, so it’s best suited for milder climates or casual settings. Expect easy care—most cotton sweaters are machine washable.

Blended fabrics combine the best of both worlds. For example, wool-cashmere blends deliver the softness of cashmere with the durability of wool, while wool-cotton blends offer a balance of warmth and breathability. These blends are often more affordable and easier to care for than pure fibers.

Alpaca wool is soft, silky, and hypoallergenic—great for those with sensitive skin. It’s warmer than regular wool but feels lighter, making it perfect for chilly days without feeling too heavy. Alpaca sweaters often have a natural luster, giving them a polished, luxurious look.

The best sweaters for men should strike the perfect balance—tailored enough to look polished, but comfortable enough for all-day wear. Pay attention to the shoulder and chest areas, which should be roomy enough for an undershirt or a button-down shirt underneath, but also not too loose and still snug and slim enough for looking elevated during standalone wear. Sleeves should hit at the wrist bone when your arms are relaxed at your sides and the overall silhouette should be neither too tight nor too loose. A well-fitting sweater not only enhances your style but also maximizes comfort and complements your body shape.

Opt for designs that work across settings, whether it’s a classic crewneck for casual days, a half-zip for sporty outings, or a cable-knit for a dressier touch. A great sweater should transition with no problem from every location to the next.

Between Style Director Christian Gollayan, who’s spent the past decade covering men’s fashion, and me, who’s tested sweaters, jackets, and everything in between over the past five years, we’ve worn enough knits to fill an entire coat check. Together, we pulled on dozens of sweaters in every fit, fabric, and price point to see which ones actually live up to the hype. We wore them to the office, out to dinner, on weekend errands, and through too many cold commutes. We paid close attention to how each sweater fit (flattering or frumpy?), how it felt against the skin (buttery soft or scratchy mess?), how it held up after a wash, and whether it layered neatly without bulk. After plenty of wear, tear, and mirror checks, we narrowed it down to the sweaters that truly earn their keep—sharp, comfortable, durable, and ready for anything winter throws your way.

The key lies in understanding the different styles of sweaters and pairing them accordingly for various occasions. For a casual, laid-back look that you can wear every day, try a classic crewneck sweater with your go-to pants—perfect for running errands or grabbing coffee with friends. V-neck sweaters are ideal for smart-casual or business-casual settings, whether you're at the office or at dinner, since they layer beautifully over collared shirts. (Zip sweaters also work as such, by the way.)

Cardigan sweaters are easy to dress up: layer a button-down shirt beneath a well-fitted cardigan for a sophisticated, professional-looking appearance, or pair them with khakis and tailored trousers to achieve a preppy look. Similarly, turtlenecks exude refinement and work for cocktail and business-casual attire, easily paired with tailored trousers and blazers for a polished, upscale look. For a more rugged, outdoorsy vibe, opt for a chunky cable knit or fisherman sweater.

#4806. Range Rover is axing its two cheapest SUVs, making way for a new entry-level EV

Range Rover is pulling the plug on its two most affordable models, the Evoque and Velar, as a new entry-level EV steps in.

For decades, the Range Rover name was viewed as a status symbol, mostly used by wealthy buyers, high-powered executives, and even royalty.

That started to change with the launch of the Evoque in 2011 and the Velar in 2017, making the iconic British luxury brand a little more accessible.

In the US, the 2026 Range Rover Evoque starts at $49,900, and the Velar starts at $61,600. That’s considerably less than the Sport and flagship Range Rover SUVs, which start at $83,700 and $107,400, respectively.

Range Rover’s accessible luxury era is reportedly drawing to a close. Martin Limbert, Range Rover’s managing director, confirmed to Autocar that the Evoque and Velar will officially be discontinued, with production set to end in 2027.

While it has no direct replacement planned, the new Range Rover GT will serve as the brand’s new entry-level vehicle.

Range Rover revealed the GT in July, presenting it as the fifth and newest member of the lineup. Unlike the distinct SUV design Range Rover has built the brand on, the GT is a low-slung grand tourer.

The electric GT is “a captivating new expression” of the brand, Range said, describing it as “the most technologically sophisticated” model it’s ever designed.

It’s expected to be among the first vehicles based on JLR’s new EMA platform. Initially, the Range Rover GT will launch as a battery-electric vehicle (BEV), but Range Rover plans to add a full-hybrid (HEV) option later in the lifecycle.

Production of the Range Rover GT is set to begin in the first half of 2027 at JLR’s Halewood, UK plant, following the flagship electric SUV and smaller Sport EV model (shown below).

The Range Rover GT is expected to start at around $90,000 with an EPA range of at least 300 miles when it goes on sale as a 2028 model. In the UK, it will likely be over £75,000 ($100,000).

Range Rover’s flagship electric SUV starts at $140,450 in the US, and the smaller Sport EV will likely be a bit cheaper at around $120,000 to $130,000.

At $90,000, the electric GT isn’t what most would consider an “entry-level” vehicle, but it’s part of Range Rover’s push into higher-end, more profitable models.

#4805. Heart Failure Is Becoming More Common in Adults Under 65, Report Finds

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

An estimated 56 million people worldwide were living with heart failure in 2023, more than double the number in 1990, according to a new Global Burden of Disease (GBD) analysis published September 30 in JAMA Cardiology.

Heart failure is a chronic condition in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body’s needs. Despite its name, heart failure doesn’t mean the heart has stopped beating.

A separate 2026 report from the Heart Failure Society of America (HFSA) found that heart failure contributed to more than 450,000 deaths in the United States in 2023, with particularly sharp increases in mortality among adults under 65.

Approximately 7.7 million U.S. adults (3%) are living with heart failure, according to the HFSA report. That number is projected to rise to 8.7 million by 2030, 10.3 million by 2040, and 11.4 million by 2050.

The GBD researchers said the findings highlight the growing burden of heart failure associated with population growth and aging, as well as the need for prevention and treatment strategies targeting common causes such as ischemic heart disease and hypertension (high blood pressure).

Between 2010 and 2022, heart failure hospitalization rates increased among adults under 65 while declining among those 65 and older. Between 2001 and 2020, estimated heart failure mortality rates more than doubled among adults ages 25 to 44 and nearly doubled among those ages 45 to 64.

“I think we’re seeing the impact of cardiovascular risk factors developing earlier in life. Conditions such as obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and sleep apnea are affecting younger adults at higher rates than in previous generations,” Kevin Shah, MD, Program Director of Heart Failure Outreach at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the analysis, told Healthline.

“When those risk factors are present for decades, they can eventually lead to heart failure at a younger age,” he said.

Amit Blumfield, MD, a cardiologist at Manhattan Cardiology in New York City who was also not involved in the analysis, noted that improvements in early detection may also play a role.

“Our tools to detect early heart failure are also improving with time, and as a result, patients may receive an earlier diagnosis and can hopefully start medical therapy to prevent progression or possibly even reverse the process entirely.”

Heart failure contributed to 452,573 deaths in the United States in 2023, accounting for approximately 14.6% of all deaths that year, according to the HFSA report.

Age-adjusted heart failure mortality rates increased by approximately 37% between 2010 and 2023, with preliminary 2024 data suggesting the upward trend is continuing.

This increase appears to have reversed more than a decade of previous progress in reducing heart failure mortality.

Ischemic heart disease and hypertension were among the most common causes of heart failure in older adults, according to the GBD report. However, the underlying causes varied considerably by age group and region.

Among children and young adults, congenital heart abnormalities and rheumatic heart disease (RHD) were common causes of heart failure. Heart failure associated with alcohol use was most prevalent during middle adulthood.

The analysis also identified regional differences in the underlying causes of heart failure:

The global burden of heart failure is expected to grow as populations age.

While not all cases of heart failure can be prevented, managing certain risk factors can help reduce your risk. These include:

According to Shah, other important steps to help prevent heart failure include maintaining a healthy weight, staying physically active, and managing conditions such as diabetes and high cholesterol.

He added that regular medical care is important because many of these risk factors can be identified and treated long before heart failure develops.

“Heart failure is often treatable and may even be reversible with early diagnosis and treatment. It is important for patients to seek help early if they have concerning symptoms, such as exertional shortness of breath, chest pain, leg swelling, or anything else they’re concerned about. Talk with your doctors early and often,” said Blumfield.

#4804. ‘The Gilded Age’ Star Ben Ahlers and Todd Snyder Know the Power of a Good Uniform

For the label’s latest campaign, the 30-year-old actor takes fall style to Scotland’s Isle of Islay.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

TODD SNYDER makes some of our favorite menswear, and for its latest collaboration, the New York brand crossed the pond to Scotland. The draw? Lagavulin, the distillery that’s been making smoky Scotch whisky on the island of Islay for more than 200 years.

The partnership marks Snyder’s 15th anniversary, with clothes that borrow from Islay’s rugged landscape. Standouts include a brown suede jacket lined in Lagavulin’s own tartan and Fair Isle zip-ups in the earthy shades of the Scottish moors. Pretty great reasons to look forward to sweater weather.

Fronting the campaign is Ben Ahlers. As footman-turned-businessman Jack Trotter on The Gilded Age, the 30-year-old actor knows his way around heritage menswear. Still, these relaxed layers are pretty easy to picture on the streets of New York. We caught up with him about what playing Jack taught him about getting dressed—and which piece he’d bring home.

MEN’S HEALTH: You spend a lot of time in period costumes on The Gilded Age. Has anything from Jack’s wardrobe made its way into how you dress off-screen?

BEN AHLERS: Jack has a consistency to the way that he dresses. As a footman, he had a uniform, and as a young businessman, he has a pretty steady throughline through his looks—a base structure with really well-made clothing and then accents like a tie or a tie pin or a ring that can allow for a sense of creative expression. I find that I like a level of consistency in my own personal dress as well.

More than anything, the greatest benefit of living inside of the clothing that Kasia [Walicka Maimone, the show’s costume designer] and her incredible team make for us every year is this awareness of the way clothes not only make you present to the world but also how they make you feel within them.

MH: Is there a menswear trend from that era you wish more guys would embrace today?

BA: I would love to see some of the creativity come out in menswear and in the accent work, like a tie pin. Some of the tie pins we have on this show are just so well-crafted and specific. The heads of canes the men wore back then also have such an artistry to them, and there aren’t a lot of avenues for that sort of expression in modern menswear. It’d be nice to see that creative voice or risk-taking come through in the subtle accents that we wear in our day-to-day life.

MH: Your role in Death of a Salesman got people talking about your physique. How did you prepare?

BA: For Death of a Salesman, I knew earlier on in the development process that they wanted to go the direction that they did for the top of the show, and so I knew that I was going to be kind of exposed every night. I really tried to go to the gym during the rehearsal process because I knew once we opened the show that it was going to be hard to stay as active—the show was just so draining.

The couple of months up to opening, I really made a practice of five days a week of cross-training, lifting, running, and yoga, and trying to keep my body as nimble and buoyant as possible, because the subject matter and the daily grind of showing up to the theater every day can really take a toll.

During the run, a lot of my focus was on rest, recovery, sauna, cold plunge, diet, stretching, because I’d already built the foundation of the physicality. Throughout the five-month run, it came down to being sure that I was healthy and recovering as best as I could.

MH: What happened between takes on the Todd Snyder shoot that we’d never know from looking at the campaign photos?

BA: Between takes, I had a blast with Boo George, our photographer. He is such a character and one of the best energies on set, and really delivered in the work. The whole crew from Todd Snyder and Lagavulin were so supportive, and it was such a fun little escape for all of us to exist on this island in the most beautiful landscape imaginable.

I really enjoyed getting to know a lot of the locals there. Many of the people there worked at the distillery, and I got to see firsthand how the whisky was actually made. People were so proud to share their culture as well as their craft with the world.

MH: Which piece from the collection would you wear back home in New York, and what would you pair it with?

BA: My favorite piece from the collection is the Todd Snyder x Lagavulin suede stable jacket, inspired by the texture and color of the mossy peat that coats Islay. It’s a perfect fall jacket, and I’d pair it with Todd Snyder’s relaxed barrel jean in khaki, which I think would really pop.

#4802. Meta's Billions Won't Fix Youth Mental Health on Its Own

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

If I had $17 billion dollars from Meta in the settlement of one social media addiction case, I know exactly what I would not do with it. I would not spend it the way states have been spending their opioid settlement money.

Over the past several years, tens of billions of dollars have flowed to states from opioid settlements meant to save lives through prevention, treatment, and recovery. While opioid-related deaths have declined, how much of that decline is attributable to settlement-funded initiatives is unclear. This is a fact researchers partly trace to the glacial pace of spending, fragmented efforts, and a lack of transparency.

Now, states face a smaller-scale version of the same test, this time over youth and social media. In late August, Meta agreed to pay $12.1 billion to resolve a lawsuit brought by 47 states and the District of Columbia that claimed Facebook and Instagram were designed to hook young users at the expense of their mental health. A chunk of that money is earmarked for youth online safety and mental health initiatives and will be paid out over the next ten years, pending court approval. Meta is dangling an additional $5 billion if other major platforms match the restrictions in the settlement.

Meta agreed to numerous product changes, including stronger age verification, parental controls, and an end to overnight use. But few states are relying on that alone, taking matters into their own hands. California, for example, passed bipartisan legislation on September 20th, 2026, banning infinite scrolling and personalized algorithmic feeds for youth under 16.

That said, as a clinical psychologist, Yale professor, and youth mental health expert, I know the devil is in the details, not the celebratory headlines. What gets done with this money, and how quickly, is still an open question. But if states take a few real notes from the opioid settlement, they can handle this one differently.

First, we have to get real. The Meta settlement was an important exercise in accountability for technology companies, but this money will not solve the youth mental health crisis. It can't. Social media is only one thread of a much larger knot of problems affecting youth mental health. While Meta plays a role here, it is our collective responsibility to improve equity in mental health support availability, access, and quality.

Second, one of the clearest critiques of the opioid settlements is the absence of any national requirement that states report where they spend the money. At a minimum, every state receiving Meta settlement funds should publicly share what it funds, what it's learning, and what isn't working, on a recurring timeline. Minnesota runs a public dashboard breaking down settlement spending, and North Carolina requires local governments to report spending annually through a public portal. Beyond spending transparency, with different amounts per state, implementation and outcomes transparency is also key. California, which helped lead the case, stands to receive the largest final payout, in excess of $2 billion. That puts California and other large recipient states in a position to share their implementation strategies, pilot data, and model resources that other states with smaller amounts can use.

States must also be disciplined. With healthcare budgets under pressure from federal Medicaid changes, especially for access to mental health services, the temptation to backfill budget holes is understandable. But this approach is unlikely to produce sustainable change. Even the roughly $56 billion states and localities receiving over 18 years in opioid settlements doesn't come close to covering what's been lost elsewhere, according to published analyses from the Bipartisan Policy Center’s Opioid Crisis Task Force. This money was never going to replace existing investment, only add to it. That's why at least a dozen states have written explicit restrictions into law against using opioid settlement funds to backfill existing budgets, and states handling the Meta settlement should adopt that restriction from day one.

Finally (for now), young people must be included in whatever gets built on their behalf from these dollars. Their lived experience is vital expertise, and its absence is a documented missed opportunity in the opioid settlements. According to reports, only about 7 percent of people on opioid settlement advisory committees nationally had lived experience for the crisis they were advising on. Alternatively, Washington state required at least four members with lived experience to be appointed members to the settlement committee and compensated for their work. States building out Meta settlement advisory structures should build from this model. Implementation of any solutions is certain to be more successful when young people, their communities, and priorities are centered.

I don't have $12 billion settlement dollars, and neither does any single state on its own. But every state that's about to receive a piece of this Meta settlement has more control over what happens next than the opioid settlements ever gave states credit for exercising. The difference this time isn't the dollar amount. It's whether we treat the last decade of settlement spending as a cautionary tale or as a blueprint we already have in hand.

#4801. VisionQuest Reveals Wanda Maximoff’s Return in Avengers: Doomsday and Hallelujah for That

Elizabeth Olsen’s return is a major revelation.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

The following story contains spoilers for VisionQuest.

LIKE WandaVision AND Agatha All Along before it, VisionQuest turned out to be among the best Marvel projects to be released in the post-Endgame era. And given that the series was billed as the conclusion to the trilogy that those prior two shows set up, that should come as no surprise. While many Marvel Cinematic Universe movies and shows in the last five years have struggled to figure out what works and what doesn’t—and what manages to resonate with audiences over time—these shows, released over the course of a nearly six-year span, have clearly understood that the recipe for success is pretty simple: a slightly raised concept, and some characters people really love.

VisionQuest took a formula that felt like something of a hybrid of what made the other two shows successful and rode it. Where WandaVision had a super high concept (Wanda turning her world into a surreal series of sitcom references), returning stars (both Elizabeth Olsen and Paul Bettany led the show), and new characters people became obsessed with (Kathryn Hahn’s Agatha), Agatha All Along then introduced the idea of bringing in a vital new character in Wanda and Vision’s son Billy (Joe Locke) to go along with the returning Agatha.

VisionQuest splits the atom by pairing Bettany with a returning James Spader as Ultron (truly fantastic throughout) and introducing Ruaridh Mollica as Tommy, Wanda and Vision’s other superpowered son. The show’s consistently strong, surprising, and well-paced writing from showrunner Terry Matalas—to go along with fun new characters like the Paladin (Todd Stashwick) and E.D.I.T.H. (Emily Hampshire)—made it an easy, fun, watchable hit. And it helped that in the end, it came with a punch.

The show continued to expand on Vision becoming human, something Bettany has proven to be brilliant at during the course of his time in the MCU, but it also gave layers to Spader’s Ultron, proving that the franchise can allow some of its iconic villains to stick around and play in shades of moral gray.

By the end of the show, Vision, Tommy, and Billy have made it through the adventure, discovered themselves, and reunited as the family unit we’ve long known they were meant to be. There was just one lingering question: Where’s mom?

VisionQuest asks the question near the end. Elizabeth Olsen’s Wanda Maximoff was the most popular character (and briefly became one of the best villains) in the MCU in the aftermath of Avengers: Endgame; WandaVision was a massive smash, hitting during the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic and becoming the closest thing to water cooler talk material that anyone could get at the time. Olsen’s performance, nominated for an Emmy, was one of the most important reasons why.

She took a more sinister arc in the following year’s Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, and—spoiler alert—appeared to be “dead” at the end of the movie. Which puts a serious wrinkle into the possibility of her reuniting with her robotic husband and immaculately conceived sons.

But this is the Marvel Cinematic Universe, and we’re talking about stories based off of comic books. There’s always a way.

Of course she is! Wanda Maximoff is one of the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s most beloved characters, and Elizabeth Olsen’s performance as her is truly fantastic. You didn’t think Kevin Feige would leave her alone beneath a mountain, did you?

Sure, it’s been more than four years since we last saw the Scarlet Witch at the end of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, but as the credits scene for VisionQuest (likely a moment taken right out of next month’s Avengers: Doomsday) shows us: She’s back. Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.) picks up the bit of mountain she was crushed underneath, and her eyes rocket open in a Jon Snow–esque awakening. “Scarlet Witch, awaken,” Doom says. “Your power will be mine.”

It’s not hard to read into what’s going on here. It’s clear that in Doomsday, Doom is recruiting from some of our existing and most powerful Marvel heroes in an attempt to fuel his own takeover of the world. In the 2015 Secret Wars comic, Doom saves the universe from destruction after incursions (the collision of parallel universes) threaten to destroy everything; the result finds unexpected allyships as Doom takes his place as God Emperor. In that story, Doom’s second-in-command is Doctor Strange… someone we’ve already seen have quite the experience with Wanda (in Multiverse of Madness). Will they wind up allied once again in Doomsday?

The news of Wanda’s return also comes as we learn that her on-screen hubby will also be in Doomsday. “I got to hang out with Paul Bettany, who I love,” Anthony Mackie said in a recent interview, spilling some of the beans.

If VisionQuest was the conclusion of the WandaVision trilogy—and a darn good one—it sounds like Doomsday could feature a full-on Wanda and Vision reunion. And what Marvel fan who’s been along for this ride (and stuck it through to this point) wouldn’t be excited for that? Let’s get the family back together, shall we?
