#4800. Ford Fathom EV pickup prices will range from $28,350 to the high $30Ks

Ford’s upcoming Fathom electric pickup will be among the most affordable EVs in the US, starting at $28,350. Even pricier trims will start at under $40,000.

After announcing the name of its new midsize electric pickup this summer, Ford said the Fathom will start at just $28,350 for the standard-range model.

Even with the $1,595 delivery fee, prices will start at under $30,000. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week, CEO Jim Farley said the Fathom, Ford’s first vehicle off the Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform, remains on track to launch in Q4 2027.

Last Tuesday, a day before earnings, Farley said he had the chance to test-drive a prototype and that it “completely blew me away.”

The 0 to 60 mph, huge room inside, and the hands-free, ADAS experience was like “something I’ve never experienced,” Farley told investors.

Ford’s CEO added that the Fathom is a “breakthrough product” that’s highly capable and affordable. The MSRP under $30,000 and low cost of ownership, Farley said, is perfect for today’s market.

The electric pickup will use a zonal electrical architecture and a 48-volt system to cut costs. It will also offer bidirectional charging, enabling it to power your home to save on energy costs or during an outage.

When asked how the company plans to upsell the Fathom beyond the $28,350 starting price, Andrew Frick, president of Ford Model e, offered some insight.

“The starting price of $28,350 is just that,” Frick said. “We’ll have a range that goes to the high $30,000 range. And we’ll have a couple of different offerings within that,” he explained.

Frick said it’s too soon to share more about the offerings themselves at this point, and more details will come closer to launch.

According to Farley, the embedded Apple Maps is a “game changer” for any EV, but especially for a vehicle starting under $30,000.

“That is going to be the most exciting upsell opportunity,” Farley said, “it’s really the long-term subscription and digital experience for the customer.”

Apple Maps will be directly integrated into the navigation system. All Fathom models will be BlueCruise-capable for hands-free driving with standard Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

We still haven’t seen the interior, but Ford claims the Fathom has a “large touchscreen display” with easy-to-use navigation.

I almost feel like the Fathom will be utilized similarly to how the Maverick is utilized and possibly become a big seller as well. It seems well suited for a small business work vehicle as well with fuel savings by going electric to add to the appeal.

The midsize electric pickup will offer more interior space than a Toyota RAV4, and that’s not including the frunk (front trunk) or truck bed. Ford also said the Fathom will cost less to own over five years than a three-year-old used Tesla Model Y.

We also know the Fathom will have an NACS port after a prototype was caught at a Tesla Supercharger a few months ago.

Ford is set to open preorders in early 2027, with an official launch expected in the fourth quarter of 2027.

#4799. Viola Davis Says Shingles Pain Was a ‘9 Out of 10’: How It Changed Her Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, and Tony Award-winning actress and producer Viola Davis was 50 years old and at the height of her career when she developed shingles.

“All of a sudden, I got a rash in the middle of traveling and juggling [back-to-back] movies that started in the middle of my stomach [and] wrapped around my back,” she told Healthline. “And the pain was definitely at a 9 out of 10.”

Focused on work, Davis didn’t see a doctor right away. Her symptoms eventually subsided but later returned on her upper back.

“That is when I was like, ‘Oh, my goodness, I just got bitten by a poisonous spider,” said Davis. “It felt like really bad nerve pain…then someone mentioned the word shingles.”

After seeing a doctor, Davis learned she had shingles, which is caused by the same virus responsible for chickenpox. She also learned that the risk increases with age as the immune system naturally weakens.

“It can also lead to herpetic neuralgia, lifelong pain that can result from a shingles outbreak,” Robyn Liu, MD, member of the board of directors at the American Academy of Family Physicians, told Healthline.

Shingles can affect daily life, including work and sleep.

“Many people don’t realize that shingles can be associated with nerve pain, and for some, that pain can last for months or even years after the rash has resolved due to potential long-term complications,” Jennifer Caudle, DO, family medicine physician and associate professor at Rowan University School of Osteopathic Medicine, told Healthline.

Nearly one in three people in the U.S. develops shingles in their lifetime.

“Anyone who has had chickenpox can get it, but the risk goes up as we age,” said Liu.

After learning about shingles, Davis said she realized that she could no longer ignore her body.

“You just cannot. I mean, I know that people say it at nauseam, but, for me, it meant slowing down,” she said. “But then the shingles slowed me down…even though I was getting up, I was working out, [the] pain and the sluggishness was awful.”

Now 61, Davis has teamed up with GSK for its “Shingles, actually” campaign to raise awareness about shingles.

“[I’m] sending the message out there for women to really honor themselves and honor their bodies,” she said. “Their bodies literally speak. They’re the other character in their lives.”

After her experience with shingles, Davis began scheduling regular annual checkups.

“Before that time, I did absolutely go to my doctor, but only when it was absolutely necessary, you know, to get my colonoscopy, get my mammogram, but I never went if something felt odd,” said Davis.

Now, whenever she feels off, she doesn’t hesitate to see her doctor. She makes it a point to be honest with them about what’s going on with her body, and she is not shy about asking questions.

“I feel that it’s my job. It’s what I owe myself, and not only [do] I owe myself, it’s what I owe my daughter, it’s what I owe my husband, it’s what I owe my elderly mom, who is in advanced dementia [and] I take care of her,” Davis said.

Caudle stressed the importance of bringing questions to your doctor.

“That’s what we’re here for. Sometimes patients ​tell me they don’t realize they can ask questions or introduce a topic that their healthcare provider didn’t bring up first,” she said. “But a simple question like, ‘Am I at risk for shingles?’ can be a great place to begin.”

Davis has made stress reduction a priority. When she developed shingles, she was juggling an intense workload and adjusting to life as a new mom after adopting her daughter.

“I was someone who just ignored stress,” said Davis. “[When] we meet each other, it becomes a contest: Who can work through their stress the best? I felt like I had to strike while the iron was hot.”

Today, Davis makes stress reduction a priority through activities such as spraying her pillows with lavender, taking Epsom salt baths, meditating, going to therapy, exercising, spending time outdoors, using vagus nerve stimulation, and connecting with family and friends.

“It’s like I overdo it now because I feel like I have to overdo it in order to compete with my schedule. But that’s what I owe myself,” Davis said.

Still, her profession can be intense and time consuming due to shooting and promotional schedules. She still makes time to de-stress and focuses on projects that bring her joy.

“Your career is only as important as how much you enjoy it; how much it adds to your life,” said Davis. “[For] me, it used to be something that I felt defined my worth. I don’t feel like it defines my worth now…I feel that I’m already worthy… I was born worthy. That’s how I see it.”

Vaccination is the best way to protect against shingles, Liu said. The shingles vaccine is more than 90% effective at preventing the disease.

“For children, that protection begins with the chickenpox vaccine, which can be given along with other routine childhood immunizations. Preventing chickenpox also lowers the risk of developing shingles later in life,” she said.

Liu recommends two doses of the shingles vaccine for adults 50 and older, as well as adults 19 and older with weakened immune systems.

“Some patients may have more questions because side effects can be more noticeable than with other vaccines, so it’s important to understand the tradeoff: short-term discomfort from the vaccine versus the risk of lasting complications from shingles,” said Liu.

Side effects may include headache or redness, swelling, itching, and soreness where the shot was given.

“I tell my patients that these reactions are common and usually clear up within a day or two. They’re a normal sign that your body is building protection,” said Liu.

#4798. GM is recalling more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs over a brake software defect

General Motors (GM) issued a recall affecting more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs because a software glitch can cause a temporary loss of braking.

The recall comes after a 2024 Cadillac Lyriq ran into a garage (at a low speed). On April 10, 2026, a GM tech expert submitted a report to GM’s Speak Up for Safety (SUFS) program for review.

After internal testing, GM was able to replicate the glitch, similar to a recall it issued in 2024. GM said the issue stems from a software glitch with the brake system control module (BSCM) that can cause a temporary loss of braking while driving under certain conditions.

When drivers lightly tap the brakes during a sharp turn and the vehicle hits a bump, the software’s slip calculation may misinterpret wheel movement.

In some instances, it can lead to a temporary loss of braking. The glitch only affects pAWD vehicles, including certain Cadillac Lyriq, Celestiq, Vistiq, and Chevy Blazer EV.

In a letter sent to the NHTSA on October 29, GM said the recall impacted 67,380 vehicles total, including certain:

According to documents filed with the NHTSA, GM found 24 field complaints related to the issue. Of these, 20 involved minor accidents, and two involved allegations of minor injuries.

The complaints were received between February 24, 2024, and June 11, 2026. GM said it has implemented software corrections in production over the past few months.

GM will update the BSCM software via an over-the-air (OTA) update or through a dealer, free of charge.

Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed out on December 14, 2026. In the meantime, you can contact Cadillac’s customer service at 1-800-333-4223 or Chevrolet’s customer service at 1-800-222-1020. GM’s recall number is N262570900.

You can also contact the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration Hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit the nhtsa.gov website for more information. The NHTSA campaign number is 26V717.

#4797. Unblending: the IFS Approach to Learning

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

Artists, writers, and musicians shape experience and hold the interest of an audience by introducing things that are unresolved, promise resolution, and offer hints along the way. A crime novel asks whodunnit; music creates gripping tension and aesthetic chills; plays and movies pose and ponder problems; paintings invite, and so on. Artists know that we stay with what we do not yet understand and we feel thrilled at discovery.

The journey from not knowing to understanding by way of curiosity and exploration is called an epistemic arc. Sometimes we’re captured by a puzzle and we understand gradually, sometimes the epiphany comes quickly. In either case, that aha! moment signifies the soft thump of the tiny dopamine hit that culminates an exploration. But to reach this moment, we have to be open to our existing ideas about identity and relationships being incomplete.

From the Internal Family Systems (IFS) perspective, we all have parts. We may see, hear, sense, or feel them. They present at different ages and, often, act in ways that don’t fit the current moment because they’re stuck in the past. When a part takes over and we see the world through its eyes, expecting what it expects, IFS says the part is blended. This can cause epochal (and often epical) cognitive confusion. Who am I? How old am I? Why do I think this way, feel this way, act this way? In contrast, when the part separates, or unblends, we can notice and relate to it. When we pay attention, parts unblend and we can get into relationship with them, ask what they fear, and meet their need for validation, connection, and love.

IFS therapy sessions follow the epistemic arc. Clients arrive in therapy puzzled by their behavior (Why do I pull away when I want connection?), but wedded to some familiar certainty, like I am bad, or no one can be trusted. The IFS inquiry invites them to be curious about their behavior and beliefs, which almost always leads to formative experiences.

The phenomena IFS calls blending and unblending illustrate a paradox at the heart of subjective experience. We can be a part or we can be with a part. When we are a part, we think, feel, and act like that part, but when we are with a part, we have choices. If, for example, a blended part expects rejection, we are likely to hear silence as rejection and view a later offer of help as untrustworthy or dangerous. The part is too afraid to try something new and our present remains a perpetual repetition of the past. But the opposite is true as well. If the part unblends and we are with it, we can explore its fear and challenge distorted and inaccurate beliefs. I can feel and hear a part that expects to be rejected, but since I’ll be okay whatever happens, I can afford to try something new.

An IFS session follows an epistemic arc, a process we can understand through the lens of neuroscience and predictive processing, which says the brain builds a world model in childhood and then, conserving energy, predicts the familiar. Ideally, the brain updates its predictive model in response to prediction errors, but fear and negative identity beliefs can get in the way. A person who expects rejection and withdraws will not get a chance to learn how others might respond if they were to stay present and express a need.

From the predictive processing perspective, blended parts block the brain’s ability to learn. In contrast, unblending clears the runway. IFS aims to persuade parts to unblend. Our compassion and respect invite engagement, parts acknowledge us, and mutual curiosity sustains investigation. Once parts feel valid, legitimate, lovable, and connected, we feel—and are—more open to experiences that disconfirm old beliefs. Expectations relax, other information gains influence, and the brain’s world model updates.

An IFS inquiry doesn’t push for change. Pressing a part to step aside or move quickly can confirm an expectation that its wishes and limits will be disregarded. Patience conveys concern and respect, and is valuable in itself. The message to parts is: You can hesitate and stay connected. You can express fear and be heard. IFS invites all parts to take time exploring their fears and needs. Faster? Slower? You’re the boss.

If you want to discover the logic behind some apparently inexplicable behavior of your own, encourage your parts to unblend. Try noticing them and getting curious. You might have a protective part that keeps everyone happy because it expects disagreements to end relationships. Or you might have a part that withdraws because it anticipates unreasonable—or unmeetable—demands. Your protectors can explain the rationale for their beliefs and behaviors. Your job is to listen with an open heart.

As you listen, you can validate protective choices but also challenge negative identity conclusions (I’m worthless… something is wrong with me). You can offer to replace old survival tactics with better options. You don’t have to undo the past, convince transgressors to take it back, or prove your worth. The part you protect is valid, lovable, and—if you let me help—loved. Your protectors may need to move toward this invitation slowly, starting with a question they can now tolerate asking: Can things be different? But those aha! moments, when they come, are transformative.

Schwartz, R.C. & Sweezy, M. (2020). Internal Family Systems Therapy (2nd ed.). New York NY: Guilford Press.

#4795. First: Volvo CE Electric equipment does the work, without disturbing the wildlife

For the first time, electric equipment assets are being put to work in the National Wildlife Refuge System, where a battery-powered, zero-emission ECR25 Electric compact excavator and L25 Electric compact wheel loader made by Volvo CE are making the wild more accessible to everyone.

Construction work isn’t exactly welcome in the wilderness – between diesel exhaust, engine noises, and the constant rumble of heavy machinery, even a relatively small project can have a big impact on the native wildlife. To minimize that impact, US Fish and Wildlife Service is turning to Volvo CE and its compact excavators and wheel loaders to get the job done, building out a new, ADA accessible trail in Virginia’s Occoquan Bay National Wildlife Refuge.

“We are excited to partner with the US Fish and Wildlife Service on this project to demonstrate Volvo’s commitment to lowering emissions and working to build the future we all want and need,” said Dr. Ray Gallant, VP of Product Management and Productivity, Volvo CE. “Projects like the one at the Occoquan Bay National Wildlife Refuge give a glimpse of how electric machines can create a more climate-friendly future for the construction industry.”

The refuge is home to a diverse array of grasslands, wetlands, and woods that attract red foxes, painted turtles, osprey, river otters, and countless other rarely seen species – and the ADA accessible path being laid down by the L25 Electric compact wheel loader will allow wheelchair-bound visitors to travel a half-mile-long trail around one of the pond. Meanwhile, the ECR25 Electric compact excavator will be digging trenches to improve drainage from the pond and helping to place a viewing platform that extends out over the water.

Keeping the machines running is a portable EV ARC solar-powered charging system from Beam Global that’s designed to drive down the project’s carbon footprint even further.

#4794. PMOS, Formerly PCOS, May Be Associated with Alzheimer's Disease Risk

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), formerly known as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), has been linked to changes in brain function and cognition that may overlap with those seen in Alzheimer’s disease.

However, a review published October 13 in the Journal of the Endocrine Society suggests that metabolic conditions commonly associated with PMOS, rather than PMOS itself, may help explain a potential link to Alzheimer’s disease and dementia risk.

“Researchers are exploring whether some metabolic conditions commonly seen in women with PMOS, such as insulin resistance, obesity, type 2 diabetes, [and] elevated cholesterol, could play a role in dementia, since these are already known risk factors for cognitive decline,” Yesika Garcia, MD, board certified endocrinologist with Medical Offices of Manhattan, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline.

“In other words, any potential connection may be related to these underlying metabolic issues rather than PMOS itself. I think it’s important to clarify that an association does not mean causation,” she added.

The researchers searched PubMed for studies published through 2025 examining brain structure and function, cognitive performance, biomarkers associated with neurodegenerative diseases, and dementia risk in people with PMOS.

Because PMOS is a newer term, the researchers searched for studies using both PMOS and PCOS.

The review identified studies suggesting that people with PMOS may experience mild differences in certain cognitive abilities, including:

Some brain imaging studies using MRI and PET scans identified differences in brain structure and function among people with PMOS. Researchers also observed hormonal changes associated with differences in gray matter.

Some studies identified elevated biomarkers associated with Alzheimer’s disease in people with PMOS. These findings appeared to overlap with metabolic changes seen in type 2 diabetes, particularly those associated with obesity and insulin resistance.

The researchers also found that neurological differences were less pronounced when people with PMOS were compared with metabolically healthy control groups, suggesting that associated metabolic conditions may play an important role in these findings.

Overall, the review suggests that metabolic conditions associated with PMOS may contribute to changes in brain health, although more research is needed to determine whether PMOS independently affects Alzheimer’s disease or dementia risk.

“I think we need to be careful about drawing conclusions too early. The research raises some good questions, but it doesn’t prove that PCOS [PMOS] causes Alzheimer’s disease,” said Dung Trinh, MD, internist, of MemorialCare Medical Group and Chief Medical Officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“What it does reinforce is how important metabolic health may be when it comes to protecting our brains as we get older,” he added.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who also wasn’t involved in the study, agreed. She also added that more attention and research need to be given to PMOS, brain changes, and future risks of dementia.

There are various ways that PMOS and dementia may share pathways and overlap, according to the researchers. Some of these shared pathways include:

Trinh explained that insulin resistance may be one of the most important connections between PMOS and dementia.

Although insulin is commonly associated with diabetes and blood sugar regulation, it also plays an important role in brain function. When insulin signaling doesn’t work properly, it may interfere with how brain cells use energy, potentially contributing to problems with memory and thinking over time.

Chronic inflammation, which can occur in people with PMOS, may also play a role in Alzheimer’s disease, Trinh told Healthline.

“Researchers are looking at how these metabolic changes may affect amyloid and tau, two proteins associated with Alzheimer’s. Some brain imaging studies have even found differences in brain structure and function among women with PCOS [PMOS],” he said.

Ross added that elevated androgen levels, which are common in people with PMOS, may also play a role in dementia risk.

“An important distinction is that these risk factors are not present in every woman with PMOS, and having PMOS does not automatically mean someone will experience cognitive decline,” cautioned Garcia.

Garcia noted that many of the dementia risk factors associated with PMOS are modifiable.

“Regular exercise, including both cardiovascular activity and strength training, can improve insulin sensitivity, help with weight management, and support cardiovascular and brain health,” she added.

“A Mediterranean-style diet, with plenty of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, healthy fats, and lean sources of protein, is a reasonable place to start,” he said.

Managing blood sugar, cholesterol, and blood pressure is also important, Trinh and Garcia noted.

“Medication, like metformin, can also improve insulin resistance, which may further reduce the risk of dementia,” Ross added.

Getting adequate sleep, avoiding smoking, and staying mentally and socially active are additional ways to support long-term brain health, Garcia told Healthline.

“For someone with PCOS [PMOS], I would encourage regular visits with their healthcare provider to monitor metabolic health and address problems early,” said Trinh.

“While we cannot say that these interventions specifically prevent dementia in women with PMOS, we know they benefit overall metabolic and cardiovascular health, which are closely connected to brain health,” explained Garcia.

#4793. Could Your GLP-1s Make You Blind? Here’s What to Make of the FDA’s Latest Notice.

For years, there have been rumblings and even research about a rare but serious condition that’s been linked to taking a GLP-1 medication. Now, the Food and Drug Administration is doing something about it.

The FDA just released a drug safety communication to warn patients and healthcare providers about the potential increased risk of developing non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) when you take a GLP-1 medication. NAION is a rare condition that can lead to vision loss in one eye, and it can be permanent.

Again, this isn't the first time concerns have been raised about the risk of NAION. But it is the first time the FDA has issued a warning about it.

Given that up to 11 percent of Americans currently take a GLP-1 for weight loss, this news stands to impact a lot of people. How concerned should you be if you're one of them? Eye experts and a doctor who prescribes GLP-1s break it down.

Meet the experts: Joseph Rizzo, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear, a member of the Mass General Brigham healthcare system; Bavand Youssefzadeh, DO, an ophthalmologist with Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles and a cofounder of the Global LASIK and Cataract Institute; and Mir Ali, MD, the medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California.

The FDA's notice is designed to flag the potential risk of NAION to people who use GLP-1s. The FDA also notes that the agency will require all manufacturers of GLP-1 medications to add information about the risk of NAION to the Warnings and Precautions section of their labels.

"Patients and caregivers should be aware of a potential increased risk of NAION, a rare condition that can result in acute, painless, decreased vision in one eye, including permanent vision loss, with GLP-1 RA use," the notice reads.

The agency cited a 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology as well as its own meta-analyses and retrospective cohort study in the notice. They also noted that “NAION cases have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 RA products.”

However, the complication remains rare: incidents from the FDA’s meta-analysis were just 6.4 events per 100,000 per year for patients using the medications.

The warning is just that—a warning to patients and physicians that this could happen, explains Joseph Rizzo, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear, a member of the Mass General Brigham healthcare system. "Most outcome-related issues in medicine should be thought of as being probabilistic—there is a certain chance that events can occur," he says. "This warning indicates that the FDA has reason to believe, at least at this time, that the probability of NAION occurring is higher in patients who take GLP-1 RA drugs."

But Dr. Rizzo stresses that there's no evidence that these drugs cause NAION—just that there's a link.

So…why issue a warning if it's not proven that GLP-1s cause NAION and it's so rare? "The severity of a complication matters alongside its frequency," says Bavand Youssefzadeh, DO, an ophthalmologist with Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles and a cofounder of the Global LASIK and Cataract Institute. "Even a rare risk deserves attention when it can permanently affect vision." The warning is likely designed to give healthcare providers a heads-up that it could be NAION if a patient has symptoms, he explains.

"It's their duty to report any adverse effects, just so people are aware of them," says Mir Ali, MD, the medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California.

While NAION is scary, doctors say it's important to put the data in perspective. "It's extremely rare, but it can happen," Dr. Ali says. Given how much GLP-1s can help with blood sugar management, weight loss, and downstream health effects, Dr. Ali says that the risk of NAION is "not a reason not to seek these medications."

Dr. Rizzo agrees. "I essentially never discourage the general use of GLP-1 RA drugs," he says. "Ultimately, the risk-to-benefit assessment must be decided by the patient, but physicians should provide sufficient information to the patients to better inform their decisions."

People should stay aware of the risk without panicking, Dr. Youssefzadeh says. "It's also worth remembering that the people most likely to be prescribed these drugs—people with diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnea—already carry a higher baseline risk for NAION, so the risk isn't starting from zero," he adds.

Korin Miller is a seasoned freelance writer specializing in general wellness, sexual health and relationships, and lifestyle trends, with work appearing in Men’s Health, Women’s Health, Everyday Health, Food & Wine, and more. She has a master’s degree from American University and lives by the beach.

#4792. What Is "Emotional Regulation" for Parents?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

Before I had children, I thought it would be hard and fun. I expected to be tired. I expected to have less time for myself. But I never expected to be so challenged by the emotions I had, like guilt and anger. And I was not equipped with the knowledge, skills, and tools I needed to navigate my emotions as a parent.

The emotional lives of parents are complex and important, especially for mental health. That’s because parenting evokes some of our biggest and most complicated emotions.

Having “negative” emotions towards children doesn’t mean we’re bad. It just means we have emotions, as all humans do. And contrary to what we may think, core emotions like anger, sadness, and fear are not under conscious control.

Emotional regulation refers to a calm and balanced nervous system. When we are regulated, we can experience our emotions, deal with them effectively, and relate in connected and attuned ways. When we are regulated, we don’t feel threatened by our children’s behaviors or emotions. Our capacity for compassion and curiosity is enabled—the qualities we need as parents.

Nevertheless, as parents, we are regularly thrown off balance because our children evoke strong feelings.

When I was young, I thought the only way to feel calmer was to get rid of my emotions by pushing them away or distracting myself. This is how many people think because we aren’t taught about emotions and how to be with them in healthy ways.

The goal isn’t to become a parent who never gets angry, frustrated, afraid, or overwhelmed. That’s simply not possible because emotions are hardwired into the brain and body and cannot be eradicated. Pushing emotions down dysregulates the nervous system, stressing the mind and body, which worsens anxiety and depression.

A better goal is to learn about emotions, develop emotional awareness, and ultimately learn how to process emotions. For example, being able to recognize and name the anger, fear, shame, sadness, or disappointment that you’re feeling begins the process of regulation, helping us feel and function better.

That’s a very different approach than ignoring your emotions and simply telling yourself to “calm down.”

One very effective way to understand and work with difficult emotions is through the Change Triangle, an emotional roadmap I adapted from AEDP psychotherapy and the academic literature on emotions.

Initially, the Change Triangle helps by teaching us the ABCs of emotions and how they work in the mind and body. As a result of this newfound emotional education, we can become less fearful of our emotions and more curious about what is happening inside us.

When something upsets you, you can turn inward and find where you are on the Change Triangle. You will find yourself in one of four places on the Change Triangle.

Protective defenses and inhibitory emotions obscure deeper core emotions such as anger, sadness, fear, disgust, or joy. Naming and validating our core emotions opens the door to regulation. The ultimate objective whenever we get dysregulated is to work our way back down the Change Triangle, moving from defenses back to the openhearted state of the authentic self, which is a regulated state.

Next time you get upset, instead of immediately reacting, pause and ask yourself:

This kind of curiosity creates space between feeling and action. And that space can change how we parent.

Imagine your eight-year-old refuses to turn off the television. You feel your body tighten. Your heart beats faster. You hear yourself thinking, Why won’t this kid ever listen to me?

When you listen to the anger and get curious about why you’re angry and what you need, you might notice something underneath the anger: I’m exhausted. I feel powerless. I need cooperation.

The situation hasn’t magically changed. Your child still needs to turn off the television. But now you’re responding from greater awareness rather than simply discharging the emotion.

You can set the same boundary without making your child the target of your unprocessed feelings. That’s emotional regulation.

Instead of yelling, gently take the remote from your child, turn off the TV, and tell your child calmly, “TV time is over.”

We spend enormous amounts of time teaching children about their emotions. We tell them to use their words. We teach them to take deep breaths. We encourage them to name their feelings and calm down. But parents need these skills, too. In fact, one of the most powerful ways to teach children emotional intelligence is to develop our own emotional intelligence. When parents learn to understand and process their emotions, they become better able to help their children do the same.

Damasio, A. R. (1999). The feeling of what happens: Body and emotion in the making of consciousness. Harcourt Brace.

Edler, K., & Valentino, K. (2024). Parental self-regulation and engagement in emotion socialization: A systematic review. Psychological Bulletin, 150(2), 154–191.

Fosha, D. (2000). The transforming power of affect: A model for accelerated change. Basic Books.

Hendel, H. J. (2018). It's not always depression: Working the Change Triangle to listen to the body, discover core emotions, and connect to your authentic self. Random House.

Hendel, H.J., & Fraga, J. (2025). Parents have feelings, too: A guide to navigating your emotions so you and your family can thrive. Alcove Press.

Holzman, J. B. W., Kennedy, S. M., Grassie, H. L., & Ehrenreich-May, J. (2022). Associations between dispositional parental emotion regulation and youth mental health symptoms: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Clinical Psychology Review, 95, Article 102174.

#4791. High gas prices are pumping up used EV sales: these are FLYING off the lot

A new car affordability crisis and punishing gas prices are driving an unprecedented number of used car buyers to consider going electric, and that increased demand without a corresponding increase in supply means these used EVs are flying off dealer lots.

Days on the lot. That’s dealer-speak for the average number of days a given vehicle typically sits in inventory before finding a buyer. That’s critically important to dealers, since the vehicles on their lots are commonly financed through something called floorplan credit, and every additional day a car spends on a dealer’s lot can mean another day of interest payments and another day closer to a curtailment. Days on the lot can be even more important to dealers when it comes to cars owned outright, as well, as the dealers can have significant cash tied up in vehicles they’ve purchased outright, and every day those cars sit is another day that money isn’t working for them elsewhere.

That’s what makes this month’s fastest-selling used EVs particularly interesting, because these used EVs aren’t just selling fast for electric vehicles – they’re selling fast, period.

Dealer news sources Automotive News and Cox Automotive report that the average new car spent 82 days on the lot in October, with a 75-day target being an industry-wide benchmark. At the same time, the Audi Q4 Sportback e-tron Quattro with its 258-mile EPA-estimated range is turning in just 29.8 days. (!)

That Audi’s not alone. In a recently-released vehicle pricing study, iSeeCars reported that the Toyota BZ4x, Lexus RZ300e, Honda Prologue, and Borrás-family favorite Polestar 2 are all turning in an average of 35 days or less, with the BMW i4, iX, Kia EV6, and Chevrolet Equinox EV just a day or two behind.

“The results reveal a market where EVs are appreciating in average asking price much faster than other drivetrains, while also spending less time waiting for buyers,” said iSeeCars Executive Analyst Karl Brauer, who found that average transaction prices for EVs rose 9.8% last month as ICE-powered vehicles stayed steady, rising just 0.3%. “Hybrids are experiencing moderate improvements in price and selling speed, while gasoline-powered vehicles have seen their selling times increase,” he adds, “despite relatively stable prices.”

@Jo Borras , you forgot to mention about one more factor (besides: "A new car affordability crisis and punishing gas prices..."). Back in September last year there was still electric vehicle tax credits in the United States that has ended on September 30, 2025.

Used electric vehicles averaged a price of $32,533 in September 2026, up $2,896 from the $29,637 ATP recorded a year earlier.

#4790. The Surprising Staying Power of Adam Sandler’s Big Daddy

A24’s Club Kid makes the case for the comedy’s unlikely legacy—and social relevance—in 2026.

EARLY ON IN Jordan Firstman’s dramedy Club Kid, druggie-with-a-heart-of-gold Peter has to shepherd his surprise 10-year-old son through an apartment party. Despite knowing each other for just a few hours, the club promoter and his child hold hands as he guides the way through the bacchanal. It’s a metaphor—what isn’t these days?—and it’s also kind of a recreation of a key sequence in Adam Sandler’s Big Daddy.

In that movie, 5-year-old Julian “Frankenstein” McGrath (played by young Dylan and Cole Sprouse) holds his hand aloft before he steps off the sidewalk, looking for help from his newfound father.

Replace McDonald’s breakfasts with coke and ketamine (plus a Charlie Kirk reference), and A24’s Club Kid is the clear heir apparent to the 1999 Sandler comedy. I’m far from the first person to make the connection. IndieWire’s David Ehrlich’s first-impression response was to ask: “What if A24 made a gay Big Daddy?”

It may seem like an odd movie for a brand like A24 to mirror. However, Big Daddy is somehow the film from the peak Sandler run that has had the longest shelf life. In fact, it may be the late ’90s–early 2000s comedy with the best depiction of the 2026 way of life. For better—or for worse.

Despite the fact that it was a hit at the box office, Big Daddy was reviled at the time of its release, even winning Sandler a Razzie Award for Worst Actor.

And, sure, it’s not the most elegant film—with its near-incessant Hooters jabs and Rob Schneider’s catastrophic accent—but still, it’s managed to stick around in the public consciousness for nearly 30 years. And it’s not just Ehrlich and I who think so.

“I particularly loved Big Daddy. That was my number one,” Paul Thomas Anderson said on an episode of The Bill Simmons Podcast in 2017 when asked about casting Sandler in his film Punch-Drunk Love. “It was a little bit more polished; it was able to be sincere and [mix in] the crazy fucking dirty shit that Sandler likes to do and got the mix really right.”

In Club Kid, promoter Peter (Firstman, who wrote, directed, and stars) somehow ends up in charge of a precocious kid while flailing in both romance and his career. Peter, like Sonny, has to instantly shift his lifestyle, one that only functions when you have little to care for, including yourself. Both protagonists need an act of God to abandon their early-30s doldrums.

And honestly, it’s a sentiment that a lot of people my age (including myself) can relate to.

At the tail end of October, The New York Times published a story (which, thankfully, my parents haven’t sent to me yet) titled “Can’t Afford a Home. Can’t Afford a Baby. Can’t Afford Life. This Is 30.” The gist is that millennials feel burned out now that they know they’re unlikely to achieve the luxuries earlier generations enjoyed.

“In the past, the idea was that you would check all these boxes by 30, give or take. But the more I think about it, so much of that is incredibly out of reach,” says one source in the article. Even decades ago, Sonny Koufax would have probably agreed with the article, before ripping out part of the newspaper to clean up some spilled milk next to his third bowl of cereal of the day. Both films find the hearts at the center of their respective protagonists’ messy, work-in-progress stories. Is there anything more 2026 than that?

When you watch Big Daddy in 2026, you almost forget how much of a schmuck—but vulnerable too—Sandler allowed Sonny to be. I was pleasantly surprised that Sandler ultimately loses his chance at raising Julian by himself. It’s a small, complicated victory for a movie that uses a schlocky, heartfelt monologue about fathers to reach a contrived moral coda, but we’ll take our wins where we can get them.

#4789. RJ Mitte's Death Highlights Mental Health Challenges for People With Cerebral Palsy

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

“Breaking Bad” actor and disability advocate RJ Mitte has died at age 34.

Mitte reportedly died by suicide, his representative told People on October 12. However, local authorities have said the official cause and manner of his death remain under investigation.

Mitte, who was best-known for playing Walter White Jr. on the Emmy Award-winning television series “Breaking Bad,” lived with cerebral palsy and advocated for disability inclusion.

There is currently no evidence to suggest that cerebral palsy caused the actor’s death. Still, Mitte’s untimely passing highlights the mental health challenges that people with cerebral palsy may face.

Research has demonstrated elevated risks of anxiety and depression among those with the condition, alongside barriers to diagnosis, social participation, and employment.

“Living with cerebral palsy can affect mental health through several interacting pathways,” said Shannel Elhelou, neuropsychologist and founder of Brain Centric Neuropsychology in Westlake Village, CA.

“Chronic pain, fatigue, disrupted sleep, and the effort required to navigate daily activities can take an emotional toll. Experiences of bullying, discrimination, social exclusion, and difficulty accessing care can add to that burden. Also, the early brain injury underlying cerebral palsy may contribute to difficulties with emotional regulation, although each person’s experience is different,” Elhelou told Healthline.

If you or someone you know is in crisis and considering suicide or self-harm, please seek support:

If you’re calling on behalf of someone else, stay with them until help arrives. You may remove weapons or substances that can cause harm if you can do so safely.

If you’re not in the same household, stay on the phone with them until help arrives.

Mitte played a key role in challenging stereotypes by portraying a teenager with cerebral palsy on “Breaking Bad.”

Outside of acting, Mitte advocated for people with disabilities through organizations including United Cerebral Palsy (UCP) and Shriners Children’s.

He also led the Mitte Foundation, a non-profit corporation founded in 1994 by his grandparents, Roy F. and Joann Cole Mitte, that improves the quality of life for people in Central Texas.

Mitte’s advocacy emphasized representation, inclusion, and opportunities for people with disabilities.

The legacy he leaves behind underscores the need to recognize mental health as an essential part of care for individuals with cerebral palsy and other disabilities.

Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of conditions affecting movement, posture, and coordination.

Most people with cerebral palsy have typical intelligence, although some also have intellectual disabilities or other comorbid physical and mental health conditions.

A 2018 study published in JAMA Neurology found that adults with cerebral palsy had a 28% higher risk of developing depression and a 40% higher risk of anxiety than adults without the condition.

A 2024 study in JAMA Network Open found higher recorded rates of anxiety and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) among children and young adults with cerebral palsy.

The researchers also identified comparatively low rates of depression and suicidal ideation, highlighting concerns that these conditions may be underdiagnosed.

“Research shows that adults with cerebral palsy have an increased risk of depression and anxiety,” Elhelou said.

“However, these conditions should never be viewed as an inevitable part of having a disability. One concern is ‘diagnostic overshadowing,’ when symptoms of depression, anxiety, or other mental health conditions are attributed to cerebral palsy itself, leading those conditions to go unrecognized and untreated. Someone’s fatigue, withdrawal, or changes in behavior deserve careful assessment rather than the assumption that ‘this is just their cerebral palsy,'” she continued.

“While these findings help us understand mental health risks among people with cerebral palsy, they cannot tell us what any one person was experiencing. Many interacting factors may contribute to someone dying by suicide, and it would be inappropriate to attribute an individual’s death to their disability.”

A 2019 study published in Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology found that children with cerebral palsy had higher odds of anxiety disorders and behavioral challenges than children without the condition.

Difficulties with friendships and bullying were associated with some of these differences.

Factors that may affect well-being include:

The researchers also found that supportive friendships may help reduce some of these disparities, reinforcing the importance of inclusive schools and communities.

A 2021 study published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine found that U.S. adults with disabilities faced increased risks of suicidal thoughts, planning, and attempts compared with adults without disabilities.

The 988 Lifeline received more than 8 million contacts through calls, texts, chats, and American Sign Language videophone in 2025, according to the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration.

Federal funding for the Lifeline’s dedicated LGBTQ+ youth service ended in July 2025, removing the option to press 3 for specialized support.

After pressure from Congress, the service was recently restored at the end of September, according to the Kaiser Family Foundation (KFF).

Employment and financial independence can influence well-being for anyone, particularly those with cerebral palsy.

However, a 2024 study found that just 30.4% of young adults with cerebral palsy who participated in vocational rehabilitation programs were employed when they exited those programs.

Workplace accommodations, accessible hiring, vocational rehabilitation, and inclusive social opportunities can help address these barriers.

“Depression and anxiety are treatable, and they should never be dismissed as an inevitable part of living with a disability,” Elhelou said.

“If you notice persistent sadness, anxiety, hopelessness, or withdrawal, reach out to someone you trust and a mental health professional. You deserve a clinician who takes your concerns seriously and adapts treatment to your communication, mobility, or other access needs. Care should also address pain, fatigue, and sleep difficulties, which can affect emotional well-being.”

Organizations such as United Cerebral Palsy offer information and support for people with cerebral palsy and their families.

Healthcare professionals can also improve outcomes by screening for mental health concerns, using appropriate assessment tools, and connecting patients with accessible treatment.

Improved access to care, inclusive communities, and meaningful opportunities can help people with cerebral palsy and other disabilities thrive.

“Asking for help does not diminish your resilience or your contributions. If you are experiencing thoughts of suicide or feel overwhelmed, you do not have to wait until things feel unbearable to reach out,” Elhelou said.

“Supportive relationships, peer groups, and disability communities can offer connection and understanding. Staying engaged in activities that bring enjoyment and meaning can also help.”

#4788. BLUETTI’s flexible $1,099 Apex 200 backs up your home – and powers your RV

What do you actually need to keep running when the power goes out? For most households, the fridge, wifi, phones, and a few other essentials come first. Buying enough battery storage for every appliance in the house can come later – and that’s the appeal of BLUETTI’s latest launch, the Apex 200 portable power station.

The Apex 200 starts with 2.56kWh of storage and 3.2kW of continuous AC output, with the option to add batteries when you need longer backup. Built-in RV connections also mean it can earn its keep between blackouts.

BLUETTI launches the Apex 200 on November 4, with standalone super early-bird pricing starting at $1,099 through November 18. Electrek readers can get an extra 5% off with code ELECTREK5OFF.

Here’s how to work out which setup is worth buying for your home or RV.

The Apex 200 takes the expandable design of BLUETTI’s flagship Apex series and puts it in a smaller package.

You get a 2,560Wh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery. The 3.2kW of continuous AC output increases to 3.6kW when an expansion battery is connected or the unit is actively charging.

The enclosure holds all that in 36.2 liters and weighs 26.9kg (59.3 lb). You’ll want two hands to move it, but it’s convenient to move it between home and your camper.

BLUETTI’s UltraCell technology delivers an industry-leading energy density of 70.7 Wh/L, yet the Apex 200 is more than 50% smaller by volume than class competitors. For an RV owner, that smaller footprint frees up room for other gear.

There’s also a tilted display and four app-controllable AC outlets. That might not sound like a big deal, but when the battery is on the floor or under your desk and you want to check or redirect its charge, it means you don’t have to crouch.

BLUETTI calls its approach “Start Small. Scale Big. Power More.” BLUETTI says Apex 300 users reported liking the modular design but wanted something easier to handle day to day. The Apex 200 offers them a lower entry point, with room to add capacity rather than replace the main unit.

Before buying a portable power station, you’ll want to know how much power your appliances draw and how much energy they use over time.

For example, a 150W appliance running continuously for 10 hours uses 1,500Wh. A 1,500W appliance gets through that same amount in one hour. Running a coffee maker briefly is a different proposition from keeping a high-draw appliance on all afternoon.

A rough runtime calculation is: Usable battery capacity in watt-hours ÷ average load in watts = hours of operation.

Divide the Apex 200’s nominal 2,560Wh by a steady 150W load, and you get about 17 hours before accounting for conversion losses and the battery system’s own power use. Real runtime will be lower.

Refrigerators complicate that calculation because their compressors cycle on and off. Check measured daily energy use where possible, along with startup demand – motors can briefly draw more power when they kick on.

If your usual blackout lasts four to 12 hours, start by looking at the Apex 200 on its own.

BLUETTI estimates it can run a 150W refrigerator for 10–12 hours, or support low-draw essentials such as CPAPs, wifi routers, and mobile devices for two to three days, depending on the equipment and how it’s used. That doesn’t mean every device on that list will run together for three days. Your combined load determines the runtime.

The Apex 200 also gives you more control over where that energy goes. Four independently controllable Smart AC outlets built right into the unit – no need to buy smart plugs! – let you switch individual devices on and off through the BLUETTI App, set schedules, and apply state-of-charge controls. So if something doesn’t need power overnight, you can turn off its power at the outlet and save the fridge’s battery.

BLUETTI calls the feature an industry first for portable power stations. The system also works with Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and Home Assistant.

A UPS function switches connected equipment to battery power in 15 milliseconds. Check that switching time against your equipment’s requirements, especially for a CPAP or other sensitive device.

With AC output on and the display off, idle consumption drops to just 10.5W.

A winter freeze or severe storm can leave you without grid power for days. That’s when adding extra storage starts to make more sense.

For typical power outages, adding one or two BLUETTI B300K batteries can extend essential home backup to two to three days.

But you can go further. One Apex 200 supports up to six B500K expansion batteries, bringing its maximum capacity to 33.28kWh.

But a bigger battery still needs recharging eventually. The Apex 200 accepts up to 3kW of solar input across two independent channels:

With a correctly configured array of SORA 500 portable solar panels making full use of those inputs, BLUETTI says the base battery can charge from 0 to 80% in 50 minutes, or reach 100% in 1.7 hours using solar alone.

A solar generator setup lets you recharge during daylight. The Apex 200 can also be charged with wall AC, vehicle charging, and compatible gas-generator charging. A suitable 30A generator connection can help replenish the battery when solar production falls short.

The Apex 200 can also form part of a larger home battery backup system through BLUETTI’s Hub A1 parallel box.

BLUETTI specifies up to 6kW of continuous AC output and approximately 100kWh of storage across a parallel system using up to three Apex 200 units.

That’s a significant increase over the standalone battery, but your daily consumption still matters. A steady 1kW load uses 24kWh in 24 hours. Heavy-draw appliances can make a large battery feel much smaller.

BLUETTI positions its larger configurations for three to four days of essential-panel backup. How close you get depends on your batteries, appliances, and ability to recharge.

If you want automatic backup through your home’s electrical panel, confirm the compatible transfer equipment, supported circuits, voltage, and output for the exact bundle. Those details determine what you can actually keep running.

Start with your most likely outage, then decide whether you need more runtime, a charging source, or both.

Extra batteries extend runtime. Solar panels or another charging source recharge them. For outages that stretch into days, both can be worth having.

When shopping for a camper van or travel trailer, choosing a battery comes down to more than just capacity. Among its 10 output ports are two connections RV owners will appreciate having built in.

The native 30A TT-30R RV outlet plugs directly into travel trailer shore power inlets for 120V power.

The 12V/30A Anderson port can directly power compatible DC equipment, including portable fridges and communications gear. This avoids converting battery power to AC and then back to DC, cutting out unnecessary conversion steps.

For charging between campsites, the system can pair with the BLUETTI Charger 2, which combines alternator and solar charging support. It lets you use driving time to replenish the battery through faster vehicle alternator charging, then use solar when you’re parked.

BLUETTI’s recommended mobile bundle is the Apex 200 + SORA 500 solar panel + Charger 2. You get storage for camp, solar charging during your stay, and alternator charging on the road. Compatible campground AC gives you another option.

The Apex 200 is the better fit if you value a smaller enclosure, easier transport, native RV ports, and a lower upfront cost. You can start with 2.56kWh and expand to 33.28kWh on one unit, or approximately 100kWh across a fully expanded parallel system.

The Apex 300 is worth considering if your priority is higher native output and capacity for a system that will mostly stay at home. It offers 3,840W of output and 2,764.8Wh of battery storage, and BLUETTI positions it for more advanced home backup, including compatible 120V/240V configurations.

For someone who wants a battery for both blackouts and RV trips, the Apex 200’s size and connections make a useful combination. You can buy the storage you need now and add more when your power needs change.

#4787. Is Psychology Measuring Introversion All Wrong?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

It used to be that if you wanted to know if someone was an introvert, you handed them a personality questionnaire, and oh, by the way, it was definitely built on the Big Five model, the dominant framework in personality science since the 1980s. Their score on the extraversion scale would have told you what you wanted to know.

But newer research is challenging the Big Five’s position as the best measure of introversion. If the critique holds, it could mean that decades of findings about introverts may have been skewed in ways I’ll explain.

The biggest problem is that the Big Five doesn’t actually measure introversion directly, which very well may mean, in effect, that it is not measuring introversion at all. You see, what the Big Five does is measure extraversion and then, believe it or not, treats introversion as the absence of extraversion. So introversion, within this model, is the low end of the extraversion dial. But that kind of makes sense, right?

Yet it paints a certain picture. A person with low extraversion is (look closely at the words I’m about to use) reserved, inhibited, quiet, or withdrawn. In the words of researchers Valerie Thomas and Pauline Nelson, the Big Five assigns “solely negative characteristics” to introverts. Oh great. Thanks. In other words, it defines introverts by what they lack rather than by the qualities and functional characteristics that they actually possess.

That’s like defining calm as “low anger,” by the way. Which would miss something essential about the experience of being calm, wouldn’t it?

So, in 2014, psychologist Jonathan Cheek and colleagues proposed the STAR Introversion Scale, measuring four distinct flavors of introversion (Cool, Jon et al., 2014):

In a 2025 study published in the Journal of Personality, Thomas and Nelson put these two approaches head-to-head, examining which better predicted solitude-seeking behavior, arguably the most signature introverted tendency (I also so argue).

Big Five introversion showed no relationship at all with positive motivation for solitude. None. Zero. Zilch. It didn’t predict wanting to be alone, and worse, under the Big Five, it was low introversion (meaning higher extraversion) that predicted actually spending more time alone. Crazy, eh? This study found that, by the Big Five’s very own logic, extraverts are the ones who are out there in the world seeking solitude for themselves, so something had clearly gone sideways.

The STAR model, on the other hand, told a coherent story about solitude. “Social introversion” predicted both the desire for and the amount of time spent alone, while curiously but understandably, “thinking introversion,” and only thinking introversion, was associated with genuinely wanting solitude, and “anxious introversion” predicted wanting solitude for negative avoidance reasons, which all makes sense to me.

When the study incorporated STAR and Big Five data and analyzed various fancy comparisons statistically, the conclusions that resulted began to indicate that perhaps where the Big Five had claimed introversion, it had actually all along been capturing something much closer to what would be better described as neuroticism. (Whoa.)

I can answer that! Well, you see, if clinical screening tools rely on Big Five-based formulations of introversion, a therapist might interpret a patient’s solitude-seeking as a symptom of a disorder rather than merely their preference. They might cast a thinking introvert who recharges alone as socially withdrawn. Alternatively, they might underestimate the functional impact of an anxious introvert’s distress given that it’s literally part of a normalized trait score, when in fact, it is an indication of clinically concerning functioning and treatable patterns. Ah, you see now?

In workplaces, the Big Five framework feeds a narrative in which introversion is a deficit to be managed, such as the stereotypical quiet employee who needs to “come out of their shell.” In reality, there is not necessarily a defensive shell at all but, rather, likely a vital interior life. Such confusion risks a perpetuation in varying forms and degrees of, in effect, pathologizing perfectly functional ways of being human.

To me, the STAR’s great contribution is carving out space for thinking introversion, a dimension completely invisible to the Big Five, for introverts who don’t avoid people out of anxiety but do also gravitate toward ideas, reflection, imagination, and, thus, toward solitude. This is arguably at the heart of what most self-identified introverts mean when they say “introvert” to describe themselves (can I get an amen?).

But still, clearly the STAR model has its own vulnerabilities. It is relatively new, developed by a small research group, and has had as-yet-limited independent validation across diverse populations (equity!). And “anxious introversion” is easily debatable. If it so strongly correlates with neuroticism, is it even an aspect of introversion, or is it really something altogether different, albeit related, that should be measured separately?

Whatever the case on the nuances, it is clear enough that the STAR is bringing a serious challenge to whether the Big Five, for all its strengths, has introversion right.

As I’ve alluded, emerging evidence suggests it does not—that it has been measuring only a shadow of introversion, defined by deficit and tinged with pathology, while missing the fuller, more textured reality, so I am appreciative of new perspectives.

This new conversation is just beginning, but for the many millions (including myself, hi) who have long felt that their introversion is something richer than “not extraverted enough,” the science may thankfully, finally, hopefully, be catching up.

Cheek, J. M., Brown, C. A., & Grimes, J. O. (2014). Personality scales for four domains of introversion: Social, thinking, anxious, and restrained introversion. Unpublished manuscript, Department of Psychology, Wellesley College. (The original STAR Introversion Scale.)

Thomas, V., & Nelson, P. A. (2025). The effects of multifaceted introversion and sensory processing sensitivity on solitude-seeking behavior. Journal of Personality. (Head-to-head comparison of the STAR and the Big Five Inventory in predicting solitude-seeking; source of the finding that Big Five introversion fails to predict positive motivation for solitude.)

#4786. What “Food Is Medicine” Actually Means, According to a Cardiologist

Plus, Chef Marcus Samuelsson shares easy ways to sneak more plant-based foods into your diet.

Despite what fitfluencers and gym bros might have you believe, eating healthy is about a lot more than counting macros and calories. Every day, scientists are learning more about how our eating habits can influence health beyond just our weight, including blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar, and risk of developing heart disease.

That's part of the idea behind a buzzy approach to health care known as “food is medicine,” which contends that what we put on our plates can be a meaningful part of preventing and managing disease.

The challenge is understanding what actually helps and turning that knowledge into meals we want to keep eating. To unpack this, Future You host and editorial director of Men’s and Women’s Health Rich Dorment sits down with Marcus Samuelsson, the acclaimed restaurateur and author of the new cookbook, Back to Green, and Louai Razzouk, MD, a cardiologist at NYU Langone Health.

Here’s a look at some of the themes covered in the episode:

Samuelsson says that beso is an Ethiopian drink that combines roasted barley with water or milk of your choice. “You just shake it and this is the best protein shake you can have,” he says. You can find the more specific recipe in Back to Green.

He grew up eating foods like beso as well as shiro, a stew made from chickpea flour, and other Ethiopian “superfoods” that he incorporates into his dishes today.

Dr. Razzouk says it doesn't mean that you can treat a disease with food alone. “It does mean that you may be able to prevent it by having a healthier and more balanced diet, and possibly minimize how many medications you need to be on,” he says.

Dr. Razzouk says that while you may still need to be on medication, food can make a “huge” impact when it comes to managing conditions like diabetes or high cholesterol. “Food impacts our level of inflammation, our insulin sensitivity, our weight,” and our blood pressure, he says.

The first warning sign that a patient’s diet may be less than ideal is if they get most of their food from Uber Eats or another delivery service. “Most of the stuff that we order in, especially living in New York City, contains a lot of saturated fats, a lot of added salt, and a lot of processed food,” he says. He discusses a couple more red flags in the episode, including meal timing.

In his early 20s, traveling in Southeast Asia and Singapore opened his eyes to a new way of eating—and the idea that there’s great food to be found all over the world.

A plant-forward diet doesn't have to exclude animal protein, he says, pointing to the Mediterranean and DASH diets as examples of eating plans that incorporate some meat. “What I tell patients is that typically if you have a choice between getting a source of protein from an animal source versus from plants, then I would try to get it from plants,” he says.

“What I tell patients is that I want you to enjoy your life,” Dr. Razzouk says, adding that fad diets typically don’t work. “What we would like you to do is find a balance,” he says, eating in a way that's enjoyable and that benefits your health.

It's a lentil salad with a coconut turmeric vinaigrette—and Samuelsson breaks down why the flavors work so well together, plus ingredients you may have in the fridge or pantry that can level it up even further.

He’ll often bring home new ingredients (e.g. spirulina) and encourage his son to look up the health benefits before they cook with it together.

Dr. Razzouk says diets high in fiber not only may lower your risk of colon cancer, but they also may lower your level of LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, which impact your risk of cardiovascular disease. It also helps keep you full.

Cooking together can be an enjoyable family activity, Samuelsson says. “When I cook waffles and pancakes with my kids, we have fun,” he says. “The kitchen is a mess, but iPads are down, we're spending time together.”

Samuelsson suggests chickpeas, sea moss, and the fruit soursop. Dr. Razzouk suggests nuts (walnuts in particular) and extra-virgin olive oil.

Caitlin is a health and fitness journalist based in New York City. She writes for publications including The Wall Street Journal and Runner’s World. She's completed 12 marathons, including the six World Marathon Majors, is semi-fluent in French, and volunteers as a greeter on The High Line. Follow her on Instagram or LinkedIn.

#4785. Pope Leo XIV Diagnosed With Lung Cancer After Surgery to Remove Part of Lung

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer following a successful surgery, the Vatican said.

The Pope, 71, underwent surgery at Agostino Gemelli University Policlinic in Rome on October 13 to remove a nodule from his right lung. This was determined to be pulmonary adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

The surgeons removed the lower lobe of the Pope’s lung to “ensure a radical procedure; the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique,” said Dr. Luigi Carbone, the Director of Vatican Healthcare Services, and Professor Stephano Margaritora, the lead surgeon, in a press release.

“An intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, as suspected from the preoperative examinations,” they said.

Pope Leo was in the operating room for 3 hours, while the operation itself lasted around 90 minutes.

The doctors noted that it was a successful operation with no complications.

According to Matteo Bruni, the Director of the Holy See Press Office, the Pope asked for dinner after the surgery and spent the evening with his secretaries and other Vatican staff.

In a press release on Wednesday, the Vatican said that the Pope’s postoperative recovery is progressing well.

According to Vatican News, Pope Leo had a calm first night following his surgery.

In the coming days, exams will be conducted on the removed tissue. There has currently been no change in the initially announced week of hospitalization.

On October 14, the Pope underwent blood tests and chest X-rays that were scheduled following his surgery. The results of these tests confirm that his postoperative recovery is progressing as expected, and the values are within a normal range for the type of operation performed.

Pope Leo has also undergone some respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking around his room, the Vatican said.

It has not yet been announced whether he will require any further treatment.

Adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of lung cancer globally. It accounts for around 40% of all lung cancer diagnoses.

Adenocarcinoma is a type of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), which accounts for about 80–85% of all lung cancers.

Lung adenocarcinoma begins in the epithelial cells that produce mucus. It is the most common type of NSCLC.

Adenocarcinoma can be classified further by the genetic changes driving the tumor. For example, EGFR-positive lung cancer is found more often in people who have never smoked and can often be treated with targeted therapies, which is why biomarker testing of tumor tissue helps guide treatment decisions.

Treatment for NSCLC is generally determined by the stage. However, it typically involves one or a combination of:

Surgery is generally the first step in treatment for this type of lung cancer. The right lung has three lobes, or sections, and the left has two.

A doctor will often remove the entire lobe that has the tumor in order to remove the tumor and improve the outlook.

The body eventually adapts in order to compensate for the loss of function.

According to the American Cancer Society (ACS), for NSCLC that hasn’t spread outside of the lung, the 5-year relative survival rate is 67%.
