#4784. This Is Still the Best Water Bottle I've Ever Used

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

YOUR WATER BOTTLE is an expression of yourself. Sure, you're buying the thing for its functionality and design, but you’re also buying into what the water bottle represents. Whether you’re in need of an all-metal wide mouth for outdoor trekking, an insulated squeeze bottle for home gym power hours, or a smart water bottle that can track your daily intake, we've got the best water bottle to fit your hydration needs below.

Most importantly, you're buying a water bottle to nourish your body and give it the liquid it requires. Now, precise water intake depends on the person and how active they are. We do know that it's not always easy to throw back the H2O, but the benefits are many and there are easy tricks to drinking more water, which will only benefit the body. Having a high-functioning, reusable water bottle you enjoy using will keep you high-functioning as well.

As a study last year found, most adults are not getting enough in terms of daily water intake. That may seem trivial, and perhaps even equate to fewer trips to the bathroom, but there are real health concerns there. Proper hydration can reduce the risk of disease and injury, aid with recovery, and much more. So, let us embrace making it as easy as possible to get the right amount of water we all need.

The Yeti Yonder water bottle has been a go-to for several of our editors for a few years now. The chug spout and cap design is perfect for everyday use, not too narrow or wide. The BPA-free plastic construction is so tough that it's been through drops onto concrete from 10 feet high (it accidentally fell off the top of an SUV when one editor was visiting family in Kansas City). Another big reason why we chose a plastic water bottle as our best overall pick is due to weight—the Yonder is much lighter than its metal counterparts. Unless you're doing some serious hiking or camping, the Yonder will essentially serve multiple uses without any questioning of keeping liquid cold or durability.

The Yonder hardly ever leaks either, no matter which cap you choose. We personally like the add-on Yonder Tether Cap. It makes the bottle a little more streamlined and takes off even more weight. But, the traditional cap it comes with is solid too and might actually be easier to carry by itself. And we've found the 25 oz size to be the sweet spot.

Last detail to point out is price and number of colors available. Sometimes Yeti gear can get expensive. This is not the case with the Yonder water bottles. Pick and choose from all the new colors the brand releases over time. Build a small collection. Gift a few. This is our favorite water bottle we've used over the years.

This is a more practical version for on-the-go guys who want to see what the Stanley craze is about. The slim design makes it slide into backpacks and gym bags with ease, and its pop-top cap is simple and secure. The cap design actually uses a two-step locking process to help avoid accidentally opening (which is a huge plus for those of us who've used these types of water bottles in the past). But it's not like cracking a safe, as the thing opens with relative ease for that quick pull of water when you need it right away.

The Quick Flip Go's double-wall-insulated design means it can keep cold drinks cold and hot drinks hot. One of our editors has even used it to sip morning coffee from time to time. We imagine it would even keep some white wine chilled in a backyard setting, too.

So why is this water bottle not our top pick? It comes down to weight. The Quick Flip Go is just a tad heavier than the Yeti Yonder. If you can get over the weight detail, though, then this pick is just as valid as a top choice.

Can a water bottle be playful? The radiant color scheme here suggests so. And why not, this is the tool that should accompany you on a lot of joyous outings, from cycling through country roads to hiking in the woods. Choose from a host of three sizes (24 oz is our preferred capacity) and enjoy the FreeSip Spout, which pivots to and from big gulps and sipping from a straw seamlessly.

The carry loop is ergonomic and folds into the bottle and push-button access means no leaks. While relatively slender overall, we found that the bottle had no problem taking on scoops of ice with the lid fully off. And once that ice is in place, you're set for 24 hours of polar temperatures. About the only scenario in which this bottle struggles is for athletes competing in helmet sports, as the broad mouth can't get through a lot of face guards. But you could also just take that helmet off before hydrating.

With so many rave reviews in favor of this bottle, it was a little hard to approach it as a skeptic. But that's what good testers do, and we came in thinking there was no way it could match the hype. Almost immediately in our testing we were proved wrong. This is a contemporary water bottle for the contemporary world and once you have one, you never want to go back to the old way.

Why does it slap? Aesthetic, durability, and a high-functioning nature. The handle is one of the best we've used, the build is sturdy, and the associated app is all kinds of helpful. It self-cleans in a single minute, insulates for a full day, and there's even a hydration tracker to keep you swigging when you should be.

The handle is detachable and the bottle itself filters the contents, making for a clean sip every time. The look is among the best out there and the color options are great too. Complaints? Few and far between, although the drinking sensors can be a little buggy and the nozzle is tricky to clean. But overall, it's a gem.

Basic squeeze water bottles for the gym are okay for use, but if you're looking for a much more enjoyable way to stay hydrated while working out then you'll want to try the Camelbak Podium. This water bottle is under $20 (sometimes even lower depending on the sale) and comes with an insulated design that keeps cold water from covering the outside of it—which means no condensation will be soaking your hands in between sets.

The spout and cap design is another huge sell for why we love the Podium for the gym. The top is designed to keep away dirt for mountain bikers, but when transferred to the gym it means there's no leakage when falling over and no gross gym dust and germs floating where you put your mouth. The spout is also similar to drinking out of a Camelbak backpack, which a few of our editors found novel.

The Podium is a little outside the box for what you'd think of as a gym water bottle, but its insulation and high level of leak-proofing makes it seriously good for all types of active settings. It doesn't hurt that it has a cool design, too.

Familiar, durable, and affordable is what makes Nalgene so good after so many years. The brand offers a ton of fun colors, designs, and patterns, so you have a full array of ways to express yourself. However, we realize the design of your Nalgene might not matter as much if you plan on layering it with all the cool stickers you collect on your travels.

Does it have insulation or specialized cap designs for sipping? No, but that's not the point. Nalgene water bottles are all about keeping things minimalist. Over time, it might start to leak a little bit or get beaten up by the dishwasher. If that happens, find a way to recycle and buy a new one for less than $20. Overall, this is a modern classic of a water bottle that's about as durable as they come. We've even run them over with mountain bikes and small cars and didn't even put a dent in 'em. The simplicity means it's also noticeably easier to clean.

Toughness with a simple design that appeals to the bare-bones hydrators out there. We like to think they’re just old enough now they’ve become somewhat iconic, earning a following for all camps, from classroom commuters to weekend warrior backcountry hikers.

If there was a water bottle we might want to bring to a deserted island, this might be it. That's because it excels in versatility, able to do just about whatever you need it to do. We appreciated the wide mouth, which delivered big swigs after long jogs or paddles on a SUP. There was never any spilling thanks to a leakproof spout and the hinge lock is a nice accent, especially if you're on the active side and like to have your water bottle with you on those adventures.

The extra large clip is nice for outings like hikes and travel and we found the insulation to be pretty good, keeping things chilled for at least 12 hours even in warm conditions. It's easy to clean, whether by hand or in the machine, and it fits in every cup holder we tried, from cars to strollers. If you need an extra nudge of insulation, just pack the thing with ice. We found the bottle to be a bit weaker than others in terms of durability (can dent up if you're hard on the thing) but for the price, it's a nice option indeed.

You really can't go wrong with any Hydro Flask, but this 32-ounce water bottle came to be our favorite from our editors who like to hike and camp, and from those who enjoy a high-capacity water bottle. The wide mouth design at the top makes for fast drinking as well as easy pouring and cleaning. As for the material, you've got insanely durable stainless steel with double wall insulation at your service.

This water bottle fits well in most hiking backpacks and duffel bags, despite its larger size. We liked how secure the cap and handle are too, as it allows for one-handed carry when walking short distances.

You're buying excellence with this water bottle. It's going to stay strong for years, no matter what adventures you throw at it. Outdoorsy types especially should consider this model if they're in need of a water bottle.

We liked the first edition of the Hidrate Spark PRO and the second round only improves on the original. It’s an entire hydration program tied to an ultra contemporary bottle and helpful sibling app. You can customize your intake based on your activities and track your progress right down to the drop.

The bottle itself is sweatproof. We appreciated the fact that it rarely if ever slipped out of our paws, even amid a grueling workout. The double-insulation does its job and the recycled 18/8 stainless steel is a nice touch. Also, the lid performed well, even outdoors, with a protective lid, a large carrying handle, and a chug spout for when you’re really thirsty.

When you get a higher IQ bottle such as this, it can sometimes be a little demanding, Not the case here. The newest option from Hidrate does insist that you stay hydrated, but in subtle fashion, with the occasional glow or beep. It’s much better than a bottle that nudges too hard, causing the user to revolt and ignore the thing.

Smart as this water bottle is, it still requires some babying when it comes to washing. The sensor is especially sensitive and should be cleaned with care. But that’s a small price to pay for a water bottle that essentially serves as your personal hydration coach.

There are a handful of filtered water bottles on the market, but no brand has wowed us more than LifeStraw. For starters, the LifeStraw filter is one of the most trusted designs on the market. According to the brand, the two-stage filtration will eliminate 99.999999% of bacteria (including E. coli and Salmonella), and 99.999% of microplastics, sand, and dirt. LifeStraw then packed its filter inside the stainless steel bottle, which we found to be much more appealing than plastic models where you can see the filter inside.

The cost of the Lifestraw Go here is a little elevated, but you are paying for the special filter. You do need to change the LifeStraw filter inside about every 60 days, so that's an extra cost. The payoff though, from what our editors discovered, is the peace of mind you get filling up your water bottle at a public water fountain or from tap water that comes out of a sink.

Grab this water bottle if you're looking for a filtered option with excellent design. There are times when you can’t fully trust your water source but this vessel affords peace of mind (and no bickering of the gut).

To say these bottles were tested is an understatement. Over the course of several years, various Men's Health editors and I put them to work—like, overtime. We paired them up with the most active members of our team, allowing us to get a clean picture of just how well these bottles perform. Hot weather, cold weather, in the gym, out on the trail, on the saddle of a bike, on plane rides, or just commuting; we brought them everywhere.

Throughout the process, we paid close attention to various attributes. Obviously, we wanted a water bottle that looks good. But more importantly, we wanted a water bottle that made staying hydrated easy, thoughtless, and perhaps even enjoyable. We analyzed design, material, size, and special features. We waded through reputable reviews and talked up insiders in the outdoors recreation and sporting worlds for their takes. And of course, we looked at price.

In the end, the Yeti has won us over on all fronts. Durable, lightweight, packable, and super affordable, it has been a favorite among many testers since it released in 2022. But several others came close, offering different traits like filtration, improved insulation, or more sophisticated lids.

Some people prefer wide-mouth tops on their water bottles for faster drinking, while others prefer a spout design that's much smaller and easier to sip. Really it comes down to preference, but there are spout designs we tested that are more enjoyable to drink from than others. Do keep in mind that lots of companies make tops that are interchangeable in case you want to switch to a different design.

To avoid any contamination of plastics, most water bottles we reviewed came in a metal design. There are some plastic water bottles we tested, however, that were BPA-free and we found to not have any impact on taste. Our top-tested water bottle from Yeti is actually made from BPA-free plastic. Our editors have tested this water bottle for nearly two years and have found no issues with taste or with material breakdown from a dishwasher.

Material also dictates temperature retention, with things like double-insulated stainless steel keeping things nice and chilled for long periods of time. Plastic tends to not insulate quite as well, but can be quite durable (and recycled). Keep this in mind as you weigh how important an ice-cold pull of water is to you.

How much water are you going to need? Capacity is a vital consideration, as you might just be looking for a little hydration while at work (where you can continue to refill when necessary) or be out and about all weekend at the campground, potentially away from a water source. Less volume is just fine for quicker outings or when you want to be streamlined, like on a bike. But you'll be wanting additional capacity for, say, lengthy conferences, road trips, or exhausting workout routines.

There are a few water bottles we selected thanks to special features our editors love. Lifestraw, for example, provides some of the best water filtration you can buy. The fact Lifestraw discreetly hides its filter behind a stainless steel body is a huge reason why we featured it on our list. The same goes for the Camelbak Podium, as its insulated body and cap and spout design make it especially suitable for indoor gym settings.

Yes. A reusable bottle is easier on the planet for that very reason—it's reusable. Single-use plastic is wasteful stuff and, worse, it does not decompose, likely ending up in the ocean and your food supply chain (not to mention turning into microplastic). Going with a bottle like the ones listed here does require some energy and inputs upfront, but because it's your long-term bottle (don't go losing it now), the carbon footprint is less.

You can take it a step further by purchasing a bottle made with responsibly sourced materials, sometimes even made from up-cycled or recycled materials. Look for non-BPA (a bad chemical) options and preferably ones that use very little if no plastic. Glass and stainless steel are generally easier on Mother Earth. And be good to yourself by keeping the thing clean and sterile.

Here's the thing about mold: It likes wet environments. You know, like inside of your water bottle. It's a repulsive thought, but some of that gunk buildup in your vessel might just be mold. Don't fret, you can clean the thing.

Now, it would take a fair amount of mold to sicken the average person but regardless, a clean water bottle is just worth having. Wash your bottle daily, either in the dishwasher if it's permitted or by hand, ideally with hot water and a scrub to get into those nooks and crannies—water bottle brushes are a great tool.

Occasionally, consider a more intense clean. Do to the bottle as you might to your coffee maker, soaking it in a mix of vinegar and water. Even the occasional boiling water soak will help keep the bottle pristine.

#4783. Why Reconciliation Fails (and What Actually Makes It Work)

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

It seems family estrangement is showing up everywhere lately on social media. In particular, we see numerous headlines of adult children going “no contact." And, to some extent, the statistics support this observation.

A 2024 Harris Poll showed about half of American adults are estranged from at least one close relative, with 35 percent estranged from an immediate family member, such as a parent or sibling. Cornell sociologist Karl Pillemer estimates that 67 million Americans are estranged and that more than 4 in 10 will experience it at some point in their lives.

With this growing reality, reconnection often becomes a focus for one or both parties after estrangement, raising two very important questions. Firstly, why does family reconciliation so often break down, and secondly, what helps reconciliation succeed?

If you're estranged and searching for a way to reconnect, you may be feeling and carrying around a particular type of hope. Despite previous unsuccessful attempts to close the gap, you picture it going differently this time. You work to convince yourself that if you could only find the right words, everything would be fixed. But it isn’t.

After more than a decade of working in this field, I've discovered that words might not matter as much as we think they do. What actually determines how these conversations go is whether two people can stay emotionally present when words start to hurt, and to stay open, as opposed to shutting down or exchanging salvos, when things get tough.

What I see is that when one person describes your behavior in a way that’s painful to hear, you feel discomfort. In many cases, your body reacts instantly, before your mind has a chance to process the words. The other person hasn’t even finished their sentence, and you're already overwhelmed with the urge to respond, in all likelihood, with a counterattack. And most of the time, it doesn't feel like defensiveness from the inside. It probably feels like protecting yourself.

However, for the person who has worked up the courage to say the hard, painful thing, the message becomes that being honest isn't safe. And, therefore, the relationship isn't safe. And, until it is, repair cannot happen.

This is where I see many reconciliation attempts falter and stall. The fact that it’s even attempted underscores something incredibly important. Someone cares enough to give it a try. The unfortunate reality is that the well-intentioned bid for reconnection fails because of an inability to hear the other’s experience without the need to defend, deny, or deflect. This is at the heart of the problem. Only when it’s recognized and addressed can a space for genuine reconnection be created.

Let me give you an example. A woman had chosen estrangement from her mother. Over time, her mother would reach out periodically. Each time, conversations started like an apology but quickly disintegrated into explanations that felt like justifications. Recollections only accommodated one set of experiences, the mother’s. Following each conversation, the daughter felt like nothing had changed. Each failed attempt increased the gap even further.

In order to make sense of this recurring pattern, the daughter turned to therapy and, through that process, became aware that she’d allowed her own healing to become dependent on a mother who might never want to or be able to hear her in the way she needed.

She longed for her mother to listen, acknowledge her childhood experiences, and take responsibility. But, repeatedly, that craved-for moment remained painfully elusive. So, she decided to stop waiting for something external that might never come and started healing anyway.

When the next reconnection attempt eventually happened, there was little to no expectation. Once she let go of needing her mother to own the past, things changed. She still received the same excuses, and the defensiveness remained, but now the daughter viewed both in a different light. She saw armor that had always been there. Armor that, importantly, she came to realise, had nothing to do with her.

In reality, the relationship remained far from what the daughter really longed for. For years, she’d hoped her mother would turn up to the conversation without armor and had weighted her expectations accordingly. Ultimately, it had become clear to her that her mother might never be capable of staying emotionally present and open. The only way to break the deadlock was to be a different daughter.

In making that decision, she and her mother embarked on a new relationship, one where she had created her own conditions for safety. One where she was emotionally present and open, and where, little by little, repair became possible.

Strangely, this isn't unusual. Research from the Family Estrangement & Reconciliation Project found this pattern spanning hundreds of successful reconciliations. Often, the people who rebuilt their relationships weren't the ones who finally got the listening, recognition, and understanding they'd been waiting for. They were the ones who embraced the importance of letting go of never-to-be-met expectations from an irreconcilable shared past.

So, on one hand, reconciliation could be seen as an attempt to reclaim and redirect the past. On the other hand, it can also become the foundation for something new and different. And, with the latter of these two possibilities, it doesn’t mean saying everything that happened in the past was fine. Nor does it mean that one’s experiences are unimportant. It simply means that one can finally put down things that should never been carried in the first place, so that healing and growth can happen.

I don't talk about this from theory alone. I have been estranged from a parent myself. I know how long the road back to rebuilding a stable relationship can be.

It might seem counterintuitive, but wherever you are in your journey, travel as lightly as possible. Carry fewer expectations, explanations, and justifications. Before ever considering the words you might use to try and bridge the gap between you and an estranged loved one, take a look at what you’re bringing with you.

To what extent the other person meets you halfway is largely beyond your control. That said, turning up to the conversation armed with a deeper degree of self-awareness, emotional grounding, and a commitment to healing that isn’t conditional on what the other person does or doesn’t do can often bring reconciliation within reach.

#4782. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Not Be Linked to Colorectal Cancer

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Ultra-processed foods as a group do not increase the risk of colorectal cancer, according to a new study.

Researchers from the National Cancer Institute (NCI) report that they found no association between overall intake of ultra-processed foods and colorectal cancer incidence among the more than 400,000 adults they studied.

They said their findings are important because ultra-processed foods now account for more than half of adults’ energy intake in the United States. They published their research on October 15 in PLOS Medicine.

The study comes amid recent research that has connected ultra-processed foods to an increased risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and obesity.

However, the link between colorectal cancer and ultra-processed foods has been less clear.

A 2025 study reported that ultra-processed foods may increase the risk of colorectal cancer in females under 50.

A 2022 study found that males who consumed high rates of ultra-processed foods had a higher risk of developing colorectal cancer.

NCI scientists noted in their new study that ultra-processed products represent a wide range of foods.

They pointed out that foods such as whole grains and dairy products were associated with a lower risk of colorectal cancer among study participants, while foods such as processed meats were associated with a higher risk.

“We did not observe an association between total ultra-processed food (UPF) intake and colorectal cancer incidence,” said Erikka Loftfield, PhD, a former investigator with the NCI, in a news release. “However, when we looked at food groups, like whole grains, dairy, and meat, by UPF or non-UPF source, we found that associations were in line with current dietary guidance for colorectal cancer prevention.”

Experts not involved in the study told Healthline that the NCI scientists appear to be on the right track.

“While the study did not find that overall ultra-processed food intake was associated with colorectal cancer risk, the findings suggest that simply classifying foods by their level of processing may not tell the whole story,” said Marissa Shams-White, PhD, a senior principal scientist in population science at the American Cancer Society.

“One of the challenges with studying ultra-processed foods is that the category includes a very wide range of foods and beverages, and we don’t yet know whether they all relate to colorectal cancer risk in the same way,” she added.

Ketan Thanki, MD, a colorectal surgeon specializing in benign and malignant diseases of the colon, rectum, and anus at the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California, agrees.

“Just because it is ultra-processed doesn’t mean it is inherently bad or good for you,” he said. “The source of the food and the additives like preservatives, flavorings, sugars, and pigments that are added to increase palatability probably play a much larger role in increasing cancer risk.”

“A whole grain cereal and a hot dog are both UPF, but they push risk in opposite directions,” Thanki noted.

In their study, the National Cancer Institute researchers analyzed data from 461,682 adults aged 50 to 71 years who enrolled in the NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study between 1995 and 1996.

The participants recorded their eating habits using a food frequency questionnaire. Researchers then used that data to estimate each person’s intake of ultra-processed foods. The median consumption of ultra-processed foods among participants was 43% of daily median intake.

The participants were then followed until 2018, for a median of nearly 19 years. The scientists reported that 10,075 cases of colorectal adenocarcinoma were diagnosed during that period.

The researchers reported no association between overall intake of ultra-processed foods and the incidence of colorectal cancer.

However, they said their findings varied by food type. Higher intake of whole grains, fiber, dairy products, and calcium derived from UPF sources was associated with lower colorectal cancer incidence, while meat from UPF sources was associated with higher incidence.

Researchers also found that replacing 10% of gram weight from UPF intake with minimally processed foods was associated with a 2% lower incidence of CRC.

The researchers acknowledged limitations to their study.

They noted that the participants were primarily older, white Americans. In addition, UPF intake was only measured once at the beginning of the study period, so the findings cannot account for changes in eating habits or the increasing availability of ultra-processed foods.

Nonetheless, Ashkan Farhadi, MD, a gastroenterologist at MemorialCare Orange Coast Medical Center in California, who wasn’t involved in the study, said he found the results “very interesting.”

“The definition of ultra-processed foods is so broad,” he told Healthline. “It’s important to designate what type of ultra-processed foods you’re talking about.”

“You shouldn’t just go by whether a food is designated as ultra-processed,” Farhadi added. “You should go by what’s on the [ingredient] label.”

Shams-White shared a similar approach. “When it comes to diet, it is important to follow an overall healthy dietary pattern,” she told Healthline. “Emphasize a variety of fruits and vegetables and whole grains and limit red and processed meats, sugar-sweetened beverages, ultra-processed foods, and refined grain products.”

“Eating a diet rich in fiber and whole grains, dairy and calcium, and limiting processed and red meat and alcohol is what really reduces your risk of developing cancer,” added Thanki.

The American Cancer Society estimates there will be about 108,000 new cases of colon cancer and nearly 50,000 new cases of rectal cancer in the United States in 2026.

The incidence rate is slightly higher in men than in females.

The organization reports that the rate of colorectal cancer cases in the United States has declined since the mid-1980s, but they note that most of that decrease has occurred in older adults.

The incidence rate among people under 50 increased by nearly 3% from 2013 to 2022. Colorectal cancer is now the leading cause of death from cancer for U.S. adults under the age of 50.

Colorectal cancer occurs when cells in the large intestine grow out of control. About 70% of cases begin in the colon.

There are a number of symptoms of colorectal cancer. Some of the common ones include:

Diet is considered one of the risk factors for colorectal cancer. However, there are other considerations.

Farhadi said genetics, obesity, smoking, alcohol consumption, and a sedentary lifestyle can also increase a person’s risk of developing colorectal cancer.

Shams-White noted that the American Cancer Society Guideline for Diet and Physical Activity for Cancer Prevention recommended achieving and maintaining a healthy weight, being physically active, following a healthy eating pattern, and avoiding alcohol and tobacco.

Thanki points out that there are risk factors for colorectal cancer that can be modified and others that can’t.

“Among non-modifiable factors, the biggest are age, a personal or family history of colorectal cancer or advanced polyps, inherited syndromes such as Lynch syndrome, and longstanding inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s colitis),” he told Healthline.

“On the modifiable side, the evidence is strongest for obesity, physical inactivity, smoking, alcohol, and diets high in red and processed meat and low in fiber, whole grains, and calcium,” he added.

Colorectal cancer treatment outcomes improve if the disease is caught at an early stage. The 5-year relative survival for localized colorectal cancer is 91.3%. The 5-year relative survival rate for colorectal cancer caught at various stages, including cancer that has spread, is 65.4%.

Shams-White points out that the American Cancer Society Colorectal Cancer Guidelines recommend that people at average risk of colorectal cancer start getting screened at age 45.

“Screening can help prevent cancer by finding abnormal cells and polyps so they can be removed before they can become colorectal cancer, as well as detect cancer at an earlier stage,” she said.

Thanki had similar advice. “Get screened starting at 45, or earlier if you have a family history or other risk factors, because colonoscopies can prevent cancer by removing polyps,” he said. “And never ignore symptoms like rectal bleeding or a change in bowel habits at any age.”

#4781. Aniioki A9 Pro Max review: Basically an electric motorcycle that you can pedal

There are electric bikes, there are electric motorcycles, and then there are machines like the Aniioki A9 Pro Max that plant a flag somewhere in the increasingly large no-man’s-land between the two.

Technically, it has pedals. You can pedal it fairly effectively too, with the actually adjustable seat. You can even pedal it for fun, which is more than I can say for some of the increasingly motorcycle-shaped “e-bikes” I’ve tested lately.

But let’s get something out of the way right at the beginning: this isn’t a street-legal electric bicycle in the US. Not when we’re talking about dual motors producing up to 6,000W of peak power and speeds of around 45 mph.

And you know what? That’s fine. As long as we’re all honest about what this thing is.

The Aniioki A9 Pro Max is absolutely massive, and the spec sheet makes that abundantly clear.

The version I tested uses a pair of 2,500W direct-drive hub motors, one in each wheel, with Aniioki claiming 3,000W peak power from each motor. That gives the bike a combined peak figure of 6,000W and up to 250 Nm of combined torque. It’s hard to overstate how massive that is.

Then there’s the battery. You can choose between a 60V 70Ah pack with 4.2 kWh of capacity or an even larger 60V 80Ah pack packing 4.8 kWh. For comparison, many typical commuter e-bikes have somewhere around 500-700 Wh of battery. The smaller battery here is roughly six to eight times that size. That’s absolutely in the territory of legit light electric motorcycles.

Aniioki claims up to 230+ miles (370 km) of pedal-assist range, though as usual, you should take maximum e-bike range figures as best-case numbers. Using the throttle and enjoying those big motors is going to dramatically reduce that figure. Even so, with more than 4 kWh of battery underneath you, range anxiety isn’t exactly the first thing that comes to mind.

All that hardware comes with a predictable penalty: weight. The 70Ah model tips the scales at around 188 lb (85 kg), while the 80Ah version approaches 193 lb (87.5 kg). Those aren’t e-bike weights. Those are motorcycle weights. Again, you can see the direction this is going.

Here’s where the A9 Pro Max gets more interesting to me.

A lot of high-powered e-motos include pedals seemingly as a regulatory fig leaf. They’re technically there, but the geometry is so bad that nobody in their right mind would want to pedal the thing farther than across a parking lot. Even some smaller and presumably Class 2 legal e-bikes that have moto-style frames are nearly unpedalable for actual riding over any reasonable distance.

But the A9 here is actually pedalable thanks to having something that more closely resembles a bicycle seat, plus adjustability that lets riders dial in the correct seat height.

The A9 Pro Max feels more like a strange combination of an oversized fat-tire e-bike and a small electric motorcycle. There’s a Shimano 7-speed drivetrain and a huge 72-tooth chainring, meaning the pedals aren’t entirely ornamental.

I actually enjoyed pedaling it with the pedal assist engaged. You’re obviously not going to mistake a nearly 200-pound machine rolling on enormous 26 x 4.8-inch tires for a lightweight fitness bike, but there’s something fun about contributing some human power while two giant hub motors do most of the heavy lifting.

And when you don’t feel like pedaling, there’s a full-twist throttle waiting for you.

That combination is really the appeal here. You can ride it more like an e-bike when the mood strikes, or twist the throttle and treat it more like a lightweight e-moto.

And again, I don’t want to beat a dead horse here, but remember: the pedals don’t make this an electric bicycle. It’s still an e-moto, but it’s one that you can actually have fun pedaling. You can treat it like a mech suit, where pedaling translates into crazy power, as if you have super-human legs. And with the insanely large 72t chainring, pedaling at higher speeds is actually doable. Though I’ll tell you right now, pedaling at 40 mph (64 km/h) is not exactly a normal or natural feeling.

And it’s worth pointing out that at a starting price of US $2,899 (or more for the larger battery capacities), that’s a fairly reasonable price compared to most e-motos that can be more limiting in how and where you can ride them.

Fortunately, Aniioki seems to understand that putting this much power on two wheels requires more serious components than the average bicycle.

The braking setup is particularly wild. There are two massive 300mm brake rotors on the front wheel and another 300mm rotor out back, along with a linked CBS braking system. The front uses custom eight-piston calipers (the pair of quad-piston calipers) while the rear gets a custom six-piston setup.

There’s also an adjustable air-suspension fork with 110mm of travel, rear suspension to smooth out bumps at higher speeds, integrated lighting and turn signals, and a large five-inch display that even incorporates features like Bluetooth audio and a recording camera.

That brings us to the elephant in the room.

In the US, consumer-product rules generally define a low-speed electric bicycle around a motor of less than 750W and a maximum motor-powered speed below 20 mph (32 km/h), while individual states use their own operating laws that typically match the familiar Class 1/2/3 framework. A 6,000W machine capable of around 45 mph (72 km/h) blows straight through normal limits.

So please don’t see pedals and assume this belongs on your local bicycle path.

Where and how you can legally operate something like the A9 Pro Max depends on your local laws and whether it can qualify under another vehicle category. For many owners, the sensible place to enjoy its full performance is going to be private property or other areas where such vehicles are permitted.

That caveat doesn’t make the bike itself bad. It just means buyers need to understand what they’re buying.

And judged on what it actually is rather than what the word “e-bike” on the product page suggests, I had a lot of fun on it.

There are certainly riders who would look at a nearly 200-pound, 45 mph machine and say, “Why not just buy an electric motorcycle?” That’s a perfectly reasonable question.

In addition to kW power limits, the legal boundary for what is an e-bike should also include weight. Anything over 100lbs including battery is no longer an e-bike and it carries a dangerous amount of momentum once it is cruising. 190 lbs is ridiculous.

But I also understand the appeal of this weird middle ground. The A9 Pro Max retains enough bicycle DNA that you can pedal it around and enjoy pedal assist, yet has enough battery and motor underneath you to deliver something much closer to small-motorcycle performance when you twist the throttle.

Imagine going off-road and getting to fly up hills while pedaling hard, but then being able to switch to throttle once your legs get worn out. Sure, it’s not everyone’s cup of tea, but it’s a cup of tea.

This bike is big. It’s heavy. It’s absurdly powerful by e-bike standards. And it absolutely isn’t the machine I’d recommend for someone looking for a normal street-legal electric bicycle.

But if what you actually want is a big, powerful electric two-wheeler that still lets you turn the pedals when the mood strikes, the Aniioki A9 Pro Max makes a surprisingly compelling argument for this increasingly bizarre category of pedal-equipped e-motos.

#4780. The 40 Best Sci-Fi and Fantasy Books of 2026 So Far

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Featuring stories about app-based love, A.I., and way more. Sound familiar?

AS WE START to inch closer and closer to the end of the year, we know you’re going to be looking to feel cozy as the weather starts to get colder. Luckily, there are plenty of exciting sci-fi and fantasy books to curl up with a big mug of something hot with and read next to a fire.

There's new releases from mainstays like Jim Butcher and Matt Dinniman (two in fact, plus an upcoming TV show). There's all manner of space operas, cyberpunk thrillers, quests to kill gods, and even a wolf who sets out to kill the human race. And toward the end of the year, Emily St. John Mandel of Station Eleven fame returns with a new hopeful futuristic tale. As summer winds down, new books will continue to offer a much-needed escape throughout 2026.

Admittedly, there's been a lot of media begging for our attention this year, like The Odyssey, the World Cup, and soon Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three. But once the adrenaline of those action-packed watches wear off, it'll be the perfect time to crack open a new read and lock into assassins dealing with an alien invasion or a botched quest to clone the founding fathers (seriously).

Below is our list of the best reads of the year no matter what kind of sci-fi or fantasy you're interested in. Keep checking back as the year continues to progress for more updates.

A group of civilians are chosen to accompany veteran astronauts on a trip to Saturn's moon, Titan. They struggle to orbit the planet, and after some struggle, they manage to get back on course and return to Earth. But the Earth they left doesn't seem to be the planet they remember.

The 18th (yes, 18th!) book in Butcher's long-running Dresden Files series finds its titular character, Harry Dresden, struggling with grief. But Chicago is struggling, his brother is seriously ill, and he's now betrothed to a vampire. He'll have to put his own feelings aside to be the wizard everyone needs him to be.

Think dating is hard right now? Maybe you'll find solace in For Human Use, where a new app helps people find love with cadavers. You read that right. And as the app gains popularity, two men behind its funding and growth are pitted against one another.

Best known for his Dungeon Crawler Carl series, Matt Dinniman is back with a standalone novel. Oliver lives on the planet New Sonora, but when Earth decides to evict the planet's tenants, they make a deadly game of it, allowing Earth's gamers to use war machines for fun. Oliver decides to try and save his home no matter what.

Leena can see the dead, but keeps her secret closely guarded. When her brother falls ill, she decides to bargain away her secret to a dangerous merchant. Her trade leads her to a mysterious estate, where she has to fight for her life to escape the merchant's grasp.

The first in a new trilogy, Tao Wong's The First Step follows a young farmer who joins a school of cultivation, and begins a magical journey filled with martial arts, Chinese mythology, and a chance at immortality.

It's post-WWI Britain, and what people hope to be a time of peace is overtaken by a new threat. Fae are taking children, and one vet decides he'll be the one to bring them back.

If you don't normally read short story collections, now's your chance. Featuring award-winning and nominated stories, this book may be the perfect read to get you out of a reading slump with tales you can finish in one sitting.

A grief support group gets dark with the newest release from horror writer Eric LaRocca. After the death of his husband, Simeon becomes enmeshed with The Wretches, whose intense methods to process the death of loved ones leads Simeon to a mysterious man who promises they can all get one last moment with a loved one for a steep price.

The graduate of a deadly academy is the protagonist of Mark Lawrence's newest novel. Rue, now an old woman, is finally at peace with her violent upbringing. But as soon as she thinks she's entered retirement, the sins of her past come back to haunt her.

Trees can drag you to your death. Artificial monsters stalk the lands. And alien men wander around town. John Maraintha is dropped on the planet Scythia and has to find a way to adapt and survive.

Fans of classic folktale retellings will enjoy this take on The Little Mermaid. Rather than following Ariel, it centers on her granddaughter, who is awash in complex politics after the assassination of her father. To save her family's legacy, she makes a deal with the famed sea-witch Ursla.

If you're a fan of The Substance, you may enjoy this new book. A young struggling writer named Maggie meets an established producer who's looking to revive her career. The solution to both of their problems is an experimental procedure–that takes Maggie's youth and gives it to the older producer–along with a $3 million payout that helps with Maggie's money troubles. But both women quickly realize that the blood transfusion is anything but a simple transaction.

Space operas are a sci-fi subgenre that never get old. When a starship's crew returns to their home galaxy after a decade away, they find the once peaceful space they knew is now on the brink of war–and they're expected to fight in it. It's up to the ship's captain to make life or death decisions that may have irrevocable impacts on her crew.

A ten-year-old girl goes on a journey with her AI toy to reach New York in this novel all about the complex relationship between man and machine.

This debut follows a billionaire who has prepared for the apocalypse and is ready to survive in his bunker with his family. But above ground, raiders are also fighting to stay alive, and aren't too happy with their new neighbors.

Earth is in ruins. A colony ship on the way to its new home keeps its original civilians in cryostasis, while their descendants maintain the vessel on its four hundred yearlong journey to a new planet. But midway through the trip, the crew of descendants starts to wonder why they're spending their lives in service of a world they'll never see.

A beloved actor in an epic fantasy franchise where much of the characters believe the world is real makes a bold choice to break out of the false reality the studio has built, and convince his co-stars to go with him.

The eighth, highly anticipated book in the Dungeon Crawler Carl series picks up on the tenth floor, where Carl and Donut try to make sense of the system AI's mysterious plans and learn more about why it calls the eleventh floor 'A Parade of Horribles'.

If you're yearning for an epic tale of political intrigue, this new Ann Leckie read is for you. The empire of Radch is dealing with internal turmoil, and when a major decision is made on the religious site called Radiant Star, that turmoil could result in irrevocable changes to everyone in the city of Ooioiaa.

#4779. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: What Breast Cancer Patients Need When Treatment Ends

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Supporting your health & well-being at every stage of your breast cancer journey

Resources to support your emotional health and well-being

Tips for nourishing your body and mind while living with breast cancer

Navigating your next steps after diagnosis

A guide to medications, treatments, and procedures for breast cancer

Guide to symptoms, tests, and screenings for early detection

Resources to support you during remission or recurrence

Breast cancer awareness has never been higher. Every October, the world turns pink and the key messages—that early diagnosis saves lives and that knowing the risk factors reduces the risk—are hard to miss.

Breast cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death amongst women in most countries, with an estimated 694,000 deaths annually and around 8.2 million women globally living with a breast cancer diagnosis, according to 2024 data from the World Health Organization (WHO)’s Global Health Observatory.

But when October ends, and the wall-to-wall campaigns move on, what has awareness actually changed for those impacted by breast cancer?

For Marisa Weiss, MD, the answer is that there is always more to be done, and she’s uniquely placed to hold that view.

Dr. Weiss has treated breast cancer patients for more than 30 years. In 2000, she founded Breastcancer.org, a not-for-profit that provides expert-reviewed medical and lifestyle information on breast health and breast cancer to millions of people globally.

Sixteen years ago, she was diagnosed with stage 1 breast cancer, becoming, in her own words, a “dual citizen” in that moment, with lived experience on both sides of the doctor’s desk.

I had the pleasure of sitting down with Dr. Weiss as part of Healthline’s Breast Cancer Awareness Month coverage to talk about how awareness has changed care for the better for millions of people around the world, but why critical gaps remain, and how access to trusted information and community can help close those gaps.

“It’s good that awareness is high, but knowledge remains low,” she said. The misconception she sees most is the belief that breast cancer is something that happens to other families.

“Most people think they’re off the hook because it doesn’t run in their family,” Dr. Weiss explained. In fact, 85%-90% of people who get breast cancer have no known family history and no known gene in the family, “so we’re all at risk,” she warns.

For most, a diagnosis arrives as a shock. “They’re completely surprised, flattened by it. Their life is upside down, and they scramble to find what they need to know,” Dr. Weiss noted.

That aftershock caused by a diagnosis is at the core of why Breastcancer.org exists. Because the person whose life is at stake is increasingly expected to direct their own care and advocate for their needs, access to accurate and empowering information is critical in that process. “Decisions aren’t being made around the patient and for the patient in a bubble,” Dr. Weiss said. “Decision-making is supposed to be shared.”

With appointments hard to get and clinicians stretched, she said patients have to do more of the work.

In practice, Dr. Weiss says that means preparing by writing down your family history on both sides and making sure your care team knows who you are. “What’s important to you? Who’s in your life? Do you want more children? Are you planning a vacation? All those decisions can have an impact on the care you receive.”

Where Dr. Weiss sees the widest gap is after treatment ends. Speaking from personal experience, she said: “I had the best care possible, and there were still gaps. You can find yourself alone with lots of questions and fears.”

Understandably, a great deal of focus and attention is centered on diagnosis and treatment, she said. Then it stops. “When your life is supposed to go back to normal, it never does. You have to find a new normal. That quiet phase can be really lonely and difficult.”

For Dr. Weiss, the questions that fill that silence are often as practical as they are emotional: “How do I know my treatment is working? How do I tell leftover side effects from new ones? How do I go back to work, and who do I tell? How do I talk to my kids? What about that new treatment I heard about on TV last night?”

That post-treatment period can also be the first time anyone has really had a chance to stop, take stock, and start asking “what next?”

“You might think, what happened to me? Who do I want to be moving forward? How do I have a long life full of wonderful things, and remain as independent as possible?”

Some of what patients do post-care never reaches their doctor at all, with Dr. Weiss pointing to a growing amount of personal care happening outside the hospital: GLP-1s, peptides, hormonal therapies, supplements, medical cannabis, to name a few. Breastcancer.org’s annual Pulse survey shows that people reported being interested in all of those things and more, and that they tend to learn about them online rather than risk the stigma of bringing them up with their doctors.

“They don’t really trust that their doctor knows much about these things,” she said, “and they don’t want a conversation that makes them feel judged. Some patients worry about what ends up in their medical record and then everyone’s going to know.”

Dr. Weiss says the stakes are real, because some of those choices can interact with cancer medications with potential for adverse or unexpected side effects. “That is why people turn to Breastcancer.org with questions that are personal, private, and important, including “what do I need to share with my doctor, and who’s on a need-to-know basis?”

Peer communities fill part of that gap. “Breastcancer.org’s members share medical information, tips, and practical advice with people who have just had the call, or are about to start treatment and don’t know what to expect,” Dr. Weiss shared, and said that while she values that kind of support system hugely, it does come with a caveat:

The same community can also be intrusive. Dr. Weiss describes standing at a party, drink in hand, when someone asks what kind of cancer you had, what you did, and whether it came back. Her advice to patients, which she took herself: “Put up your hand and say, ‘thank you so much for caring, but I cannot hear another story right now.’”

On the topic of AI and its impact on treatment and care, Dr. Weiss is cautiously optimistic. On the treatment front, she points to tools that help radiologists read mammograms more thoroughly and assess future risk as game changers in the fight against breast cancer.

Breastcancer.org also uses AI for tasks such as finding citations and interpreting pathology reports. But like many, she is wary of misinformation. “When you’re fearful, you look for reassurance, and you don’t want to be reassured by misinformation. When it comes to health information, every word matters.”

Her final advice is for the appointment itself, which she says she has even struggled with. “When they start speaking quickly in complex medical language, you can get lost really fast. The risk is you kind of fake it. That must not happen.”

“Do your research in advance. Write things down. Bring someone you trust as a second set of ears. Ask direct questions. Don’t worry if it sounds funny or silly. It’s always a smart question when you are dealing with your health.” Just be prepared for the questions to multiply from there. “Once you get a certain set of questions answered, that raises more questions. So just write it all down.”

If breast cancer has touched your life, know that you are not alone. Healthline’s Bezzy Breast Cancer Community is a space for peer support, feel-good stories, and advice in a welcoming, stigma-free environment when your lived experience is seen, heard and valued.

#4778. What Young Adults Want Parents to Know About Them

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

I am a psychologist who helps to run an Intensive Outpatient Program (IOP) for young adults ages 18-26. These young people are facing mental health challenges that temporarily prevent them from enjoying their lives and relationships to the fullest extent they might. They also may be struggling with independence, as well as career or college progression. Here are some of the themes that I have heard consistently over the past few years. I hope it helps you to connect with and support your young adult children.

I do care about my future. If I am taking a leave of absence from college or am struggling with keeping or finding a job, it is not because I do not care. I care very much, actually. However, I am struggling with anxiety, depression, or other mental health concerns that need to be addressed before I can resume my journey.

I may not always like you, but I do love you. We have spent a lot of time together over the years, and it has not always been easy. In fact, we may disagree about a lot of things. However, that does not mean that I do not love you. Yes, I can not like you at times and still love you. Please remember that.

I want you to listen and see me for who I am. My personality and values are very important to me. I may not have everything figured out yet, and I am still learning about myself and the world, but I ask that you respect me for who I am today. Ask questions and be curious about what is important to me. If you ask in an open, loving way, I am happy to let you into my world.

I am frightened of the future, so please do not minimize the state of the world I am inheriting. Let’s be honest, the older generations have not left us with a world that is thriving and well. Selfish politicians, wars, climate change — all of this is stressful to me. So, yes, I have lost faith in “the system.” And can you blame me? Please be sympathetic when I am discouraged about the state of the world.

The world is different now than it was when you were my age (and not in a good way). It is a difficult time to be a young adult. With the introduction of AI and the comparisons on social media, life is particularly stressful for me. Yes, you had your own stressors, but please know that what we are dealing with now is new territory. No one knows where it will lead, which is stressful and scary for me.

Online friends are real friends too. I know you may not understand because the world is different today, but connecting with others online can be meaningful too. Especially while living through the pandemic, we had to get creative in how we meet and interact with others. Sometimes online connection feels safer and easier, actually.

Please, never give up on me. I know I am going through a difficult time. I may be struggling with my next steps academically, professionally, or personally. That does not mean that I have failed or that I will struggle my whole life. I just need some help and support now. I am excited for what is next but may need to heal and regroup first. Please stay in my corner as I prepare for what’s next.

#4777. DeepWay electric semi arrives in New Zealand, and gets a new name

New Zealand’s Foodstuffs North Island Limited has given its latest electric semi truck an electrifying new identity, courtesy of a second-grade student at a local elementary school.

The Chinese-built DeepWay Star began delivering chilled and frozen groceries across New Zealand’s lower North Island earlier this year – and, after a naming competition organized with students at Russell Street School in Palmerston North, the big HD EV has got a new name: Evie.

The winning name came from Year 2 (read: second grade) student named Madison, who beat out suggestions including Buzzy Bee, Lightning, and Bolt. Madison got to officially unveil the truck’s new name alongside her classmates, local officials and Foodstuffs representatives.

“Our trucks are out on the road every day delivering food to stores and communities, so we thought it would be great to get the kids involved and give our first electric truck a bit of personality,” explains Foodstuffs North Island General Manager Supply Chain, Yang Zhang. “There were some brilliant ideas, but Evie was a pretty fitting name for an EV. The best part is knowing Madison and the other students will be able to spot Evie out on the road and know they played a part in it.”

Madison was allowed to do the unveiling honors, revealing Evie’s new name alongside her other classmates, Palmerston North’s Mayor, Grant Smith, local MP Tangi Utikeri, and local PAK’nSAVE, New World, and Four Square grocers who will be receiving deliveries from Evie.

In its first few months on the road, Evie’s travelled nearly 45,000 kilometers (~28,000 miles) and avoided more than 81,000 kg of harmful carbon emissions – which the company claims is roughly equivalent to taking 35 ICE cars off the road for a full year.

As for the truck itself, it has a sort of Tesla-ish, anteater-y look, and significantly longer range than the StarWay, offering more than 500 km (~310 miles) of range from its 600 kWh CATL-built LFP battery packs that can plug into charge ports two at a time for lickety-quick charging in about 30 minutes. If that’s too long of a wait, the Star can swap its tired batteries for fresh ones in special battery-sway stations in just six minutes.

The DeepWay’s electric motors put out 491 kW (~660 hp) of power, and a positively tectonic 75,000 (!) Nm (~55,000 lb-ft) (!!) of torque – more than enough to get the 50 tons (100,000 lb.) of GVWR it’s rated for up to speed.

It is great to see electric trucks replacing Diesel. I just can’t understand why EV adoption is so slow to take off in New Zealand. It has plenty of great low cost EVs and petrol is all imported and expensive.

You can check out the pictures, above, then let us know what you think of the big Chinese BEV and it’s fun new name in the comments.

#4775. The Next Generation of Weight-Loss Drugs Is Reshaping People’s Looks—And Not in a Flattering Way

WHEN YOU LOSE weight through traditional diet and exercise, you tend to see a gradual slimming down of your face. But when you add in gray-market peptides like retatrutide, you’re expediting the weight loss process. That also includes rapid fat loss in the face, leaving a sunken and hollowed-out look people are dubbing “reta face.”

Online Reddit communities on peptides and biohacking are packed with people commenting on changes to their facial appearance after taking retatrutide—a triple hormone agonist of the GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon receptors that’s expected to become the next generation of weight-loss injections. One clinical trial found those taking retatrutide had more than double the weight loss of people taking Ozempic.

To be fair, “Ozempic face” has also been an issue. But with Eli Lilly expected to apply for FDA approval of retatrutide in early 2027 for obesity and other conditions, doctors say reta will likely cause more facial volume issues. Is there any way to prevent these unflattering side effects? We went straight to the doctors currently treating people with facial symptoms from GLPs.

WHILE RETA FACE isn’t an official medical diagnosis, it’s a real phenomenon. “The facial changes can be kind of dramatic,” says Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center. But the lack of criteria has also caused some debate over what qualifies as reta face.

On the r/BodyHackGuide community (with over 87,000 contributors dubbed “Lab Rats”), reta face before-and-after posts are recurring discussion threads. Some describe reta face as a chiseled look after weight loss while Ozempic face is the more sickly face. Others argue that “reta face” and “Ozempic face” are simply two terms to describe the sunken look from your face losing fat.

“Reta face is the new Ozempic face,” says dermatologist Gary Goldenberg, MD. “Since retatrutide is a triple biologic agonist that produces more significant weight loss than GLP peptides, patients may have an even more exaggerated appearance of a sunken, aged look.”

That means cheeks can become flat and hollow, temples narrow, and undereye areas can look sunken and dark. “Facial bones can also become more prominent as fat disappears,” says Dr. Goldenberg. “The skin can thin, as collagen and elastic fibers have less underlying fat plumping them up.”

Joshua Zeichner, MD, director of cosmetic and clinical research in dermatology at Mount Sinai Hospital, says the shape of your face changes with any significant weight loss—it’s just more apparent when someone is on a weight-loss medication.

ABSOLUTELY. DR. ZEICHNER says minimizing the appearance of facial wasting is all about losing weight slowly—even when taking a GLP-1 or reta. While you can’t target specific areas for fat loss, Dr. Goldenberg recommends pacing yourself while still getting plenty of protein on your plate and being selective about meals that have enough nutrients.

If you already have reta face and the appearance bothers you, Dr. Goldenberg recommends seeing a dermatologist. “Collagen stimulators and fillers are a very common treatment for this problem,” he says. “Volume can be restored and contouring can be improved with these treatments.”

#4774. The 7 Best Electric Toothbrushes for Men in 2026, Tested by Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Cleaner, healthier teeth with picks for every budget and style of brushing.

YOU ALREADY KNOW you need to brush at least twice a day, no matter what toothpaste or mouthwash you use. But technique matters just as much. Even for me—a grooming editor who writes about this stuff—it can feel like a chore. In the morning, I brush before coffee when I’m barely awake. At night, I’m wiped out from the day or drifting off for less wholesome reasons. That’s why I love electric toothbrushes: they simplify brushing and deliver a better clean by doing most of the work for you.

Unlike manual toothbrushes, electric toothbrushes use vibrations and automated head movement to remove plaque and debris. Many models include smart programs for whitening or gum care, interchangeable heads for sensitive or deep cleaning, and built-in timers. Some of the latest options even feature AI that tracks your brushing and suggests improvements.

But the main selling point of electric toothbrushes is their ability to clean more thoroughly and efficiently than manual options, using power and vibrations no hand can match. Top-tier electric toothbrushes can be pricey, but they’re an investment in your smile. It’s the closest you can get to a dentist-level clean at home.

For the past two years, the Oral-B Series 10 has been listed at the top of this list. It remains the best overall electric toothbrush; however, it’s currently sold out everywhere due to this demand. The model that immediately preceded it, the iO Series 9, is the next best thing. It features many of the same features and power, just with a less high-tech charging mount (which may be a benefit for some who prefer something lighter and less complicated).

Series 9 is similarly a premium electric toothbrush packed with advanced features designed to elevate your oral care routine. Just like the 10, there are seven customizable modes—including Daily Clean, Sensitive, Super Sensitive, Intense, Gum Care, Tongue Clean, and Whitening—this brush adapts to your needs, whether you have sensitive gums or want a deep clean. Its oscillating, vibrating round brush head provides a powerful yet gentle clean, and the built-in pressure sensor ensures you're brushing with the right amount of force, lighting up red (too strong), blue (too weak), or green (just right) based on your pressure.

The Series 9 pairs with a companion app to track your brushing in real time across 16 zones of the mouth, offering instant feedback and a visual map of missed areas. I’m not a huge tech junkie, especially when it comes to something like brushing my teeth, since I just want to get it over with quickly. But this is one of the few apps that genuinely adds value, with accurate tracking, clear visuals, and brushing reminders.

Even if you skip the app, the built-in display shows your selected mode and a timer, though the latter is easier to read in the app. That being said, it’s nearly impossible to achieve a 100 percent clean according to the app (I usually aim for between 80 and 90) without brushing for five or more minutes, which is not recommended because it can damage enamel. If you’re a perfectionist, this will prove annoying.

In terms of design, the Series 9 is sleek and solid, and comes with a sturdy travel case. It charges in just three hours (significantly faster than most others on this list) and comes with four replacement heads, which should cover your first year of use if you replace them every three months, as dentists advise.

If you prefer sonic, this toothbrush offers nearly the same level of features and effectiveness as the Oral-B iO Series 9. At $340, it's also one of the most expensive electric toothbrushes, but the price includes five modes and three intensity settings to fully customize your brushing experience, along with an innovative charging cup.

Interchangeable brush heads, specifically designed for tasks like whitening or tongue cleaning, also help you achieve optimal results with minimal effort. Similar to the Series 9, it also has app-enabled smart modes that provide personalized feedback on your brushing habits and overall progress. Plus, the charging travel case makes it easy to travel while protecting your investment.

Women’s Health Associate Style and Commerce Editor Shannen Zitz has been using this toothbrush for the past year and says it’s the cleanest her teeth have ever felt. “I’ve long been using an electric toothbrush, so I didn’t expect to be too blown away by this one. I was wrong.” She likes how it pairs multiple brush heads, cleaning modes, and a timer with real-time app feedback to keep her brushing technique on track. The sleek charging cup also makes storage and charging effortless, even on a tiny sink, she says.

Read More: Are Electric Toothbrushes Better?

Men’s Health Associate Producer Janie Booth says the round, oscillating head reminds her of the tool dental hygienists use to polish teeth during a professional cleaning. The brush comes with a compact stand and a travel case, both of which are easy to pack. It doesn’t include a wall plug—just a USB cord—but the battery lasts impressively long.

Booth says she’s used it for a month without recharging once. If your biggest concern is avoiding charging as much as possible, the Rev is your best bet. The battery even outperforms the Oral-B iO Series 9 and Philips Sonicare DiamondClean, both of which are roughly $300 more expensive.

I’ve used all three as my daily driver at different times, and the Rev battery lasts at least a week longer. You can expect to get at least 5 weeks from a single full charge with twice-a-day use. The rest of its offerings are pretty minimal, though, again, this will be welcomed by newcomers. It only offers three levels of intensity, but none are too strong for sensitive teeth.

However, they’re not quite as powerful as the most intense settings on Oral-B and Philips, though they are close. The Oral-B iO Series 9 offers about 10,500 oscillations per minute on its Daily Clean setting, while the Rev goes up to 9,630 oscillations per minute. Considering the $300 price difference between the two, the slight dip is a worthy trade-off.

Before I upgraded to an electric, I was a devotee of Colgate’s Active Prevention Foaming Toothbrush. The heads are as soft as they come, and the handle fits perfectly in my hand. Naturally, I was thrilled when the brand made an electric version, adding vibration to those two core features. To be clear, this is battery-powered, so it’s not rechargeable. But you also don’t need to worry about recharging it every couple of weeks. I get a little more than a month out of each set of batteries (two AAAs), so while it’s under $15 at first, I plan to spend more over time.

Still, I haven’t tried a battery-powered toothbrush that lasts that long without sputtering or losing efficiency, like Colgate’s can. It’s not the most powerful electric toothbrush, as Colgate doesn’t even list its vibrations per minute (which usually means it’s nothing to write home about). But I’ve yet to find a battery-powered toothbrush that can compete with the power of rechargeable options, so it’s inherent to the design.

No matter your background, everyone shares one truth: we all lie to our dentists about flossing. They see through it, and they roll their eyes for good reason. Daily flossing is essential, which is why Waterpik built a toothbrush with an integrated water flosser. Its all-in-one design lets you brush and floss at the same time, saving effort while leaving your teeth feeling dentist-clean.

The brush includes two intensity modes and a timer, but the standout is the built-in Waterpik. You can brush with or without the water flosser, though why skip it? While it doesn’t offer the smart features of higher-end models, the unique water flosser justifies its higher price tag. Plus, its 30,000 vibrations per minute match those of the similarly priced Zina45. In that sense, it’s like the water flosser is free.

This toothbrush offers 33,000 vibrations per minute, four custom settings, a two-minute timer, and soft, nylon bristles. It’s everything you need for a decent electric toothbrush. However, there are two features that help it stand out. For one, the magnetic USB touch charger is super convenient, making recharging as simple as any option on this list. As someone who regularly forgets to recharge his devices, I appreciate how easy this one makes the process.

It also comes with a polishing head, one of the few electric toothbrushes that do. This tiny rubber head is designed to make your teeth look smoother and shinier by focusing on surface stains and plaque removal rather than deep cleaning between teeth. I use mine after brushing, even if I brush with a separate toothbrush, to complete the full at-home dentist-level clean. It also comes with four replaceable polishing heads, so you won’t have to worry about replacing them for some time.

At first, the smaller toothbrush head on the Suri 2.0 felt less effective than the OG model, but over time, it delivers the same clean. The brush comes with a compact stand and a travel case, both designed for travel. It doesn’t include a wall plug—just a USB cord—but the battery lasts impressively long. It’s the only other electric toothbrush we’ve tested that lasts over a month on a single charge, though I find it’s a couple of days shorter than the Quip Rev.

This brush delivers 33,000 vibrations per minute yet remains whisper-quiet. Its sleek case hides a UV-C light that kills 99 percent of germs on the brush head, keeping it clean wherever you take it. Plus, the head and bristles are eco-friendly, made from recyclable, plant-based cornstarch and castor oil. Overall, it’s powerful, sustainable, and travel-ready.

When choosing an electric toothbrush, you’ll need to decide between a sonic or oscillating brush head. There isn’t one right answer; it just comes down to preference.

Toothbrushes have gone smart, too. Most models include the basics—a strong motor and a built-in timer—but many now add extras like brushing modes, pressure sensors, and even AI to track your habits and coach you to improve. The right features depend on what matters most to you.

Brushing your teeth is personal, shaped by your own needs and quirks. To find the best electric toothbrushes for every sensitivity and style, we tapped a wide group of Men’s Health testers. I spoke with dentists about their go-to brands, pulled in feedback from our original 2019 guide, and compiled a list of top contenders. I then distributed these toothbrushes to writers and editors, each of whom tested them for at least a month to judge comfort, ease of use, and long-term effectiveness. Based on that feedback, here are the eight best electric toothbrushes for men in 2026.

As with manual toothbrushes, electric toothbrush heads need to be replaced every few months. Because the latter tend to be more expensive, this makes owning electric models more expensive. I recommend buying the heads in bulk when available, as this can make for pretty substantial savings. Electric toothbrushes have more nooks and crevices than their manual counterparts, which means they require a little extra daily maintenance.

This means carefully rinsing them after every use to stave off funky toothpaste and spit residue. It’s also worth actually removing the brush head from time to time to wipe the attachment point where the head meets the handle. A cotton swab or even your old toothbrush is usually enough to do the trick.

It’s tempting to just toss old toothbrushes and toothbrush heads in the trash once they’ve outlived their usefulness. But they’re actually perfect for detailed cleaning work that requires moderately stiff bristles to clean out tight spaces. Think: Shower heads, hiking boots, bathroom grout, your dishwasher filter, bird feeders—you get the idea.
