#4773. Why One Good Thing Leads to Another

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

After reading the responses to my last post about the art of asking questions, in which I described the importance of becoming better listeners to ensure more meaningful connection with others, I’ve been thinking about something else: how one small action can set other good things in motion.

Here’s what got me thinking. A woman from a media company that uses puppets to teach elementary-school children important skills reached out. She was so excited about the idea of teaching genuine curiosity to young people that she is talking with her staff about creating episodes on asking interesting questions.

She wrote: I'm part of the team behind Sunnyside Roadshow, a daily, five-minute social-emotional learning program for elementary school children that uses puppetry, storytelling, and humor to help develop important life skills.

"As I read your article, I found myself wondering: Can we begin teaching children, at an early age, the art of being genuinely curious about other people? Kids are naturally eager to share their own experiences, and understandably so! But could we help them learn to pause, listen, ask another question, and show interest in what someone else is saying?

…Rather than simply teaching children not to interrupt and act on impulse, what if we could help them discover the joy of being genuinely interested in another person's experiences? Could we intentionally model curiosity through our characters' conversations, showing children how asking one thoughtful follow-up question can make someone feel heard and valued? If they worked on these skills together in the classroom, wouldn't we help raise more thoughtful humans?"

A post about ways to deepen conversation through becoming better listeners might lead to children learning how to show interest in others. Those children could bring that curiosity to their friendships, their families, and eventually their adult relationships. We have no way of knowing how far those ripples might travel.

Other people wrote that the post prompted them to reflect on their own conversational habits. They recognized themselves in the tendency to tell stories and talk about themselves rather than ask questions, and vowed to be more inquisitive.

That’s how it starts. Someone does something. Someone else responds. And on and on.

And it doesn’t require writing a post or creating a children’s program.

Think about the times you checked out at Trader Joe’s and were asked, “What are your plans for today?” or “Got anything fun planned this weekend?” For some customers, that might be the only conversation they have all day. What seems like a casual question can be a moment of genuine connection. And think about the difference that brief connection might make—not only for the person leaving the store, but also for the people they encounter throughout the day.

A few months ago, as I was checking out of Trader Joe’s, a clerk asked me about my plans, and I mentioned that I was having a party.

He ran off and returned with a gorgeous bouquet of flowers—all my favorite colors. He had no idea how much that unexpected kindness meant to me. And now, months later, I’m telling you about it. His gesture is still traveling.

My mother understood something about this, too. A New Yorker, she would often pay the toll for a complete stranger in the car behind her when crossing the George Washington Bridge.

Imagine pulling up to the tollbooth, reaching for your money, and being told that someone had already paid. Someone you didn’t know and probably would never meet. I loved that about her.

Did those drivers go on to do something kind for someone else? I don’t know. But my mother’s gestures stayed with me. That, too, is a ripple.

We often think that making a difference requires a grand plan, lots of time, or something extraordinary to offer. Meanwhile, we overlook the opportunities right in front of us: asking a question and truly listening to the answer, offering a sincere compliment, including someone who seems left out, or letting someone know that something they did mattered.

So here’s my challenge: Do one small thing today that might set other good things in motion.

Treat it as an experiment. Notice what happens—to the other person and to you. You may see an immediate response, or you may never know where your gesture leads.

Either way, tip over that first domino. And watch the fun begin.

And if the spirit moves you, email me and tell me what happened. I’d love to hear.

#4771. Women With Autoimmune Diseases More Likely to Be Misdiagnosed Than Men

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new international study found that women with autoimmune diseases often experience longer delays in getting a correct diagnosis compared to men.

The research, published in eClinicalMedicine on October 12, also shows that females report higher rates of being misdiagnosed, especially with mental health or psychosomatic conditions.

These findings highlight challenges in diagnosing autoimmune diseases and suggest that sex differences affect patients’ experiences in healthcare.

This is significant given that autoimmune diseases, conditions in which the body’s immune system attacks its own healthy cells, are estimated to affect around 4.6% of the U.S. population. Additionally, despite the observed disparities in diagnoses, women are almost two times as likely as men to be diagnosed with an autoimmune disease.

Researchers conducted an online survey between December 7, 2024, and March 7, 2025, inviting adults ages 18 and older who had a confirmed autoimmune or rheumatic disease.

The survey was carefully designed and tested with input from patients, charities, and medical experts to ensure it captured important information about patients’ diagnostic journeys.

Participants were asked about the time it took from when they first noticed symptoms to when they received their autoimmune diagnosis.

They also reported how many healthcare visits they made before diagnosis and whether they felt their symptoms were ever misdiagnosed as mental health issues, psychosomatic problems (physical symptoms caused or worsened by psychological factors), or another physical disease.

The survey was widely shared on social media, patient support groups, and community organizations to reach a broad audience.

Special efforts were made to include underrepresented groups such as males, younger individuals, and people from minority ethnic backgrounds.

The survey was available in five languages, and participants could complete it with help from researchers if needed.

To analyze the data, the team used statistical methods, adjusting for factors like age, type of autoimmune disease, continent of residence, and financial situation.

These methods helped compare the experiences of males and females while accounting for differences in disease types and other factors

The study included 6,607 participants, with 91.2% identifying as female and most living in the United Kingdom. On average, women were younger than men in the study.

Autoimmune thyroid disease was the most common condition reported. Non-autoimmune conditions like anxiety were more commonly reported by women, while men reported higher rates of hypertension.

One of the main findings was that women reported longer delays before getting a diagnosis. Nearly 32% of females experienced delays of four years or more from symptom onset to diagnosis, compared to about 26% of males.

On the other hand, men were more likely to be diagnosed within a year of symptom onset (nearly 50% of males versus 40% of females).

Women also made more visits to healthcare providers before diagnosis, with 26.2% having 11 or more visits compared to 18.4% of men.

When it came to misdiagnoses, women were significantly more likely to report that their symptoms had been mistaken for mental health issues (43.3% of females vs. 32.7% of males) or psychosomatic causes (33.9% of females vs. 21.5% of males).

However, there was no significant difference between men and women in being misdiagnosed with another physical disease.

The type of autoimmune disease also influenced misdiagnosis rates. Diseases with clear physical symptoms or definitive lab tests, like type 1 diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis, had lower rates of mental health and psychosomatic misdiagnoses.

In contrast, conditions such as autoimmune encephalitis or undifferentiated connective tissue disease had higher rates of these misdiagnoses (over 50%).

After adjusting for disease type and other factors, women still had higher odds of reporting mental health or psychosomatic misdiagnoses compared to men.

Other factors affected misdiagnosis rates, too. People living in continents outside the United Kingdom, those with lower household income, and certain disease groups were more likely to report psychiatric or psychosomatic misdiagnoses. Age, however, was not linked to the risk of being misdiagnosed.

Muhammad Qasim, MD, a pulmonologist and medical writer with MySleepApneaTeam, told Healthline that autoimmune diseases are often difficult to diagnose. Qasim wasn’t involved in the study.

“Early symptoms can be vague, fluctuate over time, and affect several parts of the body,” he said. “Fatigue, pain, sleep problems, brain fog, and mood changes do not immediately point to one diagnosis.”

Qasim echoed the study’s findings, explaining that similar symptoms may be interpreted differently in women versus men, with complaints being attributed to anxiety, stress, or psychosomatic causes.

However, there are probably multiple factors contributing to this phenomenon, he said.

“Differences in disease presentation, gaps in research, fragmented care, and unconscious bias can all contribute,” said Qasim. “Once a psychiatric explanation enters the medical record, there is also a risk that later clinicians view new symptoms through that same lens.”

Regarding unconscious bias, the study’s authors noted that women have historically been treated by doctors as “less credible” and more “emotional” in reporting their symptoms, which can influence how doctors interpret them.

These disparities in diagnosis are important, however, because longer waits and erroneous diagnoses can delay proper treatment and increase women’s frustration, leading them to stop asking for help.

The researchers suggest that healthcare providers need to be aware of these concerns and consider autoimmune diseases carefully when patients, especially females, present with more complicated symptoms.

Adam Carewe, MD, a physician in Boulder, CO, and a clinical informaticist with General Medicine who wasn’t involved in the study, offered guidance to those experiencing symptoms on how to obtain a proper diagnosis.

“Patients can keep an accurate symptom timeline, bring in family history, ask what else could be explaining these symptoms, ask for a plan for next steps if initial testing/treatment, do not change anything, and lastly get a second opinion,” he advised.

Carewe emphasized the value of not giving up on finding answers. “The most important thing for anyone with persistent symptoms of any kind is to continue to work with your primary care clinician and continue to advocate for yourself,” he said.

The comedian says strength training, running and consistency—not vanity—have transformed his health.

Funny and self-deprecating on screen, Romesh Ranganathan takes his health and fitness seriously off it. He's not your typical gym-goer, though. Rather than training to build a bodybuilder's physique or hit performance milestones, his focus is on staying strong, healthy and active as he gets older—and being there for his three sons.

“I got a medical when I turned 40 as I started to worry about my own mortality, not for myself, but because of my kids,” he told On: Yorkshire Magazine. “Before, when I was going to the gym or staying on top of fitness, I'd do it for some sort of vanity reason. I've long since abandoned that and have accepted that I'm never going to look good. So the second half is about my reaction to that medical.”

Now 48, Ranganathan revealed on the Wolf & Owl podcast that he's been training more consistently in recent months. He has previously said he lifts weights three or four times a week—sometimes more if his schedule allows—while also trying to keep his daily step count high.

“I started hitting the gym for weights about three to four times a week, sometimes more if I fancied, and was trying to up my step count and cardio, but my appetite for that is a struggle,” he said in an interview with Huel.

It's an approach that has helped him lose around 44 pounds over the past few years.

Running has also become a key part of his fitness journey. After initially hating it, the comedian went on to complete the London Marathon in both 2024 and 2025.

The turning point came after one piece of simple advice.

“Running is something that people had always recommended to me. But as soon as I had a go at it, I found it unbearable. I'd go out for a run and be blowing after two minutes, then start walking, run a bit more, start blowing again. I'd come back and just feel absolutely battered,” he told Runner's World.

“Then somebody gave me the basic tip of just slowing down a little bit and getting on top of my breathing. That is the single most helpful tip I've ever had; suddenly I went from someone who couldn't face running to seeing all of the benefits of it. That's not to say that it suddenly became easy.”

#4769. Why We Love Talking Animals

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

From Aesop to Orwell, from the Three Little Pigs to Bugs Bunny, our stories are full of talking animals. Foxes flatter, lions boast, and donkeys mope. For thousands of years, we have used animals to tell stories about ourselves.

But why use animals? Why not just use people?

Consider this short tale by the ancient Greek fabulist Aesop, The Fox and the Mask:

A fox broke into the house of an actor and noticed a mask in the midst of a pile of stage accessories. The fox dragged out the mask and nuzzled and swatted it for a few moments, before saying, “What a handsome face, pity he has no brains.”

Or consider this fable from the Ancient Indian Panchatantra, in which a rabbit outwits a lion:

A lion was terrorising the animals of the jungle, killing far more than he could eat. To appease him, the animals agreed that, each day, they would send him one of their number. When a rabbit’s turn came, he arrived late, telling the lion that another lion had kept him by claiming to be the true king of the jungle. Enraged, the lion demanded to see this imposter. The rabbit led him to a well, in which the lion saw his own reflection. Mistaking it for his rival, he leapt in and drowned.

The use of animals creates new and striking possibilities. It stokes the imagination, making the tale seem more original and entertaining, even charming, without which it might fall flat as moralising or patronising. We are more willing to listen to a fox than to a preacher, and more likely to remember what it has to say.

The use of animals also enables the storyteller to isolate a vice and caricature it, while at the same time providing a fresh perspective on it. Each animal becomes a shorthand for a particular human vice or trait. We are often resistant to criticism, especially when it concerns our character. But when we laugh at a vain crow or a pessimistic donkey, we may be laughing at ourselves. The animal creates a certain psychological distance, enabling us to recognise our faults without feeling accused and becoming defensive.

On a deeper level, talking animals create a continuum between human and animal, revealing us as part of nature and at one with it, while also highlighting what sets us apart from the rest of creation, namely, speech and reason (Greek, logos) and the capacity for moral reflection.

As I discuss in The Meaning of Myth, animals appeal especially to children, possibly because blurring the lines between human and animal is a form of pre-logical, magical thinking. Children readily attribute thoughts, feelings, and intentions to animals, and may find a talking rabbit or bear no more extraordinary than a talking human. For adults, the attraction is more subtle: the talking animal offers both an escape from reality and a means of understanding it, in particular, through the pleasure of analogising.

Finally, the use of animals can serve as a cover, a means of escaping censorship, or of generalising or universalising. Jean de La Fontaine (d. 1695) used the fable form to satirise French society, and George Orwell used it to satirise communism and other forms of totalitarianism, while also making us smile.

Animals delight us still today, every day, if only in cartoons and viral videos, because, as the fabulist might say, “So it is with men, too.”

You may also enjoy my companion piece, The Symbolism of Snakes.

#4767. Walking, Yoga, or Zumba? Which Exercises Help Relieve Menopause Mood Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Physical activity may help support mood and improve quality of life during the menopause transition, according to a study published on October 13 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society.

This review of 12 clinical trials involving over 1,000 people ages 40 to 65 found that both aerobic and mind-body exercises may be associated with reduced depressive symptoms and improved well-being.

It is common for individuals to experience psychological symptoms during menopause, including depression, anxiety, low mood, stress, and difficulty with thinking and memory. These symptoms can have a significant effect on quality of life, with an estimated 1 in 10 women leaving work due to menopause symptoms.

This study found that regular physical activity may help improve certain psychological symptoms and overall quality of life during menopause.

The types of physical activity in the review were broken into two categories: aerobic-based exercise (ABIs) and mind-body activities (MBAs).

The researchers found that ABIs showed the strongest effects on reducing depressive symptoms and improving overall quality of life. This may be particularly relevant during perimenopause when women may be more vulnerable to mood instability due to estrogen fluctuations.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, pointed out that there are various ways that ABIs can have positive effects.

Ross explained that aerobic exercise may help improve menopausal symptoms through several mechanisms, including the release of endorphins, reduced inflammation, improved cholesterol levels, and better regulation of body temperature and sleep cycles.

MBAs were shown to have a greater effect on improving psychological quality of life. These exercises involve mindfulness, body awareness, and breathwork. They may help improve emotional regulation.

ABIs tended to require fewer sessions. This may mean these types of exercises are easier to fit in, especially if you are facing time or energy constraints. For example, in one trial, participants were instructed to walk for 30 minutes, three times per week. In another trial, participants attended three hour-long Zumba classes per week.

In contrast, one trial using MBAs instructed participants to attend two 75-minute yoga classes each week, and another had participants attend daily one-hour yoga classes.

Stephanie Faubion, MD, Director for the Mayo Clinic Center for Women’s Health and Medical Director for The Menopause Society, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that this was a relatively small body of evidence. “While physical activity is an important component of a healthy lifestyle during midlife, I would be cautious about interpreting these findings to mean that exercise is a treatment for depression related specifically to menopause,” she said.

Research has shown that physical activity can positively affect mental health. Studies have also found that regular exercise can help improve symptoms of depression and anxiety.

Faubion told Healthline that, broadly speaking, regular physical activity may support mood through multiple pathways, including better sleep, improved physical function, and overall well-being.

However, she also noted that this study cannot tell us precisely why the improvements occurred or whether aerobic exercise is superior to other forms of activity.

Faubion said that recommending physical activity during and after menopause extends well beyond mood.

“Physical activity is important for cardiovascular and metabolic health, maintaining muscle mass and physical function, and supporting bone health,” she said.

“These become particularly important at midlife as women experience age- and menopause-related changes in body composition, bone, and cardiometabolic health,” Faubion added.

Ross agreed that physical activity is important for more than just mood and mental health improvement. She also noted that there are other types of exercise beyond ABIs and MBAs that can benefit people during menopause:

“These types of activities help with weight loss or allow women to maintain a healthy weight. If you are not ready for aerobic exercises, stretching and simple exercises help with balance and stability,” Ross said.

Faubion told Healthline that physical activity is an important part of healthy aging and should be encouraged during the menopause transition, but it should not be suggested that women can simply exercise their way out of significant depression or other bothersome menopause symptoms.

“Women experiencing persistent depression, anxiety, or symptoms that interfere with their quality of life should seek evaluation and discuss the full range of evidence-based treatment options with their healthcare clinician,” Faubion said.

#4765. Electric cars are about to overtake petrol in the UK, data shows

Battery-electric cars took 32% of the UK’s new car market in October, while petrol cars fell to just 37.2%, according to new data from the SMMT. That’s the closest the two have been.

At the current pace, electric cars will outsell petrol in the UK within a year. And it could happen as soon as this December.

The UK registered 152,730 new cars in October, up 5.4% year-over-year and the 11th straight month of growth for the overall market.

All of that growth came from plug-ins. BEV registrations jumped 32.7% to 48,858 units, and plug-in hybrids rose 30.1% to 22,898. Meanwhile, petrol fell 11.6% to 56,876 units, diesel dropped 15.9%, and even conventional hybrids were down 5%.

Through the first 10 months of the year, the UK has now registered 503,805 BEVs, up 30.4%, for a 26.6% market share. Petrol’s year-to-date share is down to 41.1%, from 47.2% at the same point last year.

We pulled SMMT’s monthly fuel-type data going back to March 2024 to see where this is heading. Note that SMMT counts mild hybrids as petrol (or diesel) in its headline categories, and that’s generally how we count them at Electrek.

In March 2024, petrol held 55.9% of the market and BEVs 15.2%. In October 2026, it was 37.2% vs 32.0%. Petrol’s share is shrinking by about half a point per month on a linear trend, while BEVs gain about 0.36 points a month. Extend both lines and they cross around August 2027 at roughly 33% each.

But that’s the slow scenario, because it ignores December.

UK BEV share spikes every December as automakers push volume to get closer to their ZEV Mandate targets. BEVs hit 31.0% in December 2024 and 32.2% in December 2025, when petrol was at 39.4%. Over the last five months, BEV share has run about 5 points higher than a year earlier, and petrol about 7 points lower. If December follows that pattern, BEVs land around 37% and petrol around 32%.

That would be the first time BEVs beat petrol in SMMT’s headline numbers, mild hybrids included.

However, SMMT’s own forecast of 27.2% BEV share for the full year implies roughly 31% for November and December combined, which would make it a much closer call. And on a stricter definition that puts mild hybrids with hybrids instead of petrol, BEVs already outsold every other powertrain in August.

Zoom out to full years and the picture is just as clear. Cars that run only on petrol or diesel, mild hybrids included, made up 72.5% of the UK market in 2021. This year, they’re at 45.5%.

None of this is good enough for the SMMT, which is using the release to push the government, again, to cut the ZEV Mandate targets.

The mandate requires 33% of 2026 sales to be zero-emission. SMMT now forecasts 27.2%. It expects 32% next year against a 38% target, and 37.5% in 2028 against 52%, a 14.5-point gap.

The trade group says automakers have spent “billions” on discounts, 0% financing, deposit contributions, and even subsidized charging to move EVs, on top of the government’s Electric Car Grant. It also slammed last week’s Budget, which confirmed a new EV-specific road tax (eVED) starting in 2028 and kept 20% VAT on public charging.

“Higher targets may force supply, but they do not create demand,” SMMT chief executive Mike Hawes said.

We’ve heard this one before. The SMMT made the same argument after September’s record 99,199 BEV registrations, and the government already opened a review of the mandate this year.

This might be the main reason why the trade group wants to slow things down. The brands growing fastest in the UK are mostly Chinese. BYD registered 6,065 cars in October, up 73%. Jaecoo more than doubled to 6,089 units, Chery nearly tripled to 3,707, and Leapmotor doubled to 1,773. MG was up 85%.

Tesla, on the other hand, registered just 282 cars in October, down 45% from 511 a year ago. The first month of the quarter is always slow for Tesla in the UK, and the brand is still up 31% year-to-date at 46,526 units after a big September. But it didn’t have a single model in October’s top 10 BEVs, which was led by the Skoda Enyaq (1,568), Mini Countryman (1,494), and Jaecoo 5 (1,465).

The SMMT’s framing is that there’s a “demand gap.” The data shows the opposite. BEV registrations are up 30% this year while petrol is shrinking every single month. That’s not a market rejecting EVs.

The SMMT is not a neutral organisation, they have been briefing against EVs for years and continue to do so.

The ZEV mandate is NOT a measure of how many pure BEVs are sold, and the SMMT know it, it's a measure of REDUCING emission against a level set in the past.

Those emissions reductions can be met by selling BEVs, or selling more efficient PHEVs or even selling more efficient petrol or diesel cars! The manufacturers can also buy credits if they choose to.

NO manufacturer has paid any ZEV fines to date (DfT announcement March 2026)

As for the "heavy discounts" and "loss making sales", well I have two data points on that.

1. The retail price of EVs has continued to climb in the UK over the past 6 years, despite the cost of any average 50kWh battery pack dropping several thousand dollars.

2. There are hundreds of main dealerships who are buying cars from the manufacturers, driving them for the minimum 3 month period, often with just a few thousand miles on the clock and then selling them with a 30-35% retail price discount, and then repeating ad infinitum. The dealerships are still making a few thousand with each transaction, so we know where the manufacturers price really sits.

And the discounts automakers keep complaining about? That’s the mandate doing exactly what it was designed to do. It forces automakers to sell EVs, so they price them to sell, and buyers respond. Hawes says targets don’t create demand, but cheaper EVs clearly do. October proves it.

Now, is the jump to 52% in 2028 steep? It is steep, but it looks achievable to me. If anything is hurting demand, it’s the government’s own moves: a new EV-only road tax and 20% VAT on public charging. That’s what the industry should be fighting. It’s too early for that.

Either way, petrol’s days as the UK’s default car are numbered. The only question is whether the milestone comes in December or sometime in 2027. Our bet is December.

#4764. Reading as a Green Flag Is a Dating Trend

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

Are you looking to date someone who's on the same page with you? Or how about on any page—as in, does the person actually read things like books and not just social media posts? Well, you may have read about how reading has become a prominent green flag—meaning that many people are actively looking for it on dating profiles and dates.

For example, after pop star Dua Lipa married actor Callum Turner, many fans seemed to get excited about the cover version, so to speak, of their meet-cute, as described by an article by Ellen Durney for Buzzfeed. Turner indicated that they had first met at a mutual friend’s birthday party and soon realized that they were both reading the book Trust by Hernán Díaz and were even on the same chapter. This apparently helped them trust each other more, with Turner claiming that he had told Lipa then, “So we’re on the same page.” And that, kids, is how Dua became a duo.

These days, whether someone reads, period, can be a dating screening criterion, depending on where you stand on this whole reading thing. That's because there is a big reading divide in the U.S. For example, the Pew Research Center found that nearly a quarter (~23%) of Americans surveyed didn't even touch a book over the past 12 months. In fact, the National Endowment for the Arts and American Time Use Survey have shown that only 16% or so of Americans may be reading on a daily basis, and over 51% may be reading absolutely no books each year.

Social media may be making this divide more obvious. Just look at how many times someone posts an opinion and the response is something like "Have you even read about this?" or even "Did you even read the link that you posted?" So, if you do fall on the regularly reading side of the divide, it might make sense to have regular reading as a minimal dating requirement.

But it could go even beyond that. The reading app Headway found in a survey that ”Some 24% of people instantly swipe right on dating profiles that show someone reading, while 75% prefer a partner who is well-read over someone physically attractive." Yep, reading could even be, gasp, sexy. That might have been a War and Peace of news to you in high school, when it seemed like all that people were interested in was looks.

But if you think about it, regularly reading stuff that's more than just cereal boxes and messages with ROFL in them can tell a lot about a person. It could suggest that the person is intellectually curious, willing to learn, and more thoughtful and mindful. There is also the standard saying that the brain is the biggest and most powerful sexual organ. The size of a person's creativity, empathy, and knowledge could play a bigger role in pleasing a partner than the size of anything else. And if you are looking for, umm, enhancement in all those areas, reading can be at your service.

Once you find someone who actually reads regularly—assuming that's what you want, since you have already gotten this far on this article—it can also help to find out what, specifically, the person reads. What someone reads can tell you a whole lot more about a person than the person's photo. That's because reading is something that takes time and effort and is done on one's own time.

So, those who will dedicate their time to reading about something are likely interested in that thing at least to some degree. For example, anyone who has read a lot of books about cats probably likes cats. Or, maybe, is preparing for the big cat government overthrow that will eventually occur. Either way, that person likely has a more informed opinion about cats.

Someone's reading materials can also be a clue to that person's point of view. Guess what reading "Surrounded by Idiots" may say about a person's current life situation. Also, the diversity of their reading materials could reflect their diversity of thought and perspectives and their open-mindedness.

All of this can be important information since a big part of dating is finding the right match in terms of personality, values, and other core qualities. A person's reading list doesn't necessarily say everything about someone. For example, when I was doing research to write an article about farts, I was reading a lot about farts. But I am more than farts. Nevertheless, reading lists can be another clue to help you read someone better.

There's a lot to be read about using reading to help gauge people, but also, to meet people in the first place. Eventbrite data did show a 33% increase in book club events in the first half of 2026. Such data also showed that the number "romantasy" events around the U.S. have gone up by 196% in 2026 compared to 2025, with attendance jumping by 237%. A "romantasy event" is a gathering that's built around the whole romantic fantasy literary genre. This is fiction that brings together mystical worlds and romantic plots.

For example, there was the three-day Romantasy BookCon in Orlando, Florida, in October. There was cosplay, author appearances, and book signings, and a variety of ways lovers of this genre could mix together. Now, while the focus of that event was not dating, who knows what can happen when lovers of the same thing come together. They might end up becoming lovers of lovers of that thing.

All of this does not mean that you should pretend to like reading when you don't. People trying to be what they are not is a big reason why there are so many mismatches and bad relationships out there. But it does mean that if you do things by the book regularly, this could end up being the book on love for you.

#4762. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Increase Dementia, Stroke Risk

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Your hub for heart health management, insights, and solutions

Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.

UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations. This category of foods includes packaged snack foods, sugary cereals, soft drinks, and frozen ready-to-eat meals.

UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

Previous research has linked these foods to adverse cardiometabolic outcomes. This new study adds to growing evidence linking high UPF intake to adverse health outcomes.

This was a cross-sectional analysis of 8,783 adults between the ages of 35 and 69 without cardiovascular disease. The participants were all enrolled in the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds (CAHHM) and Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology-MIND (PURE-MIND) cohorts.

The researchers used MRI scans to evaluate the participants’ brains. They also set out to analyze the cross-sectional relationship between UPF consumption, body fat, vascular brain injury (VBI), and cognitive performance.

They measured the participants’ habitual UPF intake using a food frequency questionnaire. Intake was expressed as servings based on a 2,000-calorie-per-day diet.

UPFs accounted for an average of 25% of participants’ daily diets. For the individuals with the highest intake, this increased to 45% of everything on their plates, compared to 16% for those who ate the least.

The researchers also noted that UPFs were not just an added part of individual diets. These foods appeared to replace whole foods.

Among people with the highest UPF intake, fruits, vegetables, grains, and other minimally processed foods accounted for 41% of their daily food intake. Among those with the lowest UPF intake, minimally processed foods made up 68% of their daily intake.

When the researchers compared the highest intake to the lowest, they found that those with a higher intake of UPFs had 1.7% more body fat. They also found that people with a higher UPF intake had higher odds of VBI.

“These findings are concerning, but it is important to remember that an association does not prove cause and effect,” said Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“From my perspective as a preventive cardiology dietitian, these findings reinforce the importance of nourishing our blood vessels to support both cardiovascular and brain health.”

Although researchers found no significant differences in cognitive performance, the signs of vascular brain injury observed in the study have been associated with an increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline.

These findings suggest a possible link between UPF intake and signs of brain changes. However, participants were only assessed once and weren’t followed over time. This means the researchers were unable to determine whether UPFs directly caused the changes.

“While we can’t conclude from this study that limiting UPFs would improve brain health, we have decades of literature demonstrating that higher intakes of green leafy vegetables, brightly colored fruits, whole grains, and lean protein sources are good for brain health,” said Suzanne Judd, PhD, Director of the UC College of Medicine’s Center for Public Health, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“So focusing more on what can be brought into the diet rather than what should be eliminated might be a good way to start,” she added.

The preservatives [in UPFs] may have a direct impact on the vascular system, while the loss of antioxidants results in a less robust response to inflammation in the body.

“Additionally, sugar or salt is often added to make the food a bit tastier so people consume it in higher quantities. Over-consumption of food can lead to weight gain and diabetes, which can negatively impact brain health,” Judd said.

Judd told Healthline that it is virtually impossible to completely avoid UPFs. Even some “health” foods, like protein powder and some yogurts, are considered ultra-processed.

It is more important to look at diet overall and emphasize consuming foods as close to their natural state as possible, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and meats purchased raw or frozen and then cooked at home.

Routhenstein recommended starting simply with one manageable swap rather than trying to overhaul your entire diet.

She said that you should identify an ultra-processed food you eat regularly and consider a more nutrient-rich alternative. It is important to account for convenience, food preferences, budget, and lifestyle so that the change feels realistic and is sustainable over the long term.

“I want people to feel empowered, not fearful, when making food choices,” said Routhenstein. “Healthy eating does not mean having to cook everything from scratch. What matters most is building consistent, nourishing habits that support both heart and brain health.”

#4761. Toyota updates the 2027 RAV4 PHEV with an NACS port and up to 52 miles of EV range

The 2027 Toyota RAV4 is bringing a few major updates, including an added NACS charge port on all plug-in hybrid (PHEV) models.

The RAV4 was Toyota’s best-selling nameplate in the US last year and consistently ranks among America’s most popular vehicles alongside the Ford F-Series and Chevrolet Silverado.

For the 2027 model year, Toyota added several notable upgrades. The 2027 Toyota RAV4 will be available with hybrid (HEV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains, with available front- or all-wheel drive (AWD).

The biggest change is that all 2027 RAV4 PHEV models now have a built-in NACS charge port with Level 3 DC fast-charging capabilities.

The NACS port is on the driver’s side and lets drivers use Tesla Superchargers without a separate adapter. All PHEV grades also include an 11 kW onboard AC charger.

Powered by Toyota’s sixth-generation PHEV system, the plug-in RAV4 has standard AWD with a combined output of 321 horsepower. The setup includes a 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine, two electric motors, and a high-capacity traction battery.

The 2027 Toyota RAV4 PHEV offers up to 52 miles of pure electric range on the base SE trim. It will be available in four trims: SE, XSE, Woodland, and GR Sport.

Toyota updated the suspension system in the Woodland grade for the 2027 model year with new springs, shocks, and jounce bumpers, giving it 9.1″ of ground clearance.

The Woodland trim adds a rugged look with standard All-Terrain tires, Roof Rails with Cross Bars, and a Tow Hitch Receiver. It also features new all-weather floor and cargo mats.

Lastly, the RAV4 GR Sport trim is for those who want a more performance-oriented, sporty style, with GT-tuned suspension and steering, sports seating, and a standard PHEV powertrain with AWD.

Inside, the 2027 RAV4 includes a standard 12.3″ digital cluster and a 10.5″ touchscreen with the Toyota Audio Multimedia system, plus wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

A 12.9″ touchscreen with a JBL Premium Audio system with 9 speakers is standard on the Limited trim and available on the XSE grade.

All 2027 Toyota RAV4s come with standard Toyota Safety Sense 4.0, which includes safety and convenience features such as Lane Departure Alert with Steering Assist, Full-Speed Range Dynamic Radar Cruise Control, Proactive Driving Assist, and a Pre-Collision System with Pedestrian Detection.

#4760. We Found the Best Adjustable Dumbbells for Every Home Gym

Looking to make more gains while taking up less space? These picks from SMRTFT, PowerBlock, and REP Fitness pack a big punch in a small package.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IF THERE'S ONE piece of home gym equipment anyone can make room for at home, it's a pair of adjustable dumbbells. These clever pieces of fitness gear require minimal space, shifting from light to heavy with a quick turn of a knob or tweak of a setting. They simplify things by tackling two challenges of working out at home: space and equipment. Think about it: A single pair of adjustable dumbbells can replace around 15 standard dumbbells.

"There's a reason dumbbells are in every single big-box gym," says MH fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., who created an arm-focused muscle-building program, All Out Arms, based heavily around dumbbells. "If you want targeted muscle—and that’s what all guys want—then you want dumbbells." Adjustable dumbbells (just like adjustable kettlebells) offer a range of weights from one compact footprint, eliminating the need for multiple sets of weights.

If you prefer working out at home (or do so out of necessity on days when you can't make it to the gym), a pair of adjustable dumbbells is a solution that helps you stay consistent with your training without leaving your home. These are effective pieces, especially when combined with cardio equipment and a great weight bench. Check out our top picks for the best adjustable dumbbells for your home gym right now.

"The Nüobell is the best blend of reliability and authentic dumbbell feel I’ve used," says Samuel, who has been using these for over three years. "The shape and design of these 'bells make them ideal for accessory motions, like skullcrushers and biceps curls, and they’re easy to hold for goblet squats too." Aside from a few scratches, they've held up great to three years of heavy use.

With a maximum weight of 80 pounds of weight per dumbbell and a feel that's nearly indistinguishable from traditional dumbbells, users can utilize the same set of weights for a complete full-body workout. Users can quickly drop down to lower weights for exercises like bent-over flies or pile on the plates for more intense squats. "It features a 'turn-and-click' design rather than just a built-in selector," notes Williams. Users simply turn the handle until they reach their desired weight.

During testing, Howell noted that the Nüobell arrived assembled and was easy to plug-and-play once unboxed. Of all the adjustable dumbbells he tried, these felt the most like actual dumbbells. "These feel like the next evolution of the traditional dumbbells we have become used to in gyms," Howell said.

The major defining features include: metal plates and handles, top-tier construction, easy click-and-go weight adjustment, and the selected weight displayed on the dumbbell itself.

However, Howell expressed some concerns about the rack it came with, feeling it might have been an afterthought. He questioned whether the tempered plastic rack would withstand the constant re-racking of the metal plates over time. Nevertheless, he emphasized that the actual dumbbells are well-crafted and feel solid as hell.

In Howell's opinion, these dumbbells are best for someone who has invested in a home gym and is serious about fitness. They are tailored for the hardcore client who likely has a squat rack and barbell in their garage as well, but wants to add an elite set of adjustable dumbbells to their training arsenal. If you’re building the mother of all home gyms and money is no object, this comprehensive premium set of dumbbells from SMRTFT might just be your best pick.

These BowFlex adjustable dumbbells adjust from 5 to 52.5 pounds in 2.5-pound increments, which replaces up to 15 pairs of dumbbells (that’s a lot of potential time and money saved). We love that the weight distribution is close to that of traditional dumbbells, and the 2.5-pound increments offer more customization in weight ranges. No matter how these BowFlex dumbbells are ordered, they arrive at your door in two separate, well-packed boxes.

The weight is adjusted through selection dials located on either side of each dumbbell. The dial system is easy to use, though not exactly as streamlined as SMRTFT's single-twist mechanism. Keep in mind that changing the weight requires docking and adjusting both sides of each dumbbell–that’s two dial adjustments for each change in weight. But I prefer them to PowerBlock dumbbells.

The previous version of the SelectTechs had a plastic casing, but these updated models now feature premium metal components that are better protected from damage. We find the design a bit wide and cumbersome for certain exercises, such as triceps extensions. "In my experience, these work best for chest-supported rows and overhead presses," says Samuel.

These dumbbells have been in regular use in my garage for half a year, I haven't had any issues with wear or tear. That said, it's essential to handle them with care and consider your exercise preferences when incorporating them into your home gym setup. Like most of the dumbbells on this list, it's probably not a great idea to drop these on the floor after finishing a set.

The last note is that advanced lifters may feel a little constrained by the 52.5-pound max weight and may want to consider the 90-pound-max-weight BowFlex Results Series SelectTech 1090s instead.

The NordicTrack Select-A-Weight Dumbbells are sturdy and easy to use, featuring metal plates and a robust plastic casing designed to withstand the occasional drop (though we don't recommend it). With a weight range of 10 to 55 pounds per dumbbell, adjustable in 2.5-pound increments, they cater especially well to home workouts. However, they're not our top pick for accessory movements due to their relatively broad plates.

This set arrived assembled and was ready to go once unboxed. "I appreciated that it came with a tray that gave it a home and an easy-to-store footprint," noted Howell. "Making changes in weight by 2.5-pound increments was fairly easy, and they felt really sturdy and safe even when adjusted to heavier loads—the knurled metal handle helped with this."What Howell didn't love about these was that there was no way to confirm what weight you were using once the 'bells' were removed from the rack. Only the rack is labeled with weight numbers, not the actual dumbbell."I think this is an ideal product for someone who knows their way around a gym and is looking for a solid addition to their home to supplement," says Howell. "They're perfect for an intermediate client."

In terms of sound, while "these are quieter than other adjustable dumbbells on the market, they make more noise than the PowerBlocks," explains Samuel. Additionally, if you wish to incorporate barbell movements into your home workout routine, we've found that these dumbbells work seamlessly with the Hyperbell.

One of my favorite equipment makers, I was surprised how long it took REP Fitness to come out with a viable adjustable dumbbell option. But it seems like they were waiting to create something special, and that's what they've done with the QuickDraws.

The plates can be adjusted in 2.5-pound increments, spanning from 5 to 30 pounds. For those heavy lifters, 30 pounds might not be enough, but for the average user looking for a quick pump in the arms or lighter weights for perfect accessory movements, this is a great pick. For anyone who wants to increase the weight, REP Fitness offers heavier options with the same streamlined design, for up to 60 pounds.

They've patented their Lock-N-Load adjustment system, which is straightforward and lets you change the weights by flipping a switch on each dumbbell. This system allows you to swap weights quickly, so you can change the load between dumbbell exercises and avoid stalling.

For our testing, the dumbbells arrived in two boxes and require minimal assembly, making them an ultra-accessible choice for delivery and home use.

PowerBlock adjustable dumbbells are an ultra-sturdy set designed for lasting performance, perfect for executing heavy-duty moves like dead stop rows, Romanian deadlifts, and heavy presses. At just 12 inches long with the storage stand, these dumbbells offer decent compactness and versatility.

The Pro 50 Adjustable Dumbbells cover a weight range of 5 to 50 pounds per dumbbell, with adjustments in increments of 2.5 pounds. This weight range suits beginners well, and more experienced lifters can expand the weight by opting for additional expansion kits. For those who find 50 pounds per dumbbell insufficient, PowerBlock offers heavier models such as the Elite USA (up to 90 pounds per dumbbell) or the Pro 100 EXP (up to 100 pounds per dumbbell). Most models of adjustable dumbbells by PowerBlock feature the same pin-and-lock adjustment mechanism, which is easy to use and avoids jamming issues found in some other systems.

In his testing, Howell pointed out the compact structure of the actual dumbbell, noting the plate-like weights, which are more like weighted frames than traditional circular ones. Howell found this design "genius", as the square nature of the dumbbell makes it easy to lay down once done using it without it rolling away or requiring a rack to rest it in. He also appreciated that they arrived assembled and were fairly easy to unpack and begin using.

However, Howell expressed concerns about the durability of certain components, such as the handles and the "clip" that allows you to lock your chosen weight in, which are made of plastic. He believes these dumbbells might not be robust enough for consistent use, particularly for hardcore gymgoers.

Despite these concerns, Samuel praises their adjustability and durability, stating, "I've never encountered a more durable adjustable dumbbell. I love them for farmer’s walks, heavy DB lunges, and thrusters, and rely on them anytime I do a metcon-style workout at home." Samuel also shared he’s dropped these from three or four feet up after tough sets of incline presses, "and they hold up just fine." (Although it's not advisable to make a habit of dropping any adjustable dumbbells regularly.)These dumbbells feature comfortable contoured handles that enhance grip during workouts. However, they do not provide the same weight distribution as traditional dumbbells, as Samuel points out: "If you’re looking to use a set of adjustable movements for plenty of accessory movements, go with something more dumbbell-shaped."

Look for a weight range that meets your fitness goals. Most adjustable dumbbells can be adjusted in 2.5- or 5-pound increments, so it's important to consider a weight range that fits your needs.

Adjustable dumbbells come in different shapes and sizes. Consider the size and shape of the dumbbells and make sure they feel comfortable in your hands. Basically, does the dumbbell feel "good" or natural to you? Again, this comes down to personal preference and might involve some trial and error.

Some adjustable dumbbells distribute the load differently than traditional dumbbells (atypical), changing how it responds to certain movements (particularly accessory movements). A good rule of thumb is if you're looking to perform heavier exercises (farmer's carries, RDLs, rows) you can consider an adjustable dumbbell that doesn't distribute its weight like a traditional dumbbell, such as the PowerBlock option featured above. If you're planning to do more accessory movements (like biceps curls or skull crushers), opt for a traditional dumbbell-shaped option.

There are a few different mechanisms adjustable dumbbells use to switch weights, with some being easier or more user-friendly.

This mechanism uses a dial on the end of the dumbbell handle to adjust the weight. To change the weight, you turn the dial to the desired weight, and the mechanism will lock in the appropriate weight plates. Some adjustable dumbbells must be docked in their storage base to change weight using a dial, while others can be adjusted outside their docking station.

This mechanism uses a pin to select the desired weight and can take some practice to get used to if you're new to it. To change the weight, pull out the pin, select the desired weight, then reinsert the pin into the corresponding slot to lock it in.

This mechanism uses a twist-locking mechanism to secure the weight plates. To change the weight, you twist the handle to unlock the weight plates, remove or add weight plates, and then twist the handle back to lock in the new weight.

Warranties reflect a manufacturer's confidence in its product. And with some of the best adjustable dumbbells priced at or above $500, you want to be sure your investment is protected. So, it’s important to purchase from a manufacturer that offers a clear, comprehensive warranty. They vary widely across the industry, with the most budget-forward brands offering just 90 days on some parts, and others boasting generous five-year warranties on everything. Again, the more you spend upfront, the better the warranty is likely to be. And, if there’s anything that isn’t clear to you about the stated warranty, be sure to ask. It’s your money, after all.

As the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men's Health, it's my job to test the latest and greatest training equipment, including adjustable dumbbells. To build this guide, I tested more than 30 adjustable dumbbells over the past five years, drawing on my experience and that of my fellow MH fitness editors, including Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., and Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM. Samuel utilized the top-performing adjustable dumbbells featured in this guide in fitness programs with several of his advanced clients.

We also enlisted the help of Maillard Howell of Dean CrossFit in Brooklyn, to test and assess how well these dumbbells performed in the real world (read: a high-traffic training facility). In addition, we sought insights from trainers from both our MH Advisory Board and our Strength in Diversity class for further anecdotal and experiential perspectives on the top adjustable dumbbells.

Each dumbbell was rigorously tested in a variety of categories, including durability, weight distribution, ease of shifting between weights, and aesthetics. All dumbbells were tested with three types of exercises: explosive exercises (such as cleans), multi-joint strength exercises (such as bench presses and Romanian deadlifts), and accessory movements (such as biceps curls and lateral raises). All dumbbells were also dropped from a standard bench to test baseline durability (no adjustable dumbbell should ever be dropped from shoulder height), and they were monitored for signs of rust over a three-month period.

Adjustable dumbbells pack a ton of perks compared to regular dumbbells, with the most obvious being their space-saving design: No matter which adjustable dumbbells you choose, you can guarantee they'll take up less space than the sets of traditional dumbbells they replace.

Another attractive benefit of adjustable dumbbells is that they're more cost-effective than multiple sets of traditional dumbbells. A lot of the options on this list aren't exactly budget buys, we know. But building out a weight rack with 5-15 sets of high-quality traditional dumbbells can add up in cost even quicker.

This comes down to three things: space, personal preference, and how you plan to use your dumbbells. If you have unlimited space, you can definitely consider standard dumbbells.

"If you're building out a home gym and especially if you like to train accessory motions and work through a full range of motion, you still can't beat standard dumbbells," explains Samuel.

"They're going to be more durable, have better weight distribution for most moves, and, as cool as some adjustment dial might be, there's nothing more efficient than literally putting a 35-pound dumbbell down and picking a 40-pounder up."

But if you're in tight confines or like to work out on the go, opt for a good adjustable option. "You can load a pair of Powerblocks in your trunk much more easily than you can load 10 pairs of dumbbells for a road trip."

You'll also want to consider how often you'll drop your dumbbells. Even the best, most durable adjustable dumbbells on this list still have weight-switching mechanisms and won't hold up to being routinely dropped from a few feet in the air after a set of shoulder presses as well as standard dumbbells.

The weight of adjustable dumbbells depends on your fitness level and goals. Typically, they come in two main categories: those that max out at around 50 pounds per dumbbell and those that start at 50 pounds and get way heavier.

For beginners and folks looking to engage in moderate strength training at home, a set that maxes out at 50 pounds per dumbbell should suffice. They offer a range of weights for a wide variety of exercises and are a great starting point. Beginners can work on everything from biceps curls to overhead presses to squats with these.

Now, if you're a seasoned lifter, powerlifter, or someone aiming to build strength, opt for a pair of adjustable dumbbells that can go well above 50 pounds per bell. Adjustable sets from SMRTFT can offer a max of 80 pounds and 100 pounds per bell, respectively. For experienced lifters, added weight means greater versatility in tackling heavy exercises and challenging yourself.

Just like standard dumbbells, adjustable dumbbells are safe when used correctly and with proper form. But, as with any type of fitness equipment, there are some safety considerations to keep in mind.

It's important to choose adjustable dumbbells that are well-made and constructed from durable materials. If you're using an old-school model with removable plates, make sure they're securely attached to the handle before you start your lift.

The shape, feel, and weight distribution of adjustable dumbbells can take some getting used to, depending on the model you're working with. Because they may feel different compared to standard dumbbells in movements you do regularly, it's important to focus on slow, controlled movements and proper form throughout your workout (especially as you acclimate to them).

#4759. New Jersey is putting 10 MW of community solar on warehouse roofs

Warehouse roofs are prime real estate for solar, and Faropoint is putting more of that underused space to work in New Jersey. The industrial property owner has started construction on the first of 16 community solar projects totaling more than 10 megawatts (MW).

First up is a 1.6 MW rooftop array at 19-05 Nevins Road in Fair Lawn. Another 15 projects, totaling about 8.5 MW, have been accepted into New Jersey’s Community Solar Energy Program, and nine are already cleared to start construction.

That’s more solar going onto buildings that are already there, with participating households set to get savings on their electricity bills.

Large warehouse roofs offer something solar developers need: lots of flat space. Putting panels up there gives the same building the job of generating electricity without taking up additional land.

Faropoint specializes in industrial properties used for local deliveries and distribution. “Utilizing previously unused portions of our buildings allows us to support the communities where we invest,” said Brian Nave, Faropoint’s vice president of asset management and renewable energy.

Faropoint and its independent solar adviser, SolarKal, expect the 16 projects to generate around 12.7 million kilowatt-hours (kWh) of electricity annually once they’re operating. They estimate the portfolio will avoid about 8,500 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions a year.

Faropoint says at least half of each project’s capacity will be reserved for low- and moderate-income households. New Jersey’s program requires a minimum of 51%.

#4758. Pornography Perception: Shame Intensifies Distress Over Use

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

How much pornography is too much? People often assume that the more someone watches, the more likely they are to develop an escalating, progressive addiction.

A new study by psychologist Joshua Grubbs and colleagues complicates that story. Their findings suggest that understanding perceived problematic pornography use requires looking beyond frequency to people’s beliefs about what they are doing. The researchers also found that periods of unusually high perceived problems tended to be followed by a return toward the person’s usual level, challenging assumptions of inevitable worsening.

Published in the flagship Journal of Psychopathology and Clinical Science, the study followed American adults across five assessments over two years. Its analyses included 2,903 people who reported pornography use during at least one assessment.

Researchers measured how frequently participants watched pornography, how strongly they morally disapproved of it, and their self-reported problematic pornography use, or PPU. That last measure assessed experiences such as feeling unable to stop using pornography. It measured perceived problems rather than establishing a clinical diagnosis.

The central concept was moral incongruence: the shame and conflict people experience when their behavior violates their values. Someone who believes pornography is wrong but continues watching it may experience distress and interpret their distress over doing something they regret as evidence of addiction.

The researchers examined both differences between people and changes within the same person. That distinction matters. Asking whether frequent viewers report more problems than occasional viewers is different from asking whether someone feels more troubled during periods when they watch more than usual.

People who morally disapproved of pornography generally watched it less often. Among those who watched porn, however, greater moral disapproval was associated with more perceived problems.

Moral disapproval also amplified the relationship between viewing frequency and perceived problems. When participants watched more than their own usual amount, the association with perceived problems was roughly three times stronger among people with high moral disapproval than among those with low disapproval.

As Grubbs explained in an emailed statement about the findings:

“It's not just that people who disapprove of pornography more are more likely to interpret their own use as problematic; it's that people interpret fluctuations in their own use in light of those deeply held moral beliefs.”

Imagine two people who each increase their viewing by a similar amount. Someone who regards pornography as acceptable might experience little additional concern. Someone who believes it is morally wrong might interpret that increase as evidence of losing control.

An important qualification: the study did not find that frequency mattered only when moral incongruence was present. The association remained positive at lower levels of moral disapproval. The finding was that underlying moral disapproval substantially strengthened that relationship.

The broader message remains consequential: frequency alone cannot tell us whether someone has a pornography problem. The meaning people attach to their behavior helps shape how problematic it feels.

Because this was an observational study, it cannot prove that moral beliefs caused the reported problems. It does show why simply counting viewing occasions provides an incomplete picture.

Another finding challenges a familiar narrative: that pornography problems necessarily become progressively worse.

When participants reported PPU above their own usual level, they tended to report relatively lower PPU six months later. The researchers described this as regression toward the mean.

In everyday language, an unusually bad period tended to be followed by a less extreme one, probably because men often increase use of porn when they are struggling emotionally due to life events, and such life events often subside or lessen over time.

Likewise, watching more pornography than usual at one assessment did not reliably predict greater perceived problems six months later. The relationship between increased viewing and increased concern appeared primarily at the same assessment, rather than demonstrating a clear chain of future deterioration.

These findings are inconsistent with a simple story in which every increase in viewing signals a progressive downward spiral.

They also require careful interpretation. Returning toward one’s usual level does not necessarily mean the person has no struggles with pornography use. Someone’s usual level may still involve considerable distress. Overall differences between people were fairly stable, and the study did not establish that everyone improved or that persistent problems resolve without help.

This was also a community sample, rather than a study specifically of patients seeking treatment. Its findings cannot determine the course of every severe clinical case.

Still, a temporary spike in perceived problems should not automatically be treated as evidence of an escalating disorder.

People distressed about pornography deserve to have that distress taken seriously. Understanding its source is essential.

A useful assessment explores whether someone is experiencing persistent difficulty controlling their behavior, concrete consequences, conflict with personal values, or some combination. Moral conflict and difficulties with control can coexist.

Addressing distress rooted in moral incongruence should respect the person’s values while helping them examine shame and frightening interpretations of their behavior. Assuming that every unwanted viewing episode proves addiction risks reinforcing the very distress bringing someone into treatment.

This research encourages a more careful question than “How often do you watch?”

Instead, let's ask: What happens in your life when you watch—and what does watching porn mean to you?

Reference: Grubbs, J. B., Floyd, C. G., Carrasquillo, K. D., & Kraus, S. W. (2026). The dual-level dynamics of moral incongruence: A multilevel analysis of problematic pornography use. Journal of Psychopathology and Clinical Science. Advance online publication.

#4756. A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?

A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.

Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.

While the findings suggest that pistachios may support sleep, the evidence is inconclusive and warrants further study.

“Pistachios are compelling for sleep research because they bring together several nutrients and plant compounds connected to sleep physiology within one whole food,” said study author Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research in the Department of Medicine at Columbia University Institute of Nutrition, in a news release.

“Rather than focusing on a single ‘sleep nutrient,’ this review provides a rationale for studying how the complete pistachio food matrix may affect sleep-related pathways,” she continued.

The narrative review examined existing research on pistachios and sleep-related biology.

The researchers explored whether the combination of nutrients in pistachios could promote quality sleep.

Rather than identifying pistachios as a sleep remedy, the researchers outlined biological pathways through which their nutrients and bioactive compounds might influence sleep.

“We were particularly interested in pistachios because they are particularly high in phytomelatonin, polyphenols, and carotenoids, which we noted were plant-derived components that had been shown to have sleep benefits in preclinical studies,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“We also noted their high content of tryptophan and vitamin B6, which are relevant to melatonin production in humans,” she continued.

Pistachios contain several nutrients associated with sleep, including melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Other studies examining the effects of some of these nutrients on sleep offer further context.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of tryptophan supplementation found that it may reduce wakefulness after sleep onset, particularly at doses of at least 1 gram (g) daily. However, an ounce of pistachios supplies only about 71 mg, which is much less than the doses examined by the researchers.

Additionally, a 2023 review of dietary polyphenols led by St-Onge identified potential links between plant compounds and sleep outcomes, although results varied across studies.

Neither review established that polyphenols or tryptophan from pistachios specifically affected sleep quality.

“I was not surprised that pistachios may help support sleep, given their combination of nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” said Michelle Routhenstein, MS, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“Pistachios provide tryptophan, an amino acid the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin; vitamin B6, which supports these pathways; and magnesium, which plays a role in nervous system function and sleep regulation,” she told Healthline.

The new review highlights the concept of the “food matrix,” or how nutrients and bioactive compounds interact within a whole food.

Instead of investigating tryptophan, magnesium, or melatonin individually, researchers were curious about the combined effects of consuming them together in pistachios.

Laboratory and simulated-digestion research offers clues about how fiber and plant compounds in pistachios and peanuts interact with gut microbes. However, these findings do not establish that eating pistachios changes sleep quality in real-world conditions.

Broader nutrition research also points to a relationship between diet and sleep.

A 2021 review in the Annual Review of Nutrition examined evidence linking dietary patterns and individual nutrients to sleep outcomes. The findings suggest a relationship between sleep and diet, but note that more research is needed to determine cause and effect.

In a nutshell, the current evidence builds a compelling case for pistachios as a sleep aid.

However, it’s too soon to recommend pistachios as a sleep remedy, as many factors may affect sleep quality and insomnia.

“Sleep difficulties can have different underlying causes,” Routhenstein noted. “If inadequate intake of these nutrients is a contributing factor, pistachios may help, but they may not address sleep issues related to other nutrient deficiencies or other causes.”

Much of the supporting evidence cited in the review comes from studies of individual nutrients, other foods, laboratory experiments, or biological mechanisms rather than from trials involving whole pistachios.

Researchers have also reported significant variations in the melatonin content of pistachios, making the amount in a typical serving difficult to pinpoint.

Additionally, the review received support from American Pistachio Growers, and the corresponding author, St-Onge, serves on its advisory board. Larger studies and clinical trials are needed, ideally without industry funding, to ensure well-rounded results.

Indeed, the authors call for randomized controlled trials examining whether eating pistachios affects sleep outcomes, including sleep quality, duration, and melatonin levels.

“This was a review; we noted that the complete profile of pistachios would make them well-suited to support healthful sleep, but research is needed to evaluate this,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“This is the next step, and something we are actively working on. We also need to better understand what dosage and frequency of consumption would be optimal.”

Regardless, a handful of pistachios is still considered a healthy choice as part of a balanced diet.

“A small handful, about 1 ounce of shelled pistachios, is an appropriate portion,” Routhenstein said. “Enjoy them during the day or as a light afternoon or evening snack when you’re hungry.”

If nutrients like tryptophan help promote sleep, it’s possible that other nuts could yield similar results.

“Other nuts, such as almonds and walnuts, may offer similar benefits because they also contain nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” Routhenstein said.

“Early research is encouraging, but it’s too soon to say how much they might help.”

Other foods, like turkey, also contain tryptophan.

“For someone allergic to nuts, foods such as tofu, beans, oats, eggs, dairy, and fish can provide tryptophan, which the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin,” Routhenstein said. “The goal is to meet their nutrient needs rather than rely on one food to improve sleep.”

Sleep health depends on multiple factors. As such, Routhenstein recommends a personalized approach to getting better sleep, from what you eat and when you eat to addressing any nutritional gaps.

“I would also encourage regular, balanced meals throughout the day to support blood sugar management, especially for those with diabetes, while avoiding large meals close to bedtime,” Routhenstein said. “Caffeine later in the day and alcohol in the evening are also worth considering as possible sleep disruptors.”
