#4754. Segway launches new electric motorcycle that’s so safe it has seatbelts

Segway came to EICMA this year with a surprisingly broad lineup of new electric motorcycles, ranging from high-performance concepts to off-road machines. But perhaps the most interesting of the bunch is also the one that looks the least like a conventional motorcycle or scooter.

Meet the Segway X Cruiser, an electric two-wheeler that takes motorcycle safety so seriously that it has a roll cage and seatbelts.

Or at least, those are among the configurations Segway is showing as it develops the new machine for production.

The X Cruiser is Segway’s attempt to bring more automotive-style protection to a single-track vehicle, essentially asking how much of a car’s safety envelope can be wrapped around a motorcycle without adding another pair of wheels.

From the looks of things, the answer is quite a lot.

Segway says the X Cruiser’s design was informed by automotive crash scenarios, with cage and semi-cage structures, four-direction collision protection, staged energy absorption, and seatbelt restraints intended to improve rider protection. It also gets active safety features including standard blind spot detection and lane change warning.

The company showed several ways that basic idea can be configured, ranging from a more conventional partially enclosed scooter-like setup to versions with significantly more structure surrounding the rider. One of the most striking configurations uses a heavily bolstered race-car-style seat and seatbelt along with protective framing around the rider, while another adds a roof for even more enclosure.

It’s a fascinating approach because motorcycles have traditionally relied largely on the rider wearing the protection. Helmets, jackets, gloves, boots and sometimes airbag vests form the safety system, while the motorcycle itself generally offers little physical protection during a crash.

The X Cruiser effectively flips part of that equation by building some of the protective structure into the vehicle itself.

There’s an important caveat here, though. Segway specifically notes that its descriptions refer to the vehicle’s current design and equipment and do not mean it has completed automotive-style crash certification. Final equipment and certification will depend on individual markets, so it sounds like the company is holding short of making any major certification claims. Still though, it’s easy to see how having what is effectively a racing seat and roll cage surrounding the rider could seriously contribute to better protection in a crash. Just remember to keep your hands and feet within the vehicle at all times.

And unlike plenty of wild EICMA showpieces, this one isn’t merely destined to live under convention-center spotlights. Segway says the X Cruiser has a confirmed mass-production plan, with launches planned for China and Europe between 2027 and 2028. There’s no US availability announcement yet.

Underneath all that protective hardware is a fairly serious electric touring platform. Segway is using its CTB (cell-to-body) battery integration to help improve structural rigidity and battery packaging, with the company targeting nearly 200 km (124 miles) of range.

European versions are expected to feature 4.5 kW Type 2 AC charging, while the Chinese version will offer optional higher-power DC fast charging. The bike rolls on 15-inch front and 14-inch rear wheels wearing Michelin City Grip tires, and riders get a 10.25-inch TFT display along with an optional 55-liter electrically operated top box.

Interestingly, the X Cruiser also incorporates certain two-wheeler intellectual property and know-how licensed from BMW Group, though Segway stresses that it is responsible for the vehicle’s development, integration, validation, production and certification.

The X Cruiser may be the weirdest – and thus perhaps the most interesting – of Segway’s EICMA debuts, but it was far from alone.

The company also unveiled the Segway Orca Concept, a futuristic high-performance electric maxi-scooter concept built around an 800V electrical architecture and a nearly 20 kWh battery.

Segway is targeting up to 300 km (186 miles) of range, a 0-100 km/h (0-62 mph) time of 4.5 seconds, and the ability to add 200 km (124 miles) of range in 20 minutes. The concept also features front and rear multi-link suspension, electronically controlled multi-mode damping and a battery-integrated CTB chassis. Those figures are engineering targets rather than promised production specifications, and Segway currently describes the Orca strictly as a concept.

Its a BMW C1 reborn as electric! They were a bit of a cult thing, but underpowered for the weight. Never made it to the USA.

The biggest benefit is not really safety, its comfort.

Then there’s Segway’s expanding X Series, which moves the focus away from urban riding and toward dirt. The lineup includes the Xaber X1000 and Xaber 350, along with different Xaber 300 variants for the US and European markets. Segway is also partnering with Michelin for its Dakar Rally Factory Team, using the brutal rally environment as a real-world development and validation platform for electric off-road motorcycles.

Taken together, it’s quite the showing from a company whose name many people still associate primarily with those funny two-wheeled self-balancing machines from the early 2000s.

Segway has already expanded heavily into electric scooters, e-bikes, go-karts and powersports vehicles. Now it seems increasingly serious about becoming an electric motorcycle company as well.

And if motorcycles with roll cages, roofs and seatbelts are part of that future, things could get pretty interesting… pretty quickly!

#4752. The Sadness of Borrowed Dogs

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

In Ron Howard’s new documentary Avedon, the internationally renowned photographer Richard Avedon recalls “the sadness of borrowed dogs.” Throughout his childhood, his family borrowed dogs from neighbors to complete the happy family photos.

"We were not satisfied with the way we were,” Avedon says, while reflecting on his sister, Louise, who suffered from mental illness. She was eventually admitted to a psychiatric hospital after becoming increasingly withdrawn from reality due to schizophrenia.

The borrowed dog is a small detail that reveals a larger family dynamic. John Bradshaw called this staged domestic harmony a shame-based family system: a family organized around hiding its defects. In my view, these polished photographs of the happy Avedon family are what shame looks like when an entire family maintains the pretense. The photos show the family as it wants to be seen.

Photographs are one way to keep up appearances. Another way, which is common in families affected by addiction or abuse, is living by three unwritten rules: don’t talk, don’t trust, and don’t feel. Those rules keep the outside image intact. I hear versions of these rules all the time from clients who grew up being told “children should be seen and not heard,” “don’t make waves,” or “keep the peace.”

Children who are exposed to these messages learn to make themselves small to avoid being singled out, perhaps by an alcoholic parent who flies into rages. In that house, shrinking is a survival skill the child learns: their needs don’t matter, and safety depends on staying unseen.

They carry it with them, hiding their defects, and it becomes armor. The armor goes with them when they leave home. Some go on to build successful lives despite this armor. But they do so at a cost: They never let themselves live an authentic life, because if the armor slipped for even a second, someone might see them. And that feels dangerous.

Avedon’s son says his father adored Louise but never visited her in the institute where she languished. Perhaps Avedon feared finding her somewhere like the hospital he photographed in 1963. That February, he spent time at the East Louisiana State Mental Hospital and made his Mental Institution series. This unflinching set of pictures was meant to support that year's mental health reform movement. When they appeared in Nothing Personal, his 1964 book with James Baldwin, the critic Robert Brustein accused Avedon of offering “a titillating peek into the obscene and ugly faces of the mad.”

Unlike Brustein, who saw exploitation, I see the borrowed-dog snapshot turned inside out. The family album hid Louise’s illness, and the asylum photographs refused to look away from it. Avedon’s career is proof of that refusal.

As a child, Avedon posed with a borrowed dog. As an adult, he spent his career photographing everything his family had taught him to hide, except the one person he couldn’t bear to visit.

Avedon, R., & Baldwin, J. (1964). Nothing Personal. Atheneum.

Black, C. (1981). It Will Never Happen to Me! Children of Alcoholics: As Youngsters, Adolescents, Adults. M.A.C. Printing and Publications.

Bradshaw, J. (1988). Healing the Shame That Binds You. Health Communications.

Howard, R. (Director). (2026). Avedon [Documentary film]. Imagine Documentaries; Fifth Season; Netflix.

Richard Avedon Foundation. (n.d.). Mental Institution, East Louisiana State Mental Hospital, Jackson, Louisiana, February 1963 [Photograph series]. https://avedonfoundation.org/the-work

#4751. BYD’s newest EV is about as big as a Toyota Camry, but brings a lot more tech for $23K

BYD launched the new Seal 07 in China, where it starts at around $23,000. It’s about the size of a Toyota Camry, but brings a surprising amount of tech and premium features for the money.

After introducing the updated first-generation Seal 07 in March, BYD launched the second-gen model on Thursday.

The second-generation Seal 07, which BYD calls the “new choice for a class-leading luxury experience,” is available in battery electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains.

BYD offers five variants, including two PHEVs and three EVs, starting at 139,900 yuan (about $21,000) for the plug-in hybrid and 149,900 yuan (around $22,500) for the fully electric version.

The new Seal 07 EV uses a 76.7 kWh second-generation BYD Blade LFP battery, providing a CLTC range of up to 481 miles (775 km).

It comes standard with a single rear-mounted electric motor producing up to 328 hp (245 kW) and 269 lb-ft (365 Nm) of torque, which BYD says enables it to accelerate from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 5.5 seconds.

All plug-in hybrid variants use BYD’s latest DM-i system, which features a 1.5L turbocharged engine with 154 hp (115 kW) and a 214 hp (160 kW) front electric motor.

The new Seal 07 PHEV has a smaller 37 kWh battery that provides up to 205 miles (330 km) of pure electric CLTC range. That’s a considerable jump from the 143 miles (230 km) of electric range the previous generation offered.

Thanks to BYD’s latest Blade Battery 2.0 and Flash Charging technology, the vehicle’s battery can recharge from 10% to 70% in just 5 minutes. To go from 10% to 97%, it takes just nine minutes.

Both versions are 5,080 mm long, 1,960 mm wide, and 1,495 mm tall, with a 2,960 mm wheelbase, which is slightly bigger than the Toyota Camry.

Inside, the new Seal 07 adopts BYD’s latest cabin design, including a 15.6″ floating center infotainment screen, a 10.25″ instrument cluster, and two rear passenger entertainment screens.

BYD added several premium extras, including a built-in 6.8L smart refrigerator, zero gravity seats, and driver headrest audio. It also offers the most rear passenger space and the largest frunk (160L) in its class, according to BYD.

The Seal 07 debuts BYD’s Smart Ecosystem 2.0, including “Diva,” a smartwatch that can interact with the vehicle and let drivers manage functions remotely.

Higher-priced models offer BYD’s God’s Eye B intelligent driving system, with a roof-mounted LiDAR available as an option. The setup provides safety and convenience features such as Navigation on Autopilot in the city and on highways, plus full-scenario intelligent parking.

BYD is offering a limited-time “Super trade-in price” promo, starting at 145,900 yuan ($22,000) for the new Seal 07 EV and 135,900 yuan ($20,500) for the PHEV version.

#4749. ACOG Strongly Recommends Hormone Therapy for Menopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.

These expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date. They include new clinical guidelines for menopause hormone therapy (MHT), nonhormonal medications, and nonpharmacological treatment of vasomotor symptoms (VMS), which include hot flashes and night sweats, and sleep and mood changes.

According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.

Around 16%–66% of females in the United States report menopause-related sleep issues, and more than one-third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal females report experiencing depressive symptoms.

“In recent years, misconceptions about the risks of hormone therapy have been widespread, which has made some clinicians reluctant to prescribe it and some patients hesitant to use it,” Bruce Pier, MD, clinical professor and associate fellowship director at the University of North Carolina and collaborator on the ACOG clinical practice guidelines, told Healthline.

“This guidance offers a comprehensive review of the evidence to support individualized counseling and shared decision making. Our hope is that it clears up those misconceptions and expands access to treatment.”

The ACOG is also developing companion guidance for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, expected in 2027.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of MHT with estrogen and progestogens (or estrogen alone for people without a uterus) for both VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbance, in individuals who can use hormones.

It also conditionally recommends conjugated estrogen plus bazedoxifene (Duavee) as an alternative for these issues.

According to a meta-analysis from 2021 that was cited by the guidelines, estrogen therapy, with or without progestogens, significantly reduced VMS frequency and severity compared to a placebo or no treatment. A 2017 meta-analysis ranked transdermal estradiol plus a progestogen as the most effective option for reducing VMS frequency.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis, also cited by the guidelines, found that MHT was associated with improved self-reported sleep quality. Once again, transdermal therapies showed some of the largest effects.

The ACOG recommends initiating MHT before age 60 or within 10 years of the onset of natural menopause..

It also suggests that the decision to start MHT for VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances should be based on a shared decision making discussion about an individual’s symptoms and the benefits and risks of therapy. Consideration should also be taken regarding an individual’s:

Research shows that factors such as race, culture, socioeconomic status, gender identity, and sexual orientation can influence how individuals experience menopause and the care they receive.

According to the SWAN study, Black women reported more menopause symptoms than white women but were less likely to be treated for them.

“This updated document shines a light on these inequities. Clinicians can proactively help right now by asking every patient in midlife about symptoms, rather than waiting for them to bring it up. Long term, we hope this document drives more research funding to understand these gaps and begin closing them,” said Pier.

The ACOG stated in the guidelines that, “The available evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against the use of estrogen–progestogen or estrogen-only MHT for the treatment of menopause-related depressive symptoms.”

It recommends that perimenopausal and postmenopausal individuals who meet the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD) or those whose most noticeable symptom is depression should be treated according to depression management guidelines.

Current treatment guidelines for depression include therapy, medication, or a combination of the two.

Psychological treatments for depression include psychotherapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), while antidepressants are among the most commonly prescribed medications.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) for the management of menopausal symptoms like VMS and depression in individuals who don’t want to use MHT or can’t use it.

Currently, paroxetine is the only antidepressant that is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of VMS.

The ACOG also strongly recommends the use of neurokinin receptor antagonists to manage VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances in people who don’t desire hormone therapy or can’t use it.

There are currently two neurokinin receptor antagonists approved by the FDA to manage menopause symptoms. Fezolinetant (Veozah) was approved in 2023 to help manage hot flashes. In 2025, the FDA approved elinzanetant (LYNKUET) for the management of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.

Another nonhormonal treatment for VMS that the ACOG conditionally recommends is gabapentin.

There are various nonpharmacologic treatments that the ACOG conditionally recommends for the management of VMS, vasomotor-related sleep disturbances, and mood changes. These are treatments that don’t involve the use of medications.

The nonpharmacologic treatments conditionally recommended include:

It is generally recommended that these interventions are used alongside hormonal or nonhormonal medications.

The ACOG noted that there is not enough evidence to support the efficacy or safety of phytoestrogens, such as soy isoflavones, or herbal supplements, which are not regulated by the FDA in the same way medications are for safety, purity, or efficacy.

“Menopause is finally getting the attention it deserves, and this document shows what evidence-based care should look like in this space. It lays out a range of safe, effective options for managing menopause symptoms. My message to anyone struggling with these symptoms is simple: talk to your clinician. You don’t have to suffer through them,” said Pier.

#4748. The 7 Best Wired Headphones for Your Runs and Workouts

No more charging, no more lost Bluetooth connections, and no more chasing a bud under the squat rack.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

WIRED HEADPHONES ARE popular again. The cords are showing up in NBA arena tunnels, where Golden State Warriors point guard Steph Curry walks in with them hanging from his ears. Bears quarterback Caleb Williams wears corded headphones as part of his pregame routine. Bose felt they were worth bringing back, too. In October, it started shipping the $99 Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds, its first new wired headphones in years.While our favorite wireless workout headphones are more advanced than ever, they still have problems at the gym: connections drop, audio crackles, and you have to constantly manage the battery. And we've all had a bud knocked loose by a burpee and watched it bounce across the floor and under a squat rack. Just me? A wired pair avoids all of that. Sound travels through the cable, so there are no Bluetooth dropouts, and if a bud slips out, it hangs from the cord instead of hitting the ground.

Wired earbuds also have no battery. You'll never get to the gym and find out your headphones are dead, and a pair that's been sitting in your bag for a month still works as soon as you plug it in.

Sure, the cord can have its own drawbacks. It can snag on a rack in the gym, and when you run, it can bounce around into your body and arms. Its weight also pulls the buds downward, which can put pressure on your ears.

Most picks below have a way to keep the buds in place, including ear hooks, stabilizer wings, or a cable that runs over the top of your ear. Most also come with the right plug for your phone, so you don’t need an adapter. These are the best wired headphones you can get right now.

The Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds are the only pair on this list with active noise canceling. Each bud has two microphones that pick up the clang of plates and the music on the gym speakers, then cancel that sound. With the room quieter, you can keep your own music at a lower volume. Hold the button on the inline remote to switch to Aware mode. It uses the same mics to pipe in outside sound, so you can hear cars and cyclists on an outdoor run.

Noise canceling works best when each bud seals your ear canal, and silicone wing-tip stabilizers keep that seal in place while you move. Bose’s wings press against the inner ridge of your ear, so the buds don't shift during jumps or sprints. You get two wing sizes and three ear tip sizes, and you can remove the wings if you don't need them. The thick, rubbery 4.2-foot cable connecting them is durable. It tangles less than the thin cords on cheap USB-C buds, and it makes less noise when it rubs against a shirt.

Partway down that cable sits the remote, which holds volume buttons, a multifunction button (tap to play or pause, double-tap to skip, hold to change noise modes), and the call mic. All that hardware can be heavy, though — enough that you'll feel it pull on the buds during jumps and sprints. Running the cable under your shirt collar keeps the remote from swinging.

The noise canceling also determines what you can plug these into. The earbuds draw power from your phone to run the mics and processor, so they need a USB-C port. Any iPhone 15 or newer works, and most current Android phones do too. A 3.5mm jack, like the one on a treadmill screen or an airplane seat, won't work, even with an adapter. Once they're plugged in, the IPX4 rating protects them from sweat and splashes from any direction, though not from a dunk in water. They come in black, white, and a limited-edition mint.

Read more: Best Workout Headphones, Tested by Us

The JBL Endurance Run 3 costs $25 and carries an IP65 rating, the highest on this list. That means no dust gets in on dirt trails and sandy beach runs, while they can survive water sprayed from a nozzle. A downpour or a sweat-soaked HIIT class won't hurt them, either.

JBL's FlipHook design gives you two ways to wear them. With the cable hanging straight down, they sit like regular earbuds. Rotate the hooks upward and the cable runs over the top of your ear and down behind it. That takes the cable's weight off the bud. It also stops the wire from thumping against your chest while you run and jump. The TwistLock tips sit into the bowl of your ear, so a bud stays put when you turn your head fast.

The remote has one button and a mic, handling play, pause, and calls, and a long press brings up Siri or Google Assistant. You can adjust the volume through your phone. The standard Run 3 plugs into a 3.5mm jack. JBL also offers the Endurance Run 3C USB-C, which has a three-button remote and costs a little more. The standard Endurance Run 3 has a 3.5mm plug and a one-button remote.

The MEE Audio M6 Sport uses memory wire, a thin, bendable wire inside the cable near each bud. You bend it around the back of your ear once, and it holds that curve. It works like a custom-fit ear hook that stays put through box jumps and hill sprints, and it also takes stress off the buds.

The three-button remote on the braided cable does more than most wired sport buds. The outer buttons raise and lower volume. The center button plays, pauses, skips tracks, answers calls, and starts your voice assistant. The IPX5 rating protects against heavy sweat and rain.

MEE Audio tunes the M6 Sport for heavy bass. The USB-C version works with modern smartphones, and it comes with a shirt clip and six sets of ear tips, so you can get the exact fit you want. You can also get them a with a 3.5mm jack plug..

The SE215 earphones are in-ear monitors, the same style of earphones musicians wear on stage to hear themselves over a loud crowd. The low-profile shells sit flush inside your ear. The cable runs up and over the back of each ear, pulling the cord's weight off the buds and keeping cable noise out of your music when you move. The included foam tips expand to fill your ear canal, and Shure says they block up to 37 decibels of outside noise, enough to drown out a gym's speakers.

The SE215 delivers deeper bass than other wired headphones we’ve tested. Beyond sound, the earbuds have also been designed with durability in mind. The SE215's cable is Kevlar-reinforced and detaches at MMCX connectors, so if it breaks, you only replace the cord. Shure also sells a Bluetooth adapter that makes the same buds wireless.

Shure doesn't give them an IP rating, though, so you should wipe them down after sweaty sessions. The standard 64-inch cable has no mic or remote and comes only in a 3.5mm configuration, so a USB-C phone needs a dongle.

Apple’s EarPods are the pair you see a lot of people using in TikTok videos, holding the mic close to their mouth. At $19, they’re a great pair to keep in your bag for the day you forget your main headphones. The remote has volume buttons and a center button to play, pause, and answer calls. Apple says they're protected against sweat and water, though it doesn't list an IP rating.

The EarPods have hard plastic shells shaped to rest in the bowl of your ear, with no silicone tips sealing the canal. That makes them comfortable for long walks and lets outside sound in. But nothing holds them in place for more rigorous movements like burpees and jump rope. Still, they're steady enough for walking, the elliptical, and light lifting.

Read more: Our Review of the Apple iPhone Duo

The Avantree C171’s ear hooks are molded to curve over and behind each ear, so unlike the MEE Audio M6 Sport, no wire needs to be bent into shape. The cable runs down behind your ear instead of hanging from the bud, so it’s more out of the way when you’re moving.

A four-button remote controls volume, playback, calls, and your voice assistant, so you can keep your phone in your pocket. Avantree sells similar sport earbuds with USB-C, Lightning, and 3.5mm plugs; the C171 is the USB-C model, and the brand’s C171 manual includes troubleshooting for Galaxy S24 users who run into audio detection or distortion issues.

They don’t have an IP rating, but if fit is your main concern, these shouldn’t fly out of your ear during a HIIT workout.

The Avantree Resolve's speakers rest just outside your ear canal instead of sealing inside it, so you can still hear traffic and cyclists coming up behind you on a run. With no tip pressing into your ear canal, you'll also feel less soreness that builds up over a long session.

Since nothing sits inside your ear to hold the speakers in place, flexible hooks wrap over each ear to hold them in place. That grip won't be as snug as an in-ear tip, so the speakers can shift more when you move. Avantree makes a Small-Medium size for ears under 2.5 inches long and a Large size for everyone else, so measure your ear before you order.

While there is no IP rating, you do get inline remote controls for playback, volume, calls, and your voice assistant. Avantree sells 3.5mm, USB-C, and Lightning versions.

Wired headphones are better if your workouts keep getting cut short by dead batteries or bad Bluetooth connections. Without a battery, wired headphones play as soon as you plug them in, no matter how long they've sat unused. There's also no battery to wear out after two or three years of charging, which is when many wireless earbuds start dying mid-run.

Wireless buds are the better choice when you need total freedom of movement. Rolling on the floor, kipping pull-ups, and jump rope can all snag a cord. If your workouts are mostly lifting, steady running, or cardio machines, a cord rarely gets in the way.

Like any earbud, whether it’s wired or wireless, they can fall out of your ear. The cable's weight pulls on each bud with every step, so look for one of three fixes: ear hooks, like the memory wire on the MEE Audio M6 Sport or the FlipHook on the JBL Endurance Run 3, loop the cable over your ear. Stability wings, like those on the Bose, brace the bud against the ridge inside your ear. Over-ear cable routing, as on the Shure SE215, takes the cable's weight off the bud entirely. Plain earbuds with no tips or wings, like Apple's EarPods, are the most likely to fall out.

Yes, if you match the plug to your phone. USB-C earbuds plug straight into an iPhone 15 and later and most Android phones. Their digital-to-analog converter is built into the plug or cable, so you don't need an adapter. Since most modern smartphones no longer have a 3.5mm jack, earbuds with a 3.5mm plug need a USB-C-to-3.5mm dongle, and on a run that dongle adds weight and can snag on equipment. Choose a USB-C version when one exists.

The thumping you hear when the cord bounces against your shirt is called microphonic. Vibration travels up the wire into the earbud. Routing the cable over your ears is the most effective fix because it breaks the straight path from your chest to your ear canal. Running the cable under your shirt collar also stops it from swinging. A thicker, rubberized cable, like Bose's, transmits less noise than a thin plastic one.

IPX4 is the minimum for sweaty workouts. An IP rating has two digits. The first is dust protection on a scale up to 6, and the second is water protection on a scale up to 9. An X means the product wasn't tested for that category. IPX4 protects against splashing water from any direction, which covers sweat. An IPX5 rating means the headphones can withstand water jets, but it doesn’t guarantee protection in every condition, such as heavy rain. IP65, the JBL Endurance Run 3's rating, adds full dust protection for trail running.

Water and dust resistance is one area where wireless earbuds are well ahead. Most wireless workout models are rated at least IPX4, and many are rated IP55 or higher. Only three of the wired picks here have a rating: the Bose, the JBL, and the MEE Audio. If your pair doesn't have one, they can still survive light sweat, but remember to wipe them dry after each session.

I use Apple’s EarPods every day and have spent years testing wireless headphones and earbuds. That experience shaped what I looked for here. For this guide, I picked models based on factors like fit, durability, compatibility, and inline controls. The rest of the Men's Health team also reviewed and contributed to the list.

First, I looked at fit. A cable pulls on the buds every time you move, so I looked for ear hooks, stabilizer wings, or cables that run over the ear. I favored pairs with an official IP rating over vague "sweat-resistant" claims. I also checked that each pair is sold with a plug that fits current phones, because a 3.5mm-to-USB-C adapter is one more thing that can come loose mid-run. Inline controls mattered as well, since a remote you can reach mid-set means you don't have to dig your phone out.

It’s time to pack away most of your three-season hiking gear and bust out your dedicated cold-weather kit.

Prepping for winter hiking is all about staying dry, warm, and comfortable. Whether you’re looking to upgrade your current outerwear—everything from jackets and hats to hiking boots and socks—or this is your first winter hiking season, we’ve rounded up the best cold-weather hiking gear to help you tackle the trail this year. As a seasoned hiker who’s explored all seven continents over the last 30 years, this is what I recommend in 2026.

The result is a setup that’s designed to keep cold water cold in the summer, but with the added benefit of keeping warm water warm for winter hikes. It also helps ensure that your water supply doesn’t straight-up freeze in deep cold conditions.

I’ve been a fan of Icebreaker’s RealFleece blend for years—it’s softer and more luxurious than traditional wool but with all the benefits of natural Merino. This midweight top makes this the perfect in-between top that layers well (on top or underneath) in colder weather. The half-zip design is also great for quickly dumping heat on the go.

The OG Buff is arguably the most versatile piece of apparel in my pack. This winter-ready version upgrades to Polartec fleece that’s warm, buttery soft, and fast-drying. The stretchy construction allows for wearing it any of ten different ways, and UPF 50 protection shields your neck and face on harsh sunny days.

I appreciate a pair of midweight gloves that balances reliable warmth and weather resistance with enough dexterity to allow me to still use my phone, camera, and do the things that heavyweight ski gloves often make impossible on the trail. The Denali checks all of these boxes while adding a silicone grip and touchscreen-friendly fingertips to boot.

Arc’teryx’s Bird Head Toque brings a dash of understated cool to winter hiking headgear, and is amongst the most popular beanies you’ll find right now. I love the oversized classic “dinosaur bird” logo and bold color options. And the blended Merino/acrylic construction ensures that it’s soft, warm, quick-drying, and moisture-wicking—perfect for long winter days on the trail.

Fancy rainshells can be obscenely expensive. Spyder takes most of the next-gen technical features of the best shells I’ve personally tested—four-way stretch, solid DWR, and excellent breathability—and packages them into the surprisingly affordable Clutch that’s available for under $200. Bonus: It ditches the “crinkly plastic bag” vibe of most other rain shells, keeping you quieter on the trail.

Hyperlite leans heavy on next-gen Dyneema Woven Composite 3.9 fabric, ensuring the Southwest 40 is lightweight, extremely durable, and completely weatherproof—all essential for intense winter hikes. I love the roll-top design that keeps things dead simple with just the right amount of organization and nothing more. (I also like that it’s available in 55L and 70L variations for longer expeditions.)

All modern hiking apparel is made from natural fibers, synthetic fibers, or a blend of the two. Merino and alpaca wool are my two favorite natural options, as both offer excellent thermal regulation, breathability, and odor-resistance. They’re fantastic for longer trips, allowing you to pack less and travel farther while staying dry, comfortable, and stink-free. In most cases, however, they tend to be more expensive than their synthetic counterparts.

Synthetic fibers like polyester, nylon, and polypropylene all dry faster than Merino, are typically lighter weight, and more budget-friendly. However, they don’t offer the same odor resistance, and they’re all petroleum-based products. So, they’re hardly eco-friendly.

The key is regulating your body temperature with proper layering. Start with a thin base layer that feels good against the skin and fits closely without being too restrictive. Add an insulating midlayer like a half-zip or full-zip fleece. In especially cold conditions, adding a down shirt or full down jacket will help provide extra warmth. Top it off with a final layer that’s designed for weather protection (to fend off wind and precipitation) in the form of a hard or soft shell. Gore-Tex is the gold standard for this last layer as it offers the best protection, however, it’s also the most expensive. To maintain a comfortable body temperature and ensure you don’t overheat (and sweat), shed or add layers as necessary throughout your cold weather hike. This is where having a little extra room in your pack allows for stashing those extra layers.

There are a lot of individual factors that determine which jacket is right for you, including the quality of down used and how cold or hot you tend to run personally. But fill power is often the most straightforward spec to consider when determining the warmth of a puffy or down jacket. In general, 700 to 800 fill power will keep you warm for most cold-weather hikes. Upgrade to 850-plus fill power for extreme, subzero winter conditions.

It’s also important to consider the face fabric construction. Denier measures both weight and durability. For example, a 7D to 10D down jacket will be lighter and more packable, but also more prone to damage on the trail. Upgrading to a 15D-plus puffer adds weight but also durability. There’s no right answer as it depends on your budget and style of hiking.

Boot insulation is often measured in grams. A winter hiking boot with 200 grams of insulation should suffice in most cold weather conditions, while a 400g+ alternative is better for subzero temps, hiking in snow, or if your feet run cold. A waterproof membrane (again, Gore-Tex is best) is essential for winter boots, especially if you know you’ll be hiking in wet or snowy conditions. Finally, look for an outsole with a winter-centric tread compound with multi-directional lugs (I love Vibram Arctic Grip) for maximum traction in snow and ice.

As an avid hiker and adventure travel writer for more than two decades, I've tested countless outdoor products from all of the world's most recognized brands. Whether that’s a weeklong car camping trip or backpacking throughout Utah’s national parks, I’ve assessed outdoor gear in countless different scenarios and climates. I also consulted with Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower on top options, research, and his own personal testing in the winter months.

While testing cold weather hiking gear, we've been sure to take thorough notes on comfort, warmth, ease of packing, weight, durability, functionality, performance, and necessity.

Mike Richard has traveled the world since 2008. He's kayaked in Antarctica, tracked endangered African wild dogs in South Africa, and survived a near-miss great white shark attack in Mexico. His travel advice has appeared on the websites for Forbes, Travel + Leisure, CNET, and National Geographic. He loves the great outdoors and good bourbon, and (usually) calls Tulsa, Oklahoma home. Mike also enjoys speaking in the third person.

Ryan Brower is the Senior Gear and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, where he tests the best products in outdoor gear, tech, running shoes, and more. He has written about the outdoors for nearly two decades and was previously the Managing Editor, Content Performance at Gear Patrol. He holds a B.A. in Sport Management and is a Certified Beer Server, having previously covered the craft beer industry. Ryan currently lives on the water in New Jersey with his wife and their dog.

#4746. Can AI Really Make Us Feel Seen?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

MIT professor Sherry Turkle’s new book Artificial Intimacy explores what happens when people turn to chatbots for the kind of understanding we used to seek from each other.

In one exchange she describes, a man asks his chatbot whether his former girlfriend was right that he was emotionally unavailable. He brings a painful judgment about himself to a machine that is likely to offer a fluent, sympathetic response, instead of asking another person whose reply might be more unpredictable.

Turkle has studied our relationships with technology for decades

Today people use chatbots as companions, therapists, confidants, and romantic partners. “Pretend empathy" is the term Turkle uses to describe the sympathetic replies of the chatbots. Through her own experiments, she acknowledges just how powerful their responses can feel. She argues that because talking to a chatbot feels so easy, people may come to prefer it to human relationships, which take more work and can sometimes be uncomfortable.

Most people like hearing that their reactions make sense, especially when they are upset or hurt. It's harder to hear that we contributed to a problem, misunderstood something, or missed what someone else was trying to tell us. Another person who knows us may notice a pattern we have missed or remember an encounter differently. It can be unsettling to be shown something about ourselves that we couldn't see for ourselves. We often learn more about ourselves from knowing how our words and actions landed with someone else.

A chatbot's reassurance can soothe us when we are upset while leaving our account of events unchallenged. Validating a person's feelings doesn’t necessarily mean endorsing their version of what happened. But with a sympathetic reply, the two can easily blur. That's what’s called the sycophantic pull. This is when the chatbot’s agreement feels like insight, even when the response only reinforces the user's version of events. This helps explain the preference that Turkle describes. Of course, we want to return to the listener who always seems to agree with us.

One thing that can make the pull even stronger is that the chatbot can sound like an objective observer. But the chatbot knows only what we tell it. For instance, when we describe an argument, we choose the details and frame what happened, and the chatbot works only from the information we provided it with.

A therapist also starts with one person's account, but then brings independent judgment and experience to it. A therapist or confidant may notice what we leave out or question how we tell our story. A chatbot's polished answer can sound like a second opinion, but it’s really just our own account handed back to us in more confident language.

There is also a difference in who has to live with the consequences of the advice given.

A chatbot's sympathetic replies can sound like concern, but the program has no feelings about us and won't be affected by the outcome.

If the man acts on its answer, whether by reaching out to his former girlfriend or by deciding she was wrong about him, the chatbot won’t wonder how things turned out or bear any responsibility for the outcome. Professional ethics guide therapists. A friend has lived with the advice they gave, and with us, afterward.

When someone who has to face us afterward tells us something we don't want to hear, they are risking their relationship with us to say it. But a chatbot's agreement costs it nothing. That’s why the difficulty and awkwardness of human relationships is so essential. Another person may see us differently from how we see ourselves. If we turn to a chatbot's soothing agreement instead of risking disagreement and repair in real relationships, we miss chances to see our behavior from another’s perspective.

I explore these ideas in my forthcoming book, Being Seen: The Psychology of Visibility – Its Promise and Peril. Other people can help us recognize parts of ourselves that we can’t see for ourselves. Another person’s view can be painful or mistaken, but it comes from someone with an independent mind and one who cares what happens to us. A chatbot can soothe us with an answer that feels personal, but it has no independent point of view from what we tell it and nothing to lose if its advice goes wrong.

#4745. The 91 Best Movies of 2026 So Far (and 14 More We Can't Wait For)

With Christopher Nolan, star-studded epic romance, and major Marvel events, this list is a behemoth. And it also features a movie called Behomoth!.

AS A HUGE fan and follower of both movies and sports, the former has one major advantage: There's always something to look forward to. As a fan of the New York Jets, I don't always have that luxury. As a fan of watching films, though, not only is there always something worth my time on the big screen or streaming, but there's always several flicks down the line that will sound great or intriguing for one reason or another. Will they all turn out great? Of course not. But with sports and movies alike, excitement tends to be all about hope.

After a particularly strong 2025—movies like One Battle After Another and Sinners proved to be true standouts—how does 2026 pick up? With strength and energy, that's how. The year has been filled with all sorts of great movies, from horror (like 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple and Obsession) to epics (like The Odyssey), to some pretty great comedies (like Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie and The Invite). It’s been a good year.

But we always like to look at not only what’s been good to date, but also what we can still be excited for—and that includes everything. We’re talking stuff on the calendar already, stuff we suspect could come out this year, and even stuff making noise in places like the Sundance Film Festival. Throughout the year, this list evolves from our most anticpated movies into our favorite movies, and always looks quite different in December than it did in January.

For now, we've got a lot we’ve loved, but still a lot to look forward to as well. Below, we've listed nearly 100 movies on our radar that we think you'll be really interested in seeing.

If you're interested in a killer chimpanzee B-movie slasher, then Primate is for you. The movie delivers what it promises. Ben the chimpanzee does some very terrible things on screen but it makes for quite an enjoyable experience.

28 Years Later: The Bone Temple is a direct sequel to last year's 28 Years Later. And while the great Danny Boyle doesn't return to direct, the movie is helmed by the more-than-capable Nia DaCosta and once again counts Alex Garland as its screenwriter. The real assets, though, are the movie's leads: Ralph Fiennes and Jack O'Connell are sensational, magnetic every minute they're on screen amidst all sorts of post-apocalyptic chaos. Bring on part three.

Here's a quick pitch for The Rip: Matt Damon and Ben Affleck. The longtime friends team up once again for The Rip, a cop thriller in the vein of movies you've probably seen several times before... but done particularly well. This twisty crime story involves a police team finding a ton of money in a stash house (the titular rip), and figuring out who may or may not be corrupt. In addition to our beloved duo, the cast is shockingly stacked: Steven Yeun, Kyle Chandler, Scott Adkins, and One Battle After AnotherAcademy Award nominee Teyana Taylor are all on board.

SAM RAIMI FANS, ASSEMBLE! For the first time since 2009, the master of gross effects and frenetic cameras is back with an original horror story in Send Help. Rachel McAdams plays a Survivor superfan who gets stuck on an island with her dickhead boss (Dylan O'Brien), and then the antics begin. Think Cast Away meets Misery meets Drag Me to Hell. It's great stuff.

Jason Momoa and Dave Bautista are a pair of cool dudes who, with The Wrecking Crew, set out and did exactly what they intended to do: Make a badass buddy action comedy. The movie finds the pair playing estranged brothers who reunite in Hawaii to investigate their father's mysterious death; From there, we get lots of jokes, and a lot of (very violent!!!) action. It's a good time! Honestly, if they want to make a couple sequels to this, I'd be her for it.

Part This Is Spinal Tap, part Josie and the Pussycats, and part Curb Your Enthusiasm, The Moment is Charli XCX's movie for anyone who enjoys her music, persona, or both. A really fun movie about music, stardom, and celebrity in 2026.

Pillion was technically released initially in 2025 (and was also included on our list of favorite movies of that year), but we didn't want to miss an opportunity to recommend it to people once again. This unique film follows a man (Harry Melling) who engages in an unexpected BDSM relationship with a biker he meets at random (Alexander Skarsgård). The movie is quite the tonal balancing act, at times funny, intense, raunchy, and heartbreaking, but it all comes together by the end. A delightful movie, and a great showcase for both leads.

The classic novel comes to life on the big screen once again, this time from Promising Young Woman and Saltburn director Emerald Fennell, and with Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi in the lead roles. Fennell, an Academy Award winner for her work on Promising Young Woman, has both big fans and big detractors at this point—but her take her, while book purists haven't been thrilled, is a big, visually stunning epic romance. Robbie and Elordi are both up to the task as well, bringing a charged energy to roles that really need it. Alison Oliver, who recently shined on HBO's Task, is another major highlight in a supporting role. An original soundtrack from Charli XCX helps to set the anachronistic mood and feels like a real cherry on top.

This action-thriller, based on a book by Don Winslow, looks like a very solid entry in the genre that we're going to call "Somewhat Resembles a Michael Mann Film." And reviews have confirmed as much—the movie has often been compared to Heat, and while its tough to compare to Mann's 1995 masterpiece, we'll take just about anything in that vein. Look: If someone tells you there's gonna be a crime thriller in the vein of Heat with Chris Hemsworth, Mark Ruffalo, Halle Berry, and Barry Keoghan leading the cast, how could you not be on board?

One of our coolest directors, Gore Verbinski, makes his grand return with Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die—his first movie since 2016's A Cure For Wellness. If you don't know Verbinski by name, you should know several of his movies: the original Pirates of the Caribbean trilogy, The Ring, and Rango are among the standouts. Good Luck follows Sam Rockwell as a man who claims to be from the future and fighting off a rogue artificial intelligence. While the movie takes some pretty tough and labored tangents into on-the-nose satire, Rockwell's performance and the practical effects keep the movie afloat as a fun sci-fi romp.

Despite the title, you don't need to know anything else about Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie before going to see it. Sure, this story of two inept dudes in a band who just want to play music at a bar—and go through all sorts of ordeals, including time-travel, to do it—has existed before in both web series and television series form. But you can just go in and laugh and the absolute madness of the movie. Trust us—you'll have a good time with this one if you're into "madness that makes you laugh." This is a long-term passion project of Matt Johnson, who became well known recently for directing the underrated BlackBerry. His brash talent is again on display here.

We're always in on Glen Powell, and How to Make a Killing marks his first foray into A24's world as a leading man. This black comedy neo-noir comes from Emily the Criminal director John Patton Ford and follows Powell as a man who decides to take out a few members of his family in order to increase his chance at making a whole bunch of money via inheritance. The supporting cast joining Powell isn't too shabby: Margaret Qualley, Jessica Henwick, Ed Harris, and Topher Grace are all along for the fun.

The Napa Boys is a very specific cut for comedy fans. Remember when all those nondescript American Pie direct-to-video sequels were coming out? "American Pie Presents:.."? The Napa Boys imagines itself as one of those: self-impressed raunchy comedy with little tact—crossed, naturally with the wine bro nature of 2004's Sideways. As a result, we get a movie that presents as a sequel to a franchise that both has long been running out of juice, and, in our world, never was. If you get the truly absurd brand of parody being presented here, you're going to get a real kick out of it.

Hoppers feels like a throwback to the golden age of Pixar. Not only is it an original story (at a time when the legendary animation studio has often been leaning into sequels, prequels, and more), but it's a sweet and funny one at that. Following an animal-lover who uses Avatar-style technology to transfer her consciousness into a robotic beaver body that can discover what animals are thinking and saying, Hoppers actually turns into something of a conspiracy mystery story. With a voice cast that includes Jon Hamm, Dave Franco, and Meryl Streep among others, it's a fun one for the whole family.

Look. This is one of those movies that you really don't have to overthink. It's Alan Ritchson—Reacher himself—taking on a giant alien robot monster thing. This is as much of a throwback to '80s-style action filmmaking as we're ever going to get, and it delivers as promised. The fact that the rest of the cast includes staples like Jai Courtney, Esai Morales, and Dennis Quaid is just a bonus.

Undertone has been positioning itself as A24's next huge horror hit—and we'll see how it lands. The filmfollows a supernatural podcaster who gets sent some particularly spooky recordings; Its soundscape has brought tons of hype, with many calling it the scariest experience of the year. A simple premise like that sometimes makes for a very solid horror movie.

Based on the novel by Andy Weir(who also wrote The Martian), Project Hail Mary is a story of space exploration and a regular guy (played by Ryan Gosling) who gets involved. Phil Lord and Chris Miller (who are responsible for the Spider-Verse movies and directed 21 Jump Street) are behind the camera for this one, which has already proven to be a big, big hit. Gosling is basically on his own out in space for most of this, but it also includes a fun little alien guy named Rocky and a nice supporting performance by Anatomy of a Fall star Sandra Hüller. The visuals here are worth seeing on the biggest screen you can find.

2018's Ready or Not was one of the most fun horror films of the last decade, and now eight years later we get to see Samara Weaving's lead sucked back into the same twisted, bloody, violent games. The supporting cast—including David Cronenberg (!!!), March MH Flex star Elijah Wood, Sarah Michelle Gellar, and The Pitt's Shawn Hatosy—is fantastic. The movie kind of keeps with the form of the first Ready or Not, so if you liked that one, you'll certainly have a fun time with this one.

Forbidden Fruits follows a secret coven of witches operating in a shopping mall. Like, guys, some premises you just have to accept for how good they are and see them out. The movie is a campy, fun, twisty turny ride. Understand what you're getting into—a little bit of horror, a little bit of satire, and some fun twists—and it's going to be a good time.

Zazie Beetz (Atlanta, Deadpool 2) gets to lead her own horror/thriller movie with They Will Kill You, where she plays a woman who answers a help-wanted ad for a housekeeper in a luxury apartment building, only to find herself fighting for her life. The movie is pretty similar in tone to fellow horror/comedy Ready or Not 2, which we just talked about. But They Will Kill You leans more into its John Wick-style action and Kill Bill style plot, which sets it apart. The supporting cast, which includes Patricia Arquette, Heather Graham, and Industry star Myha'la, make it extra worth it.

#4744. Tesla wants its sworn Cybercab answers to NHTSA kept entirely secret

Tesla has answered NHTSA’s Special Order demanding it prove, under oath, that the Cybercab meets federal safety standards. The response landed on the October 30 deadline, and Tesla asked the agency to keep all of it confidential.

The only part of the filing the public can read is a 30-page guide for firefighters. Everything about how a car with no steering wheel, pedals, or mirrors was certified as compliant is blacked out.

We reported in September that NHTSA had ordered Tesla to show its work on the Cybercab’s certification. The order came one week after the company started charging for Cybercab rides in Austin on September 3 and put 21 questions to the company, with civil penalties of up to $139 million for an incomplete answer and criminal exposure for a false one.

Tesla first tried to buy time. On September 18, it asked for eight more weeks, until November 20, citing “the voluminous nature of the request” and the work of searching its records and writing “thorough narrative formats in response to each question.” NHTSA gave it 30 days instead. The new deadline was October 30, and Tesla met it.

Three Tesla documents now sit in the AQ26002 docket, and two of them are empty.

The first is Tesla’s response letter, dated October 30 and addressed from 1 Tesla Road in Austin. It is one page long. The only text is: “The entirety of this file is confidential business information.”

The second is a placeholder for Tesla’s answer to Request 8, which asked the company to explain, standard by standard, how it determined the Cybercab complies: which subpart it certified to, and whether it ran physical tests, simulations, or engineering analyses. Per NHTSA’s note, the responsive documents carry a confidentiality request “for the entirety of each document.”

The third is the only substantive document: Tesla’s Cybercab First Responder Interaction Plan, version 1.2, dated September 3. It’s a real document with useful information in it. It’s also something Tesla has had on its website since July, aimed at police and fire crews, not regulators.

So the public gets a tow-truck manual, and the certification argument stays sealed.

The Special Order wasn’t a fishing expedition. It named the rules the Cybercab doesn’t obviously meet, and it seeks to understand how Tesla believes it can get around it.

FMVSS 135 says “the service brakes shall be activated by means of a foot control.” NHTSA has stated in public that a manufacturer of a vehicle with no foot brake can’t certify to it, then asked Tesla how it did. FMVSS 108 requires a turn-signal control that cancels itself when the steering wheel turns. FMVSS 111 requires mirrors. And the agency wanted to know whether Tesla certified the car with temporary driver controls bolted in and then removed them, which would run into the Safety Act’s “make inoperative” prohibition.

It also asked how the Cybercab is legal without a Part 555 exemption, the route Amazon’s Zoox took for its own steering-wheel-less robotaxi in July. Zoox applied, made its case, and got an exemption capped at 2,500 vehicles a year. Tesla self-certified and started charging for rides.

Every one of those answers is now under a confidentiality claim.

The first-responder plan was written for a different audience, but it brushes against several of NHTSA’s questions.

It says the Cybercab is “not typically equipped with a steering wheel or acceleration and brake pedals.” The word “typically” is doing work there. The same document notes that a Cybercab with a steering wheel and pedals “is typically an engineering or test vehicle, and operates at SAE Level 2 autonomy,” and includes instructions for driving one. That’s relevant to Requests 5 through 7, which asked whether the subject vehicles can be driven with temporarily attached controls.

It describes an operational design domain covering “all public roadways, such as freeways, highways, city streets, and rural roads,” at all hours, in light and moderate rain, fog, and snow. That is a far wider envelope than the Austin geofence the cars run in today, and it references an “Arizona Areas of Operation Appendix.” Request 1 asked for the ODD and Request 2 for scaling plans.

And it confirms that first responders can be granted access to on-board touchscreen controls to move the car, after showing a badge to the B-pillar camera (that’s interesting). Request 20 asked whether the touchscreen can move the vehicle and under what restrictions.

Nothing in it touches brakes, mirrors, telltales, or the certification itself.

Confidentiality requests go to NHTSA’s Chief Counsel under Part 512. The agency decides whether Tesla’s claim holds, and it can order a public version released if it doesn’t. NHTSA hasn’t said anything about the request, and it hasn’t found the Cybercab noncompliant with any standard.

This is familiar. In June 2025, Tesla asked NHTSA to hide its answers about the original Robotaxi launch in Austin, a service running on supervised FSD while FSD was under investigation. Those answers never surfaced.

NHTSA’s opening resume for the audit put the affected population at about 1,000 vehicles. The Cybercab is still carrying passengers in Austin while the agency reads a filing nobody else can.

I don't see how the answers can have confidential business secrets. It is about meeting public safety standards, not asking for schematics, technical details or designs. It is about clear public safety requirement and how the vehicle qualify as meeting it.

The so called keyword from Tesla's self certification is "applicable". Tesla may argue that many of those requirements aren't applicable in their test vehicle. But I would like to see the justifications on that.

Tesla’s position in September was that the Cybercab complies with every applicable federal standard, including the one that requires a brake pedal. If that’s true, the argument for it is the most interesting document in the autonomous vehicle industry right now, and Tesla just asked the government to make sure nobody reads it.

We get why a company redacts test data and supplier details. But the legal theory for how a car with no foot brake meets a foot-brake rule doesn’t sound like a trade secret to me. Zoox’s exemption petition is public. Waymo’s safety framework is public. Tesla’s case for why it didn’t need to ask is sealed, cover letter included.

NHTSA now has to decide whether “the entirety of this file” is really confidential business information. If it says no, we’ll finally see how Tesla certified this car. If it says yes, about 1,000 Cybercabs keep driving on a certification the public isn’t allowed to check.

#4743. Music as an Intervention in Psychedelic-Assisted Therapy

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

Music has long been part of ceremonial and healing practices involving psychedelics, and it has played a role in Western psychedelic research for decades. But as researchers learn more about how music influences patients during psychedelic-assisted therapy, an important idea is emerging: Music isn't simply something playing in the background. It is part of the therapeutic intervention itself. However, a recent 2026 systematic review in the Journal of Clinical Psychology highlighted how little data has been gathered to date about the role of music in psychedelic clinical trials.

In psychedelic-assisted therapy, set and setting are at the core of the process. Set refers to the patient's mindset, expectations, and emotional state, while setting encompasses the physical, social, and therapeutic environment in which treatment takes place.

Music is an important part of that setting. Early psychedelic research sometimes involved sessions conducted in relatively sterile environments with little sensory stimulation. Over time, researchers and therapists came to recognize the importance of creating a more supportive environment, including the use of music. Even the absence of music could create a response.

One of music's most valuable functions is that it provides a sense of movement throughout a dosing session. A piece of music begins, develops, and eventually ends. Another takes its place. The emotional tone, rhythm, and instrumentation change, offering patients a reminder that whatever they are experiencing in the moment will also change.

A 2026 review published in Brain and Behavior suggested that music can intensify emotions, influence brain networks involved in meaning and imagery, and affect patterns of brain activity during psychedelic states. However, the researchers also emphasized that the evidence remains limited.

One of the challenges in selecting music for psychedelic-assisted therapy is that no two people hear music in exactly the same way. A piece of classical music might evoke peace for one person and sadness for another. Choral music may feel deeply meaningful to someone with a spiritual background but uncomfortable to someone whose religious experiences have been painful. Even a particular instrument can carry strong personal associations. For this reason, it is virtually impossible to choose music that is completely "neutral."

Every musical selection has the potential to influence a patient's experience, whether through its emotional qualities, cultural associations, or personal significance. This doesn't mean that every piece of music will have a profound effect. Some patients may barely notice what is playing, while others may find the music central to their experience.

A 2018 study published in Psychopharmacology, titled "The Hidden Therapist," examined patients receiving psilocybin treatment for depression. Researchers found that patients' responses to music, particularly their sense of resonance with it, were associated with aspects of their psychedelic therapy experience and changes in depressive symptoms. The findings suggest that how patients relate to the music may matter as much as the music itself.

One of the more interesting aspects of music in psychedelic-assisted therapy is that patients are not encouraged to avoid every uncomfortable response. In preparation sessions, therapists may discuss what to do if a patient encounters music they dislike or find emotionally challenging. For example, if a song brings up sadness, a patient might be encouraged to notice what is happening and consider whether they can remain with the feeling for a short time rather than immediately trying to escape it.

Even the experience of disliking a piece of music can offer an opportunity for observation. What happens when something feels unpleasant? What thoughts, sensations, or emotions arise? Is it possible to experience discomfort without immediately needing to change it? These questions connect to a broader principle of psychedelic-assisted therapy: learning to approach difficult emotions with curiosity rather than automatic avoidance.

But there is an important distinction between allowing space for discomfort and imposing it.

If music becomes overwhelming, distressing, or simply feels inappropriate for the moment, patients should be able to communicate that to their therapists. Depending on the research protocol, the music may be changed, skipped, lowered in volume, or temporarily turned off.

Patient autonomy remains essential. Music may be part of the therapeutic intervention, but patients should understand their options and have opportunities to express their preferences and concerns.

Music's role in psychedelic-assisted therapy may continue after the effects of the medication have subsided. Integration is the phase of treatment in which patients reflect on their experiences, explore their meaning, and consider how to apply insights to everyday life.

For some patients, listening to music from their dosing session can help them reconnect with emotions, memories, or perspectives that emerged during treatment. Sometimes, playlists are made available to participants after their dosing session. Some have reported returning to the music during quiet reflection, while others listen during ordinary activities such as gardening or getting ready for the day.

For certain patients, the music becomes a meaningful reminder of their therapeutic experience, sometimes years later. What such experiences suggest is that music may provide a connection between the dosing session and the ongoing work of therapy.

The compound is only one part of psychedelic-assisted therapy. The therapeutic relationship, preparation, environment, integration, and music all help shape the patient's experience.

Music may offer comfort, evoke memories, or help patients navigate difficult emotions. At times, silence may be more appropriate. What matters is not simply what is played but how each patient responds. By approaching music with intention and flexibility, therapists can make it a meaningful part of individualized care

Jess M. Jones, LCSWC, holds a B.A. in sociology from Wesleyan University, an M.S.W. from the University of Pennsylvania, and multiple clinical certifications in psychedelic-assisted therapy. She has specialized training in MDMA-and ketamine-assisted therapy and also serves as a trainer and mentor with Fluence.

#4742. Hyundai is recalling nearly 30,000 Kona Electric vehicles due to an airbag software defect

Hyundai issued a recall affecting nearly 30,000 Kona Electric vehicles due to a software error that could cause the airbag to fail to deploy in a crash.

In a letter sent to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration on November 4, Hyundai said it was recalling certain 2019 to 2023 Kona Electric and 2019 to 2022 Veloster N vehicles.

The recall impacts 37,901 vehicles in total, including 29,058 Kona Electric and 8,843 Veloster N models.

According to documents submitted to the NHTSA, the issue stems from a software error with the airbag control unit (ACU) that can cause the airbag malfunction indicator light (MIL) to come on and the airbag system to deactivate under certain driving conditions.

The data may become corrupted during a system reboot or power interruption while the system is writing to the ACU’s memory. When this happens, the airbag MIL will illuminate to warn drivers.

As of October 22, 2026, Hyundai is aware of 331 alleged incidents related to the issue. However, none have resulted in a crash, fire, or injury.

Owners can take their vehicle to the closest dealer, where it will update the ACU software, free of charge.

Hyundai expects to mail out owner notification letters on January 1, 2027. In the meantime, owners can contact Hyundai’s customer service at 1-855-371-9460 with any questions or concerns. Hyundai’s recall number is 311.

You can also contact the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration Vehicle Safety Hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit the NHTSA.gov website for more information. The NHTSA campaign number is 26V728.
