#4741. The 60 Best New Shows of 2026 (and 1 More We Can't Wait For)

We've got murder mysteries, stories of love and lust, and lots and lots of Yellowstone. And that's just the beginning.

THE IDEA OF "new" television shows is a little bit of a tricky one these days. Sure, we do still get a fair share of truly new, exciting, unique ideas each year—just look at shows like Severance a couple years ago and Pluribus last year. Shows like last year's The Lowdown—rich, well-written, character-focused stories—still draw major stars like Ethan Hawke and still hit in a big way for audiences that watch it. If someone was being dramatic and wanted to say original TV was dead, dying, or on life support, there's plenty of evidence out there to throw in their face.

But at the same time, they aren't entirely wrong. For one reason or another, so much of the TV landscape—even shows we're really excited for—are based around something that in one way or another already exists.

Look, we can't beat too much around the bush: People love nostalgia, people love things they recognize and remember, and it can be pretty hard to get anyone to even attempt to give their attention to something new, let alone get really into it in the way we all like to with the very best of TV. Which is why we kind of have two different options here—people need to be really trusting of word of mouth and really aware when something is a really good new, original show (because no one likes to waste their time with a piece of junk), and we just need to really hope that all the remakes, reboots, reimaginings, and re-whatevers are good.

And they should be! HBO's Lanterns is modeled after True Detective, stars Kyle Chandler and Aaron Pierre as the titular Green Lanterns, and counts Watchmen genius Damon Lindelof as a producer. Of course it’s good. Below, we're going to keep track all year. We're charting the shows we already know are good. We're charting the shows we think might be good. And we're charting the shows that may not even come out this year, but if they do... they still might not be good. But, again, say it with us: We're choosing to be hopeful.

Netflix has been really good of late at the pulpy, potboiler, limited series, and His & Hers is the latest in that winning streak. The show follows a detective (Jon Bernthal) and his estranged journalist wife (Tessa Thompson) as they both hunt for answers when a local woman—whom they both have a close connection to—winds up dead. Based on Alice Feeney's book of the same name, His & Hers is exactly how this kind of show should be: Juicy, fun, easy to watch, and filled with really good actors.

In shrinking its story down to a more intimate one that takes place between the margins of major universe events, Game of Thrones takes a page out of the Andor handbook with A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (based on George R.R. Martin's Dunk and Egg novellas). This short series, which follows a big, humble, anxious hedge knight (former professional rugby playerPeter Claffey)and his little friend/squire (Dexter Sol Ansell) is a true breath of fresh air for Thrones fans on both a story and character level. It's a delight.

Doesn't the premise of Ponies just sound fun? This spy series set in '70s Moscow follows a pair of women working with the CIA who find themselves at the midst of a vast conspiracy when their husbands both die under mysterious circumstances. And those women are played by The White Lotus's Haley Lu Richardson and Game of Thrones queen Emilia Clarke. Sometimes something that sounds like a winner just turns out to be one.

The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins (NBC/Peacock)

This show about a disgraced former football player (Tracy Morgan) and a documentary filmmaker following him (Daniel Radcliffe) comes from the team behind 30 Rock, so you know you're going to get several jokes per minute. Plus, Morgan and Radcliffe are no slouches themselves. The show had a special debut in January and will continue on a regular schedule later in February.

At the very least, Wonder Man is among the best shows Marvel ever made—and you could make a case that it's at the top of the list. Yahya Abdul Mateen II plays the titular hero (aka actor Simon Williams) as the kind of guy we love to love in this sort of story: humble, well-meaning, charismatic, and ambitious. But when he meets fellow actor (and former fake terrorist) Trevor Slattery (Ben Kingsley) and learns that his favorite movie from childhood is being remade by an acclaimed director, everything changes. Wonder Man isn't just a good Marvel show, but a good show about people, movies, and friendship period. Let's hope the MCU takes notes from what worked so well here and keeps the streak going in the future.

One of America's great cultural institutions made its grand return in 2026: The Muppet Show! This version—coming from executive producers Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg—is directly modeled on the original Muppet Show, which means special guests, musical performances, comedy sketches, and lots of fun. The first episode, which featured special guest star Sabrina Carpenter, was an absolute delight for anyone who likes Kermit, Miss Piggy, and friends (or who just likes laughing and having a good time). For now, it's just this one episode, but if the reaction is strong enough (and it seems like it might be), the show will come back in full.

The latest entry in producer Ryan Murphy's American Story universe is called Love Story, and follows the romance and life between Carolyn Bessette Kennedy and John F. Kennedy Jr. The show is, however, much better than that tabloid-y description sounds; Sarah Pidgeon, who plays Carolyn, is a star, coming off her Tony-nominated role in the Fleetwood Mac-inspired play Stereophonic. But Paul Anthony Kelly, who plays JFK Jr., is a real discovery—it's his first role (he was previously a model), and he truly feels like a reincarnation of the late attorney/magazine publisher/dashing public figure. Of course, this is a story that ends in an extreme tragedy—so if you get invested, be sure to have your tissues ready.

This wild documentary series looks at different disputes between neighbors, telling compelling and often escalating true stories that will truly floor you in the depiction of their very-real truth. Think about this less as a story about the legalities of these disputes, and more a look into some larger-than-life characters through an often trippy, absurd lens. The series is produced by Josh Safdie and Ronald Bronstein, coming off of their recent success on the Oscar-nominated Marty Supreme.

The new season of Scrubs brings back almost all of the original cast, including Zach Braff, Donald Faison, and Sarah Chalke. And audiences who love and/or remember that trio and most of the show's original dramedy premise should be pleased with this new version of the beloved aughts sitcom. The last season aired in 2010, so we're OK with calling this 16-years-later revival a 'new' show.

DTF St. Louis follows trio of languishing adults—played by the electric trio of Jason Bateman, Linda Cardellini, and David Harbour—who get involved in a love triangle and general madness that results in one of them winding up dead. You may think you have an idea of what you're getting into with this show based on the cast and that premise, but believe us—all of your expectations will be upended. DTF St. Louis is a tonal balancing act, a show that bounces between hilarious dark comedy, compelling mystery, and gutting, relatable drama. It's one of the best shows of the year.

The second age of Yellowstone begins in earnest with Marshals, a 13-episode drama that airs on CBS (and streams on Parmaount+ either simultaneously or a day later, depending on which tier of subscription you have). The series focuses on Luke Grimes's character Kayce, and how an old SEAL Team leader (Logan Marshall-Green) recruits him into his Marshal squad. There's at least one more Yellowstone spinoff coming in 2026—Dutton Ranch—and so this is the one leading the charge.

One of the busiest men in show business these days—on both the big and small screen—is Guy Ritchie, and his newest endeavor takes him back to a world he's inhabited a couple times before. Young Sherlock follows, well, a Young Sherlock Holmes. And as you can imagine, it follows Arthur Conan Doyle's famous detective as he solves a mystery. Hero Fiennes Tiffin plays the titular character, and Colin Firth is also part of the show's cast. If you're into that, you'll have a fun time! It's an enjoyable show.

The erotic thriller is back! Or, well, juicy erotic character study dramedy? Whatever we want to call it, Netflix's Vladimir is one of the year's most exciting new shows. Based on the novel of the same name, this show follows a longtime literature professor at a college (Rachel Weisz, constantly breaking the fourth wall) who finds herself in the midst of controversy when her fellow professor husband (John Slattery) gets caught sleeping with students. She takes this as an opportunity to switch things up a bit, and so she becomes smitten with her very sexy new colleague (Leo Woodall). It's a fun, zippy, juicy time—and kind of like if Deadpool was actually about a smart woman in academia who's spinning her wheels and maybe just a little bit horny.

From the mold of Ted Lasso and Shrinking comes Rooster, which stars Steve Carell and counts Lasso and Shrinking co-creator Bill Lawrence (who also made Scrubs and Cougar Town) as its showrunner. Carell plays an author who heads to help his professor daughter on a college campus... and becomes enamored with life there. Imagine Back to School but with some middle-age soul-searching and academia at play? Sure! HBO's got another winner on their hands with this one—and maybe Carell can get the Emmy that he somehow never got for The Office.

There are 29 books in the Scarpetta series, and, now, one TV show on Prime Video starring Nicole Kidman and Jamie Lee Curtis. The series follows forensic pathologist Dr. Kay Scarpetta (Kidman) as she solves a crime—but the show is so much more than just that. In a way, Scarpetta is destined to fit into Prime Video's roster of rock-solid procedural murder mysteries, which also includes Reacher, Cross, Bosch, and plenty more. But it's got a little bit of an extra chaotic oomph—helped out by the star-studded cast that also includes Bobby Cannavale and Simon Baker—that make it worth your while and a unique, fun show.

Sunny Nights, which aired in Australia last year, now makes its U.S. debut on Hulu. The premise is simple: A pair of siblings (played by the very funny Will Forte and D'Arcy Carden) want to start a spray tan business, but wind up entrenched in the criminal underworld. Whoops! Forte and Carden have been two of our finest comedic actors for a while—with ability to play depth in addition to that humor—and the show thrives when they're at their strongest. A solid watch for anyone looking for something light but compelling.

This series—from Yellowstone super writer/producer Taylor Sheridan—follows Stacy Clyburn (Michelle Pfeiffer) and her family, as they move from the busy, stressful world of New York City to a more rustic setting out in beautiful Montana after a totally unforseen tragedy. Kurt Russellplays her husband, Preston, with his usual endless charisma, while the supporting cast includes the likes of Matthew Fox and Suits star Patrick J. Adams. Sheridan does his usual zigging and zagging in The Madison—the tone can sometimes shift from very sad to zany and comedic, and, as usual, there's a bit of social commentary speechifying buried in almost every scene. But if you're on board with the writing style he uses in shows like Yellowstone and Landman, you'll probably be OK with it here, especially if you're ready for a heavier and more contemplative tone. This show was originally planned to be part of the Yellowstone connected universe, but those plans have since been changed; It's now a new story, but with that Montana setting, you still get to look at all sorts of beautiful landscapes.

After striking gold a couple years ago with Jury Duty, Prime Video gives its grand Truman Show-esque experiment another try with a second season called Company Retreat. This time around, we follow a regular guy who thinks he’s working as a temp for a hot sauce company and joining them on their annual company bonding retreat. Of course, everyone around him is actually an actor in a scripted, engineered situation. It’s a little goofier than the first season, but seeing how everything plays out is compelling, often very funny television nonetheless. A worthy follow-up, and, honestly, we might just watch these as long as they feel like making them.

Riz Ahmed is the creator and star of Bait, a show about an actor who thinks he's about to get offered the role of a lifetime—James Bond!—and the madness that spirals out of such a revelation. If you're a fan of Ahmed's (and why wouldn't you be?) this will be a fun ride.

Something Very Bad Is Going To Happen (Netflix)

Camila Morrone (Daisy Jones and the Six) and Adam DiMarco(The White Lotus) are set to get married in this horror series from showrunner Haley Z. Boston (who worked on the very underrated Brand New Cherry Flavor) and producers The Duffer Brothers. And not to oversell, but Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen is the best horror show I've seen in quite some time. While the show plays with familiar settings and tropes—you may think of Ready or Not or Midsommar during the show's eight episodes—it's so filled with Ari Aster-esque dread and stunning, striking camera work that it doesn't even matter. Horror fans are in for an absolute treat with this one.

#4739. Why Shame Matters in Politics

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

In the November 2026 American midterm elections, campaign advertisements were relentless. Across broadcast television and digital media, a record 573.2 and 500 million dollars were spent on Texas and Ohio campaigns, respectively.[1] Americans received a combined 60 billion political text messages, an average of 170 messages per person.[2]

The quantity of messages was startling, but so was their content, which frequently transgressed the bounds of decorum. Many campaigns involved insults and unsubstantiated rumors, meant to undermine the credibility of candidates.[3] These were cases of mudslinging—the exchange of personal insults or abuse, especially unjust ones, to damage the reputation of an opponent.[4] While the delivery of unsolicited messages directly to our iPhones was a novel experience, mudslinging itself is not a new American phenomenon.

For example, in the 1796 U.S. presidential election, John Adams and his supporters called Thomas Jefferson an atheist, and Jefferson’s supporters referred to Adams as “His Rotundity” and an “old, querulous, bald, crippled, toothless Adams.”[5] In the presidential election of 1828, Democrats accused John Quincy Adams of the misuse of public funds, and Whigs attacked Andrew Jackson’s military record and character.[6]

There are helpful ways to criticize a political opponent in an election. Examples include drawing attention to a poor track record of leadership or patterns of equivocation in policy statements. But personal vitriol, fabricated attacks, and ridicule are not among them. Mudslinging is often at odds with virtues such as charity and honesty. It distracts from substantive policy conversations. When a candidate campaigns in this way, he has shown himself to be undiscerning, cruel, and sometimes shameless.

To be shameless is to avoid moral censure or be unapologetic in wrongdoing. The shameless person intentionally flouts moral norms—doing the wrong thing, even though he knows better. Alternatively, he may be unaware of moral norms—even though he should have known better. In either case, the shameless person is blameworthy yet fails to experience the sting of a moral sanction.

I provided a recent example of shamelessness in American civic life—campaigns built around dishonesty and personal vitriol. But shamelessness is not just a problem during election cycles. It is a problem in daily governance, such as when leaders demean others or abuse power for personal gain. It is a problem on social media, where people overshare personal information and make inappropriate jokes. And shamelessness is a problem in corporate America. Examples include fraud, bribery, and flagrant violations of environmental protections.

So, why does shame matter in politics? Here are three reasons.

Shame is a negative-valence, self-conscious emotion, characterized by a critical self-evaluation.[7] It construes oneself as problematic. Shame is not an emotion that people like to experience. It is popularly regarded as “guilt’s ugly sister” and a disposable emotion.[8] We would rather do away with shame entirely than feel bad about ourselves. However, it is probably not a coincidence that a culture that wishes to dispose of shame is also riddled with shamelessness. If we are not sensitive to wrongdoing, how can we be expected to act well?

A better (albeit more challenging) approach is to recover shame in healthy forms. This is the approach we take with other misdirected emotions. An example is that, when a child throws a tantrum, we do not regard her anger as disposable or inherently unproductive. We educate this emotion toward its proper end, helping the child to experience anger in fitting ways.

I defined shame in terms of a global negative self-evaluation. This distinguishes shame from guilt, which attends to particular bad actions. Tangney (1998) puts it this way: Shame says, “I did that terrible thing,” whereas guilt says, “I did that terrible thing.” In some cases, shame’s self-evaluation makes it less action-guiding, since shame, unlike guilt, does not see a particular wrongdoing to repair. However, shame’s construal of the person means the emotion can better recognize patterns of bad action.

Additionally, shame attends to considerations of moral beauty or fineness—features of the moral life which are not neatly captured in terms of ‘good’ and ‘bad’.[9] Finally, shame attends to social standing and relational repair.[10] It aids our sensitivity to the feelings and expectations of others. Without shame, we lack the vision it provides, which helps us navigate the complexities of the moral life.

Imagine you have a rule in your home: no jumping on the couches. But you don’t enforce the rule. Maybe you see the child jumping, and instead of scolding him, you turn away or smile. The child may jump on the couch tentatively at first. Eventually he will jump freely and shamelessly, unconcerned about the rule that apparently does not apply to him.

Shame matters because it holds a leader to a standard and keeps the standard emotionally salient. This is important because it reduces the likelihood of bad actions. It also reduces the tendency toward assumptions of norm-differentiation in leadership—acting as though rules, in general, do not apply.

Finally, shame matters because we are imitative creatures. We can tell young people that moral character matters, but when those in authority are uncivil and unapologetic, or shameless in how they comport themselves in public, this is the lesson that stays with them.

#4738. Meta-backed 250 MW solar farm breaks ground in Arkansas

Arkansas is getting another 250 megawatts (MW) of solar power, and Meta has signed up to buy it.

EDP Renewables North America (EDPR NA) broke ground on Cypress Knee Solar in Chicot County, in the southeastern corner of the state, on November 4. The solar farm is expected to be completed by 2028, bringing several hundred construction jobs and an estimated $25 million in county revenue over its lifetime.

Meta’s long-term power purchase agreement helps it work toward its pledge to match 100% of its annual electricity use with renewable energy generation. Don’t confuse that pledge with Meta powering its data centers with renewables around the clock, though – Facebook and Instagram’s parent company is also backing new gas plants to meet its growing power demand.

The companies announced the deal in May. Cypress Knee is their third clean-energy agreement, bringing the total capacity covered by Meta’s deals with EDPR NA to 545 MW.

“As energy demand continues to rise, projects like Cypress Knee Solar help strengthen grid reliability while creating jobs, generating meaningful local revenue, and delivering long-term benefits to the communities that host them,” said EDPR NA CEO Sandhya Ganapathy.

EDPR NA says it has already contributed more than $77,000 during project development, including money to restore the Lakeside High School greenhouse, resources for the Lakeside Robotics team, and funding for the Lake Village food pantry.

#4737. The 6 Best Adjustable Kettlebells, Tested by Editors and Certified Trainers

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

These offerings from REP Fitness and Bells of Steel are some of the best.

KETTLEBELLS OFFER PLENTY of bang for your buck. You can use them for strength training, muscle building, and explosive movements like snatches and swings. You can achieve all of this with just one kettlebell, making it a tool that’s as simple as it is effective. Not only that, but they are actually fun to use; I've put together plenty of grueling workouts with kettlebells that had me grinning from ear to ear at the end.

If you want to get stronger, you’ll need a heavier kettlebell, and buying multiple bells can get pricey. Our favorite solution is the adjustable kettlebell, which, like the best adjustable dumbbells and the best weighted vests, is a highly versatile piece of equipment. Our editors researched and tested the most popular—and even lesser-known—adjustable kettlebells to find the six best to get for your home gym.

Our guide is competitive. Many iconic brands produce adjustable kettlebells with rave reviews and similar specs. What puts REP’s adjustable kettlebell in our Best Overall spot is that it looks, feels, and performs most like a standard kettlebell—even the handle diameter is nearly competition-grade—and the price is very fair for the equipment you’re getting.

Like nearly everything REP produces, this kettlebell sets the standard for quality. The frame is cast iron and powder-coated to improve grip. The traditional shape lets kettlebell athletes use it, so their training transfers to competition. Even the bottom of the kettlebell is covered in rubber to protect your floor—a minor detail we appreciate. Typically, you’re paying above market for this level of quality and design, but REP’s adjustable kettlebell is less expensive than other picks here.

REP offers three different weight ranges: 8-16kg (17-35lbs), 16-24kg (35-53lbs), and 10-40lbs. The kilogram kettlebells adjust in two-kilogram increments, and the pound kettlebells adjust in five-pound increments. To select your weight, turn the dial on top of the kettlebell (below the handle). Then lift the kettlebell off the weight stack, where the remaining plates will sit for the duration of your set or workout.

If you want to nitpick, other brands have said that the plastic dial feels cheap and prone to breaking. We want to highlight this detail, but our editors don’t think this is an issue unless you plan on abusing the kettlebell.

No matter which weight range you choose, you’re replacing five kettlebells. For general fitness enthusiasts, we like the 10- 40 lb option; it’s enough weight to challenge you for presses and high-rep sets of squats and rows. If you have some lifting experience and want to primarily train explosive movements like swings and snatches, as you traditionally do with kettlebells, opt for the 16-24 kg range. Unless you’re a complete beginner, we suggest those two weight ranges.

Bells of Steel created something very cool with this competition-spec adjustable kettlebell. The weight range and increments are fantastic, and the dimensions match competition specs exactly. You’ll replace 18 kettlebells for less than $300. Two reasons it’s not our overall best pick are that the adjustment process is comparatively time-consuming, and a competition-style bell isn’t for everyone.

To change the weights of the Bells of Steel kettlebell, you need a few minutes and a couple of tools. Use an Allen wrench to undo the bolt on the bottom of the kettlebell, remove the bottom half, then loosen the other screw that secures the plates with a traditional wrench. You can then add more plates in half-kilogram increments to the bolt that runs through the top half of the shell. Because the adjustment process is more time-consuming, this isn’t the best kettlebell for circuits or workouts that demand you change weights on the fly.

At first glance, you probably can’t even tell this is an adjustable kettlebell; it has a smooth cast-iron finish, no dials or switches, and a 35-millimeter handle that looks identical to standard competition kettlebells. This adjustable kettlebell is for serious kettlebell athletes. That said, if you’ve never trained with an adjustable kettlebell, be aware that the stainless steel handle can rub the hand raw (use a lot of chalk), it’ll feel more cumbersome than other picks in our guide, and the starting weight is over 24 pounds.

This is a solid choice if you’re a kettlebell athlete or want a heavier adjustable kettlebell (and you’re okay with the adjustment process).

From the company that brought adjustable dumbbells into the mainstream, BowFlex’s SelectTech 840 adjustable kettlebell is a great entry-level model for the kettlebell-curious gym-goer. It’s reasonably priced, replaces six kettlebells, and adjusts easily on the fly. The SelectTech 840 offers six different weights: Eight, 12, 20, 25, 35, and 40 pounds, enough weight to challenge you during isolation movements like curls and extensions while providing enough resistance for snatches, cleans, and rows.

If you’ve been training with kettlebells for a few years, 40 pounds will likely be too light, so you’ll want a kettlebell with a heavier top-end weight or consider buying two of this model. While it isn’t shaped exactly like a kettlebell, it feels enough like one that anyone who uses a traditional kettlebell won’t be completely thrown off. The dial on top of the kettlebell makes adjusting between weights a breeze, and the wide handle makes two-handed exercises easier.

I don’t love the plastic shell, which leaves the SelectTech 840 more prone to breaking if dropped. Also, the smooth handle makes it harder to hold onto the bell, especially after you’ve worked up a sweat. Overall, this is a basic, easy-to-use kettlebell with a moderately challenging weight range. If you’re a beginner or casual kettlebell user, you’ll enjoy BowFlex’s adjustable kettlebell.

Powerblock is best known for its rectangular adjustable dumbbells, which can hold up to 100 pounds, but the brand also makes a rugged, compact adjustable kettlebell with a decent weight range.

The 18- to 35-pound kettlebell measures 5.75″ L x 4.25″ W x 10″ H, while the 35-to-62-pound kettlebell measures 8″ L x 5.5″ W x 11.25″ H. That’s not drastically smaller than other kettlebells in our guide—in fact, Titan’s adjustable kettlebell is half an inch shorter than Powerblock’s heavier kettlebell—but its size relative to the weight range earned it the superlative of most compact.

We like a few things about this kettlebell. First, the handle is wider than most single-weight and adjustable kettlebells, which I like for two-handed movements like swings and upright rows. This kettlebell is also made from steel and feels sturdy and durable. You can drop it without worrying it will break; there aren’t any plastic parts. Lastly, the untraditional shape may throw off some kettlebell enthusiasts, but I think the sloped sides make it sit more comfortably on my wrist. Anyone who snatched or cleaned a traditional kettlebell knows the pressure that can be put on the wrist.

Unfortunately, you have to choose between a lighter or heavier kettlebell. Each model replaces just four kettlebells, less than any other pick here. With either kettlebell, you’ll get the shell plus three weights you can select with a pin. (FYI: You need the pin to choose the weights, and Powerblock doesn’t seem to sell a replacement part.) Sixty-two pounds is a substantial top-end weight for an adjustable kettlebell, and only the Titan Loadable Kettlebell Swing and Bells of Steel Competition Kettlebell offer a heavier option.

We picked Titan as the best budget option because, for this price, the equivalent of seven kettlebells is a pretty damn good deal. It looks and (mostly) feels like a traditional kettlebell, is compact, and uses cast-iron plates, which adds to the product’s durability. What we like most about Titan’s kettlebell is its price and shape. Regarding gym equipment, this is pretty affordable for almost any product. A 40-pound kettlebell from Titan Fitness is no small cost, so add six more kettlebells to your cart; it is worth it.

The shape and size are comparable to traditional kettlebells, so you shouldn’t have a hard time adjusting your technique if you switch to this model. This kettlebell starts at 10 pounds and goes up to 40 pounds, a good weight range for beginners and intermediate lifters. The weight is light enough to master movements like the snatch, clean, and jerk and to burn out the muscles during exercises like curls and overhead presses.

Unfortunately, 40 pounds isn’t enough weight for stronger individuals to get much out of movements like kettlebell swings, rows, chest presses, and deadlifts. If you want to do high-rep workouts with intensity, you can still use this bell. However, expect to outgrow this weight range at some point.

The weights on this kettlebell aren’t marked, so you need to read the plates on the inside to figure out how much you’re lifting. Ideally, Titan would paint the numbers somewhere on this kettlebell. Also, adjusting Titan’s kettlebell isn’t as easy as most other picks we've tested. You need to unlock the plates and then slide them out one at a time. But these are little nuisances in the grander scheme of what you're getting for the price.

We’ll admit that this is more of a kettlebell-adjacent tool, but we're including it because it’s affordable, you can load it up to 500 pounds, it uses weight plates, and you can use it in a few creative ways.

First, let’s be clear: Titan’s loadable handle is not a kettlebell replacement. It’s nowhere near the size of a standard kettlebell, so you can’t perform classic kettlebell movements like the snatch, clean, and jerk. As the name implies, Titan’s Loadable Kettlebell Swing is for swinging, with the main benefit being that you can load it with hundreds of pounds.

Swinging this handle will not feel like swinging a kettlebell. It’s 19 inches tall, eight inches taller than a competition kettlebell. You’ll probably feel unstable and unbalanced the first few times you swing it, since the plates are relatively far from your center of gravity. You’ll also need to assume a wider stance than you do with standard kettlebells. A competition kettlebell is 8.25 inches wide. By comparison, some metal 45-pound plates are nearly 17 inches across, and 25-pound plates are almost 12 inches across. We suggest loading 5-, 10-, and 25-pound plates onto the handle so you don’t have to widen your stance.

Even though you can’t technically replace a kettlebell with this handle, it’s still a valuable and fun addition to any home gym. Aside from heavy swings, you can perform one-arm rows, upright rows, single-arm farmer’s carries, duck walks, and elevated sumo deadlifts with this handle. We say “addition” to a home gym because this handle is an excellent buy if you own weight plates. Otherwise, you’ll need to shell out extra money for plates to load it.

If you’re looking for a pure kettlebell replacement, Titan’s Loadable Kettlebell Swing is not for you. However, with this price tag and a 500-pound weight capacity, we think serious strength athletes will love this unique tool for heavy swings, rows, elevated deadlifts, and carries.

Most adjustable kettlebells range from 10 to 40 pounds. We looked for brands that offer either a wider range of weights in one kettlebell or multiple kettlebells with different weight ranges.

For movements like swings, deadlifts, rows, and push presses, anything under 40 pounds is too light to challenge anyone who isn’t a beginner. Ten to 30 pounds is great for isolation exercises (think curls, lateral raises, and extensions), but it won’t properly challenge the explosive movements people expect to do with kettlebells.

The handle needs to be easy to grip, comfortable, and able to fit both hands for a variety of exercises. Handle size refers to both the diameter (measured in millimeters) and the width of the handle. A competition-grade kettlebell has a handle diameter of 190mm (or 7.5 inches). Unless you’re training specifically for kettlebell sport, you don’t need to worry about buying a kettlebell with those specific dimensions.

In fact, some of our testers prefer handles that are thinner in diameter (easier to grip) and longer (so you can grab it with both hands). That said, all the kettlebells in this guide are comfortable and effective, and within millimeters of competition-grade specs.

You want an adjustable kettlebell to look and function like a traditional kettlebell, so we mostly chose products that resemble single-weight kettlebells. That said, if a pick in this guide strays from the traditional shape, it’s because we still found it comfortable and/or easy to use.

You’re going to run into a handful of different changing mechanisms for the kettlebells below. The two most common are a dial and pin. For the dial, the kettlebell usually sits on top of a stack of plates. You turn the dial to the weight you want, and the mechanism automatically engages the appropriate number of weight plates. To use the pin, you’ll manually insert it into different holes in the kettlebell that correlate to a specific weight (it’s no different than using a weight stack at the gym). Both dials and pins are quick and efficient mechanisms.

Dials are often made of plastic, so they can break, but in our experience this is rare and unlikely as long as you use your kettlebell sensibly. Competition-style kettlebells may require you to ratchet open the bell with a wrench and manually add or remove metal plate weights before closing it back up. This is a pain, but the trade-off is more stability and durability, and an adjustable kettlebell that’s shaped like and performs like a traditional one. Kettlebell handles aren’t really kettlebells, but handles with an extended pole for you to load weights onto. This process shouldn’t feel too different from loading a barbell.

As a fitness writer and NASM-certified trainer, I've covered home gym equipment for years, including kettlebells. I worked with our team at Men’s Health, including a few certified trainers and former athletes, who have used dozens of adjustable kettlebells over decades in the fitness industry. The building of this guide was led by Fitness and Reviews Editor Charles Thorp, who started with the previous batch of best-performing models and then put them up against newly released options, even unreleased options that we have received early access to. We also reached out to our large network of experts, including our Advisory Board, to share their insights and any new designs they've tried.

We combined this expansive experience with targeted testing of the top contenders on the market from both upcoming and established brands. During this testing, these kettlebells were used during a wide range of workouts in a variety of environments, whether that was CrossFit WODs at our local box, kettlebell flows in the Men's Health studio gym, or HIIT workouts in our own garages.

Andrew Gutman, NASM-CPT is a journalist with a decade of experience covering fitness and nutrition. His work has been published in Men's Health, Men's Journal, Muscle & Fitness, and Gear Patrol. Outside of writing, Andrew trains in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, helps coach his gym's kickboxing team, and enjoys reading and cooking.

Charles Thorp is the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, where he shares the best product recommendations in gym equipment, recovery tools, supplements, and more. Following an early life in athletics, Charles became a NASM-certified trainer and began writing programs alongside the most respected coaches in the world.   Since entering the world of fitness content, Charles has had the opportunity to learn from and train alongside high performance individuals from the NFL, UFC, NBA, Formula 1, CrossFit, US Olympics, and Navy SEALs. When he’s not writing about training programs or gear, he can be seen at the gym or in the wild, putting them to the test.

#4736. Kia’s EV5 spotted with an updated design and a huge new infotainment display

Kia’s Sportage-sized electric SUV, the EV5, was spotted with a distinct new style and an overhauled interior, including a huge widescreen infotainment screen.

The EV5 is the fully electric SUV we want, but can’t have in the US. After launching it in China in 2023, Kia introduced the global version last year, which is now on sale in Europe, Canada, the UK, and other markets.

It has already been a big part of Kia’s comeback in China and is expected to become one of its best-selling EVs.

Kia appears to be preparing an updated version. A new EV5 model was recently spotted by ShortsCar in a South Korean parking garage without camouflage, and it’s expected to be the updated version.

You can see in the video that the design has changed quite a bit. Up front, the hood and headlights remain about the same, but new design elements like a black accent light are added.

It also features a unique bumper design, similar to that of the rugged EV5 WKNDR Concept Kia revealed last November at the Guangzhou Motor Show.

The biggest changes are inside, where the interior appears to be completely overhauled. Instead of the current large display screen spanning from the driver to the center, the new EV5 features a display that extends from the center to the passenger side.

There also appears to be an added slim display in front of the steering wheel. Since Hyundai has recently added a slim display to vehicles equipped with its Pleos infotainment system, the updated Kia EV5 is expected to feature the new setup.

However, this is still speculation and has not been confirmed. The center console has also changed. Instead of the physical buttons, it now has a cover, giving it a cleaner overall look.

According to a sticker on the back, the updated EV5 is set to launch in the Philippines. Given Kia initially launched the EV5 in China in 2023, it will be due for a facelift around 2027.

Kia has yet to confirm whether and when it will launch the updated EV5 in other global markets, such as Europe or Korea. It will likely arrive after the China-made version, like the current EV5. We should learn more details soon.

#4735. Has the Most Wonderful Moment of Your Life Already Happened?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

In a recent newsletter, Jack Maden, the founder and writer of Philosophy Break, was asked about ideas that changed how he sees the world. He cited the Vietnamese Buddhist philosopher Thich Nhat Hanh, who posed the question that is in the title: Has the most wonderful moment of your life already happened?

For Hanh, this is not about looking back on our lives through a new lens that highlights what we may not have appreciated then. No, for Hanh, the most wonderful moment of our lives may already have happened, because for him, every moment has the capacity baked into it to be that wonderful moment, but it eludes us because we’re too preoccupied to notice it. What most of us do is put our hope in the future: the “when we’s—graduate, get married, have a child—or the “only if’s—make a million dollars, get that promotion—etc. By not being mindful in the present and instead dwelling mentally on the past or future, both the opportunity and the awareness of the wonderfulness of now slip right by.

The psychology of mindfulness is, of course, well known, thanks not only to Buddhism but also to writers like Eckhart Tolle and his book The Power of Now. While Tolle does a good job, in my mind, of helping us realize that the now is all we have, all we can live in, I agree with Maden that Hanh’s question offers a different, positive, and challenging spin: that wonderfulness is always available to us, ready to be found if only we learn to pay attention to it.

Easier said than done, of course. Here, meditation and breathing exercises come to the fore as ways to build that attention muscle. This is where, 20 years ago, Carlson and Bailey, in their book Slowing Down to the Speed of Life, advocated doing things at half speed to help us take in the moment better. Something relatively easy to do and a good starting point. But learning to notice and see the wonderfulness of the now through our senses and a clarified mind is different, I believe, from proactively, more robustly creating it. Are we capable of doing that?

Yes, we can. Modern philosophers such as Hume, Nietzsche, and Kierkegaard, as well as ancients like Epicurus, advocated not dismissing logic but setting it aside, putting passion and desire on the front burner, and using them as a divining rod to guide our lives. But we can also combine them with mindfulness and the power of now: If we make present decisions based on our preferences, excitement, and passions, and support them with reason rather than impulse, we have a winning combination. We keep our ear close to ourselves, identify what we need, and act to create it, which in turn translates not only into a wonderful moment but ultimately into a wonderful life.

So, are you ready to slow down, let the present seep more fully into your life, and pay attention? And maybe, taking a step further, actively practice making these moments the best they can be?

Maden, J. (2026). Two ideas that changed my world. Philosophy Break, October, 2026. https://philosophybreak.com.

Carlson, R. & Bailey, J. (1998). Slowing down to the speed of life. San Francisco: Harper.

Tolle, E. (2004). The power of now. New York: New World Library.

#4734. Cancer Taught Dolph Lundgren He’s Not Invincible. Now He’s Finding New Strength.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

After three years with no evidence of disease, the action legend is training smarter—and living differently.

DOLPH LUNDGREN HAS had one hell of a life. From being plucked from obscurity into a modeling career after studying chemical engineering at MIT, to dating Grace Jones, to becoming one of the iconic bad guys of the 1980s, what hasn’t he done? Just one of those things would be a highlight in anybody’s life. But Dolph Lundgren isn’t just anybody.

Seemingly cut from stone and delivered to America ready-made to star in films, his path upon arrival from Sweden wasn’t always easy. In the new documentary, Dolph: Unbreakable, Lundgren gets candid about a childhood of abuse and the struggle to put that behind him. He also discusses the films he felt didn’t meet his standards after he was established as a household name thanks to roles in Rocky IV, Universal Soldier, and Masters of the Universe. While there are certainly gems to be discovered in that direct-to-video period, it's fascinating to watch the man many know as Ivan Drago, a brute with few words, open up about his life and career. Perhaps the film’s biggest revelation is that of Lundgren’s fight with cancer, a diagnosis that, at one point, gave him just a few months to live.

That fight scaffolds Dolph: Unbreakable, and it’s moving to watch a man so seemingly superhuman allow himself to be so vulnerable. Now, on the other side of that battle and going strong, Lundgren is out in the world touring with his new memoir, Fights Worth Fighting: Finding Strength in Struggle, alongside the doc. Taking a moment from his busy schedule, the 69-year-old legend sat down with Men’s Health to discuss his new fitness app, Brandon Lee and learning from Sylvester Stallone.

MEN’S HEALTH: How’s your health these days?

DOLPH LUNDGREN: It's good, man. It's good. I've been NED—no evidence of disease—for three years now. I'm doing a scan every couple of months. I mean, I still work out. I work out a lot now, actually, like I used to. I’m feeling great. I'm working on a fitness app—My friend Arnold has one. I'm going to do a much smaller personal one about exactly how I work out; It's more confined to what I do.

But physically, I feel good. Psychologically, once you have the cancer diagnosis, you're always wondering what's going to come in the future, but it keeps you honest on some level. It keeps me honest about enjoying the moments.

MH: Even in the scariest moments of your diagnosis in the documentary, you always looked like you were in great shape. How has your approach to fitness evolved as you’ve gotten older?

DL: It's gotten a little more focused. As you get older, you have more responsibilities and you have less time, especially these days with all the digital noise in the world. I think I’ve also gotten a little smarter. The cancer journey made me realize I'm not invincible, and even though I want to do crazy stuff like I used to and spar with 25-year-olds and run up the mountain, I can’t do that anymore.

I said, "No, I'm going to cut back on the crazy stuff." And I've devised this workout schedule that's based on 30- to 40-minute workouts a couple times a week, and I've distilled it down to what I think really works, what doesn't get you injured, and what you have access to. Most people have access to a gym. So, most of it is strength training. There's some cardio involved, plus a little movement and mobility from martial arts. I've come up with a pretty clever and pretty efficient program.

MH: I love how candid you get in the film, especially about your own work. You’re hard on some of your direct-to-video work, but those projects still have a lot of fans. Is there anything you think went under the radar?

DL: Look, what I would say is I'm proud of my own work, but I may not be totally ecstatic about how the films turned out sometimes. I wasn't the director. Some of the movies, however, like Command Performance, I'm very proud of. That's a movie I directed. I think what I said in the doc was that the focus wasn’t necessarily to make a good movie. It was just to make quick money. I definitely feel good about the movies I directed. I feel good about Command Performance and Wanted Man. Movies like I Come in Peace—I know a lot of people like that one. Unfortunately, we couldn’t include that one in the documentary. There’s only so much space. [Laughs] They're all testaments of their time. They may not be prominent, but they've clearly played a part in my life and my development as a person and as an actor.

MH: Showdown in Little Tokyo is an all-time favorite of mine. I love your dynamic in it with Brandon Lee. What are your memories of him?

DL: My main memory of him is that he was a great guy. We really got along very well, both off-screen and on-screen. Obviously, I was a fan of his dad's, Bruce. I think his mom, Linda Lee, was half Swedish. I think her grandmother was from Sweden. He had been to Sweden, and had a quarter of Scandinavian descent. That's why he was tall, and had those good looks—that mix between her and Bruce.

He spoke some Swedish, and we bonded over that. Then, of course, the martial arts: he did the same style as his dad, and I was doing Kyokushin karate, a different style. We had such a great time together. I was very, very upset when I got that call a couple years later that he'd gotten killed in some freak accident. He would've certainly been a huge star.

MH: You were speaking earlier about your development as an actor. You’ve always been a compelling screen presence, but you’ve become better and better as you’ve gotten older. You give incredible performances in movies like Creed II and Universal Soldier: Day of Reckoning. What’s it been like to stretch yourself?

DL: It's been great. I remember an interview with Russell Crowe where he was asked, "How do you create a great character?" And he says, "Work with a great director." It's hard to display great acting if you're not working with a great director, because he's the artist. That's why Marlon Brando made bad movies once in a while. He was usually interesting, but maybe the movie was forgettable.

As a martial artist, as an engineer, I was used to being trained from the ground up properly for years. Martial arts took seven years to get a black belt. I started acting when I was 23, and I was thrown into a big movie very quickly. The movie was a hit, and suddenly I'm in Hollywood. I'm now starring in my own movies, but I didn't have much experience. I had to learn on the job, and it wasn't easy. But think about Stallone, for instance. He’d done some great acting, but before that, he was a writer. He wanted to be a star early on. I hadn't even thought of it before Rocky IV. It took me years after that to acquire more confidence and skill.

With recent films, especially Creed II and Aquaman, I had a chance to work with better directors and actors, and play more interesting characters. I still do action stuff and action comedies where it's not as focused, but I do like to apply myself. Now, I'm interested in applying myself, post-cancer, to dramatic roles to see what happens, because I haven't done it yet. It's going to be interesting. I'm doing some of those kinds of movies this year and next year.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#4733. Ford’s electric pickup is suddenly selling like hotcakes at 50% off used

Once America’s most popular electric pickup, the Ford F-150 Lightning is finding a second life on the used market.

The F-150 Lightning is hard to pass up at 50% to 60% off sticker price, even used. With new models no longer available, Ford’s electric pickup is suddenly selling like hotcakes on the used market.

After the last model rolled off the assembly line last December, CEO Jim Farley said the decision to end production came as the “very high-end EVs, the $50K, 70K, $80,000 vehicles, they just weren’t selling.”

At 50% to 60% off, it now looks like a bargain in the used market. “When Ford was selling it brand new, the math was complicated,” Jimmy Douglas, CEO of Plug, a wholesale EV dealer, recently told Bloomberg.

On the used market, however, “the Lightning is 50% to 60% of the sticker price and that is really a sweet spot,” he added.

Used Ford F-150 Lightnings are selling in about 20 days, less than half the 44-day average for used vehicles in the US. According to Edmunds.com, prices are now up 4% to about $50,000 since the start of the year.

Douglass said that close to one-third of used models are sold by rival dealerships that would normally flip them back to Ford. However, many are opting to sell them directly because of demand.

Chase Norris from Colorado called the electric pickup a bargain. He purchased a used Lightning for around $40,000 and considers it a major upgrade from his previous gas F-150.

EV Group CEO and cofounder Alex Lawrence, which sells pre-owned electric vehicles, said he can’t get his hands on any reasonably priced used F-150 Lightnings currently.

He said many Lightning buyers use it as a second truck to save money during their weekly commute.

It looks essentially the same as the gas-powered F-150, offers instant torque, and produces zero tailpipe emissions, but the electric pickup failed to meet Ford’s expectations because of its higher price.

The base F-150 Lightning Pro debuted in 2021 with a starting MSRP of $39,974, but that was quickly raised to around $60,000 a year or so later.

According to Edmunds.com, the average transaction price for the F-150 Lightning in its first year of sales was $79,000 because Ford focused on higher-priced trims. The gas version’s ATP was about $19,000 less.

Even with the higher sticker price, Ford was losing a considerable amount on each Lightning it produced. In Q1 2024, Ford lost more than $100,000 on every EV it built.

Next year, Ford will take another crack at the electric pickup market with the Fathom, the first vehicle based on its “groundbreaking” new Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform.

Ford said the Fathom will start at $28,350 for the standard-range version. Even with the $1,595 delivery fee included, the electric pickup will start at under $30,000.

As the first vehicle built on its UEV platform, Ford promises the Fathom will be a step-change from its first-generation EVs.

According to Ford, the electric pickup will offer more interior space than a Toyota RAV4 and will be the first vehicle with Apple Maps directly integrated into the navigation system.

We also know the electric pickup will have a NACS port after a few prototypes were spotted charging at a Tesla Supercharger this summer.

Ford reportedly aims to sell around 100,000 Fathoms in its first year. CEO Jim Farley said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week that the launch remains on track for Q4 2027.

Farley called the Fathom a “breakthrough product” and said that the MSRP under $30,000 is perfect for today’s market.

At least some F-150 owners are already trading in for lower-priced options. A member of the Ford F-150 Lightning Owners Group, JF, said that although it was a great ride, “Carvana gave us just a little less than we paid new,” adding, “R2, here we come!”

When Torque News reached out, JF said he “really liked the Lightning,” but wanted something smaller. “With the current increase in resale value, the time to trade seemed right,” JF added.

The Rivian R2 (see our review) Performance with the Launch Package is now available to order starting at $57,990 with an EPA-estimated range of up to 330 miles and 656 hp. The R2 Premium will go on sale later this year, starting at $53,990

In Spring 2027, Rivian will launch the R2 Standard, starting at $44,990 with an estimated range of up to 275 miles and 350 hp.

So were they losing $100k / truck, or the average loss when all development was included ended up being $100k? Big difference. I don't believe the cost to build each one was $170k+. That makes no sense. They just priced them too high to amortize the development costs over enough vehicles to make them profitable. Every vehicle has to sell a minimum # before they start to make a profit.

Surging F-150 Lightning sales on the used market show buyers want electric pickups. But at the right price.

At $60,000 to $70,000, the Lightning wasn’t so attractive, but at $40,000 used, it suddenly is. Perhaps Ford is on to something with its next-gen EV pickup, the Fathom, set to go on sale starting at under $30,000.

Will it deliver on its promise? Ford has yet to reveal battery specs, towing capacity, range, or any other specs. We should learn more soon.

#4732. E-quipment highlight: Jungheinrich launches new forklift for Asian markets

Like many equipment brands, German forklift maker Jungheinrich has been struggling to crack the Asian industrial markets – but the company is set to change all that with the launch of a new line of 1.6- to 3-ton class electric forklifts designed specifically to navigate the region’s tight warehouses and factories.

Jungheinrich launched the next generation of its EFG MB and MC electric counterbalance forklifts, giving businesses more flexibility to match truck performance with the battery options, charging systems, and operator features that meet their specific needs.

“Different operations have different requirements,” said Lisa Jing Xue, Managing Director at Jungheinrich’s Qingpu Plant, China. “With the EFG M series, customers can configure the (forklift) truck around their application, workload and operators – whether they need greater maneuverability for confined warehouse spaces, or a stable, powerful truck for demanding transport and stacking work.”

Forklift buyers can choose between two performance packages, prioritizing energy efficiency for everyday material handling or more driving and lifting muscle for more demanding, high-throughput operations. The higher-performance package comes standard on models rated for 2.5-3.0 tons, with a choice of either lead-acid or lithium-ion batteries with 346 or 690 Ah of capacity available to suit different workloads and shift patterns. Both ship with regenerative braking tech that can recover up to 30% of the energy used in stopping and lowering loads, too, helping to keep these machines running longer between charging sessions.

“We carried out extensive customer research to understand what the market needs,” added Jing Xue. “Customers can invest in the performance required today and add further capabilities as their application demands.”

Optional features include fingertip controls, a larger 4″ digital display, upgraded LED lighting, and operator-assistance (ADAS) systems, while flexible seating and cabin configurations are designed to keep drivers comfortable through long shifts. A slim B-pillar and glass roof help visibility in busy warehouses, while the four-wheel EFG MC gets automatic cornering speed reduction as standard. Integrated telematics are also standard, giving fleet managers access to utilization data, maintenance planning and pre-operational checks from day one.

Jungheinrich says the order books for both the three- and four-wheel electric forklifts are open now, ready to be supported by the company’s 6,000+ person strong service network across the Asia-Pacific region.

#4731. Christina Applegate ‘Not Happy at All’ After Learning She Was Misdiagnosed With MS

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health update on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.

Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.

In two podcast episodes released October 20, Applegate revealed that doctors had told her she was misdiagnosed with MS.

“She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS,’ ” Applegate said as she fought back tears. “I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.”

The “Anchorman” and “Dead to Me” actor explained that her symptoms have continued to worsen, leaving her without an explanation for what she’s experiencing as doctors investigate the cause.

Being misdiagnosed with MS is relatively common. Applegate’s revelation highlights a difficult reality for people living with unexplained symptoms resembling MS. Her experience raises questions about how MS is diagnosed, why misdiagnoses may occur, and what people can do when their symptoms don’t match their diagnosis.

While MS can be difficult to diagnose, an accurate diagnosis can help people with the condition gain access to appropriate treatment. A misdiagnosis, on the other hand, may lead to unnecessary interventions and medication, and take an emotional toll over time.

“MS can be challenging to diagnose because there is no single test that confirms it in every case,” said Steve Allder, MD, consultant neurologist at Re:Cognition Health.

“An incorrect diagnosis can have significant consequences. Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may experience considerable anxiety, undergo unnecessary investigations, or receive treatments with potential risks and side effects. Equally, if MS is missed, treatment may be delayed, potentially allowing further neurological damage,” Allder told Healthline.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis underscores that MS misdiagnoses remain a concern.

Research suggests that around 15% of people diagnosed with MS may actually have another condition.

However, estimates vary across studies, with some reporting rates ranging from 5–41%.

While an accurate diagnosis can guide patients toward appropriate treatment, a mistaken one may lead to unnecessary medication, emotional distress, and years of uncertainty.

New diagnostic guidelines offer hope for greater accuracy, but they also raise important questions about how doctors can adequately distinguish MS from other conditions.

“Research has shown that MS can be both overdiagnosed and underdiagnosed,” Allder said.

“Diagnosis relies on a combination of symptoms, neurological examination, MRI findings, and sometimes, additional tests. It is also important to recognize that diagnoses can evolve as new evidence emerges. As neurologists, we must remain open to revisiting a diagnosis when symptoms or test results do not fit, ensuring patients receive appropriate treatment and support.”

MS symptoms may vary widely and overlap with several other conditions. These may include:

Because these conditions share certain features with MS, healthcare professionals should consider a patient’s full clinical profile rather than relying on a single symptom or scan.

“MS can cause numbness, tingling, muscle weakness, visual disturbances, balance problems, and fatigue. However, these symptoms are not unique to the condition,” Allder said.

“For example, numbness and tingling may indicate peripheral neuropathy, sometimes associated with diabetes or vitamin B12 deficiency. Weakness or altered sensation may result from a trapped nerve or spinal cord compression. Migraines can cause visual disturbances and sensory symptoms, while inner-ear disorders may affect balance,” he continued.

Allder noted that fatigue is particularly nonspecific and may be associated with:

He explained that, as a neurologist, he considers the pattern, duration, and progression of symptoms alongside examination findings.

“No single symptom automatically indicates MS. A thorough assessment is essential to identify the underlying cause and ensure the patient receives appropriate treatment,” he said.

There is no single test that definitively confirms every case of MS.

Diagnosis typically involves reviewing symptoms, conducting neurological examinations, and evaluating MRI scans and laboratory results.

MRI findings may be tricky to interpret. Some white-matter spots resemble MS lesions but may result from migraine, aging, or other conditions. Misapplying diagnostic criteria or overlooking alternative explanations can also lead to mistakes.

“MRI abnormalities alone do not confirm MS,” Allder said. “The diagnosis must be based on the overall clinical picture, with alternative explanations carefully considered.”

Research also suggests that MS misdiagnosis rates may differ by sex.

Research shows females are 2.1 times more likely to be misdiagnosed with MS than males, highlighting the potential for diagnostic bias and differences in how symptoms are evaluated.

The updated MS diagnostic criteria published in 2025 offer a framework for improving diagnosis.

The updated guidelines introduce several important changes.

For instance, the optic nerve (the nerve connecting the eye to the brain) is now included as a fifth anatomical location for assessing evidence of MS.

The revised criteria also include new MRI biomarkers, such as the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions. These features can help doctors distinguish MS-related abnormalities from other conditions.

These changes may help doctors diagnose MS earlier and more accurately.

If you experience persistent or recurring neurological symptoms, seek medical advice. Your doctor can assess your symptoms and, if applicable, refer you to a neurologist.

Sudden weakness, vision loss, or difficulty speaking requires urgent medical assessment, Allder said.

“Depending on the findings, investigations may include MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord, blood tests, and, in some cases, a lumbar puncture,” Allder noted.

“It is important that results are interpreted alongside symptoms and examination findings, as no single test should determine the diagnosis in isolation.”

Allder said that if you’re unsure about a diagnosis, you can ask your neurologist what evidence supports it and whether alternative health conditions have been considered.

“A second opinion or follow-up assessment may be appropriate. The priority is an accurate diagnosis that leads to the right treatment and support,” Allder said.

#4730. I’ll Be 72 When My Youngest Kid Graduates High School. I Wouldn’t Have it Any Other Way.

“I have found a way to get to do the thing I love most for as long as I possibly can,” says comedian Andy Richter.

I DON’T CONSIDER myself to be very “Hollywood,” but in terms of fatherhood, I’m practically a cliché.

It’s because I had my kids in waves. There’s my son Will, 26, and daughter Mercy, 21, from my first marriage, and my daughter Cornelia, 6, from my second and present marriage.

There are a lot of us old-dads-of-young-kids out here, and the main reason is that there are so many Los Angeles men who, after they get that first marriage out of the way, employ a sort of Benjamin Button philosophy towards the subsequent ones in that as time marches forward and the end of life moves closer, the wives get younger and younger.

I don’t lump myself in with those geezers, though, because I am 60 and my wife is 50, and the narrowness of that merely ten-year gap affords me the moral superiority of a guy married to someone with whom he can have actual conversations.

But the fact remains that I was 54 when my youngest was born. And yes, I have done all the math. I’ll be 72 when she graduates high school, 76 when she graduates college, and god knows what kind of drooling diapered mess I’ll be when I’m giving the toast at her wedding, champagne flute in one hand, the other one white-knuckling my walker.

But it is what it is. I fell in love with a single mother who, after many years of a successful career, wanted a child and hadn’t found a suitable partner to raise one with. A relationship with Jen was always going to be a package deal, and it’s the best one I’ve ever been lucky enough to gladly tumble head over heels into.

When I started letting people know that we were engaged and that I was going to adopt the then-two-year-old Cornelia (I was calling it “getting back into the toddler business”), people had one of two reactions.

The first was along the lines of Why the fuck would you do that? For so many people, and especially parents, the idea of going back to raising a pre-pre-schooler was incomprehensible. To them it was like driving through a hurricane and then making a U-ey to take one more crack at it for fun.

The other reaction was that I was some kind of saint. That to so selflessly dive back into the stress of making a person out of what is basically a little wild animal that can delete seven phone apps in less than one minute made me some sort of super dad, the menschiest of mensches.

This take was, while flattering, a little embarrassing, because years ago I figured out that all you have to do be hoisted on metaphorical shoulders and pronounced a Good Dad is about 30 percent of the work that it takes to be a Good Mom.

I also felt a little sheepish about the idea that signing up to help raise a two year old was somehow heroic because I knew that this little girl was giving me a gift: approximately 16 years of not having to figure out was I was going to do with myself.

“What should I do now?” has been a question that has plagued me for my entire life in both the micro and the macro. It’s why I smoked for almost 20 years. When you’re raising a child, you don’t have to come up with something to do—you’ve got that kid to take care of. You want a purpose? How about making a decent human?

When you are raising a child, it’s always good work. You are never wasting your time on an unworthy project. (A quick stroll through my IMDB page will show that I have done that more than a few times.)

So when a group of kindergarten girls asks me, “Are you Cornelia’s grandpa?” I just let it roll off my back, because they don’t know about the scam I’m running. I have found a way to get to do the thing I love most for as long as I possibly can.

And there’s a good chance that by the time she’s ready to head out on her own, her older brother and sister might start having children, which means I will possibly get to have a life filled with babies and little kids for a long, long time. And that is a huge win for me.

I once heard Bob Odenkirk say on a podcast, “When you’re raising little kids, you know what your job is.” I know exactly what he means, and I love my job.

Andy Richter, author of Elf Unwrapped, is a Los Angeles–based comedian, actor, writer, and host best known as Conan O’Brien’s longtime sidekick, who also hosts the Three Questions podcast and The Andy Richter Call-In Show and had a longer-than-expected run on Dancing with the Stars.

#4729. They Believe You. So Why Don't They Trust You?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

From our personal relationships to our professional lives, trust impacts how we view others and experience the world around us. Addiction can make trust particularly difficult; it may leave loved ones questioning whether they can rely on someone's word. However, being trusted is often confused with the simpler idea of being believed.

To explore this further, I spoke with Amber Hollingsworth, a licensed addiction counselor and certified provider at Soberlink with more than 20 years of experience. She provides insight on how honesty, consistency, and accountability help rebuild trust, particularly in relationships affected by addiction.

Someone may believe what you tell them in a particular moment but still question whether they can rely on you over time. For example, a spouse may believe their partner is committed to recovery but still struggle to trust that things will be different this time. Past experiences can make it difficult to feel secure, even when their partner is making progress during their recovery.

Trust can be looked at as what you feel comfortable counting on others to do. Belief is a cognitive process; when someone believes you, they may accept that a specific fact or story you have shared is true, often based on evidence or a well-supported explanation. Trust, on the other hand, is an emotional process because it involves making yourself vulnerable to another person based on your confidence in their character.

A 2025 study found that consistently demonstrating trustworthy behavior was the strongest factor in whether people learned to trust others. According to Hollingsworth, “Apologies can change minds for a moment, but consistency can actually change nervous systems."

When trust becomes damaged, it can ultimately impact how people interact with each other. For instance, a spouse may begin to pay closer attention to behaviors and look for signs of alcohol use to confirm their suspicions. This can take a significant emotional toll as time goes on.

In this situation, accountability can be extremely useful. You need to build trust in many cases during the recovery process from addiction. This can be done by showing consistency, clear communication, and providing measurable evidence where appropriate. Amber expresses that, "Trust doesn’t happen just because you promise harder. It happens when you remove uncertainty.”

Rebuilding trust takes time, and is different for everyone. Entering recovery is an important step, but loved ones may need to see consistent changes before they feel comfortable relying on someone again.

A 2025 review examined the use of remote monitoring technologies, including smartphones, breathalyzers, and wearable devices, in alcohol use disorder treatment. These tools can help track alcohol use and inform treatment, but they cannot address the relational harm caused by dishonesty or broken promises. Rebuilding trust still requires honesty, open communication, and consistent behavior.

Hollingsworth emphasizes this importance and indicates: “Openness is so important in building trust, because it shows others that we aren’t trying to hide anything. Even if you’ve been struggling, being open about your successes and setbacks can help build trust with your loved ones. Being transparent shows your intent, and that can be just as important as your actions themselves. You earn belief with a story, but you earn trust with a system. Radical honesty, non-defensive listening, and verifiable accountability turn maybes into I knows.” Ultimately, rebuilding trust is about giving people reasons to feel confident in you again, whether in recovery, marriage, friendship, or the workplace.

Rebuilding trust is not one conversation or one apology. It takes consistent effort from both people. Here are some practical action steps:

Trust cannot be fixed in a day. Words can start the process, but it is the actions people take each day that help bring it back. I ask you to consider if your actions line up with your words and what you can change to prove to the people around you that they can rely on you.

Duncan, C., Sganzerla, L., Kaltwasser, L., & Dziobek, I. (2026). Trust learning in the repeated trust game: A meta‐analytic study. British Journal of Psychology, 117(3), 1026-1055.’

#4728. Janus Electric secures battery supply deal for its battery-swap semi truck

Australian conversion specialists Janus Electric have been celebrating a growing slate of orders for their Class 8 electric truck conversions, which ditch diesel in favor of advanced battery-swap electric power – but exactly how they’d deliver all those trucks was still a question. Now, we have an answer: Electrovaya will supply the batteries.

The concept of dropping an electric power unit into a Class 8 semi makes perfect sense, as most of these trucks are built as gliders. That is, rolling body and chassis without an engine and transmission that’s ready to receive power from Cummins, Detroit, International, or Volvo Penta. That’s the role that Janus Electric sees itself occupying, and it seems to be working.

Janus’ reservation book crept past 70 units this past summer, helped along in part by California’s HVIP Program and the US EPA’s Diesel Emission Reduction Act (DERA) Grants. When the HVIP voucher is combined with the Port of Los Angeles’ “Plus” support, customers can received up to $166,000 per truck conversion. Factor in the massive fuel savings of electric and the classic good looks of square-nose Western Star truck body, and it’s easy to see why they’d be a popular choice.

As Jerry Seinfeld taught us however, it’s one thing to take a reservation – it’s another thing to deliver. To help make it happen, Janus has inked a battery supply deal with Electrovaya that will see a $26 million initial purchase orders for Electrovaya battery packs to demand for Janus’ products in the US and Canada, along with the battery company purchasing approximately $1.4 million in Janus stock with (what seems to be) actual money.

“Electrovaya is an important partner to Janus Electric, and we’re particularly pleased it has decided to invest directly in our business,” explains Ben Hutt, Managing Director and CEO of Janus Electric. “The investment is a strong vote of confidence in our technology and approach to electrifying heavy transport.”

The Janus Electric-repowered trucks carry a stout, 480 hp electric motor drawing power from a standard 310 kWh battery pack, with up to two battery packs (one on each side) of the truck. In practice, that gives the Janus trucks up to 370 miles of loaded range. After that, the batteries can be DC fast charged in under 90 minutes, or swapped for fresh ones in about four minutes without too much in the way of specialized equipment. That’s not just Janus’ killer app, it means that a battery supply deal like this one with a strategic partner who’s invested in the fledgling company’s success is such a huge deal.

“Reliable battery supply is critical to our growth,” adds Hutt, “and Electrovaya’s expanding North American manufacturing capabilities will be important as we scale. Both companies see considerable opportunity in this market, and we look forward to building on our partnership.”

For their part, Electrovoya executives seem to know their role here, and seem excited to be a part of what Janus is doing. “Class 8 trucking is one of the most exciting and demanding frontiers in electrification, and Janus has demonstrated real commercial traction with fleets in the US, Canada and Australia,” said Dr. Raj Das Gupta, CEO of Electrovaya. “Janus has developed a practical solution to one of the major challenges facing heavy transport, enabling diesel-powered trucks to be converted to electric without compromising their commercial operations.”

Electrovaya will be expanding its American manufacturing capacity with lithium-ion cell, module, and battery pack production at its new, potentially BABA-compliant facility in Jamestown, New York, which is expected to come online in 2027.
